translations.an10.13:1: "There are, monks, these ten fetters. Which ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. Which are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, sensual desire, ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: "Monks, as far as there are beings—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form, formless, percipient, non-percipient, neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them. So too, monks, all wholesome qualities are rooted in heedfulness, converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:2: "Monks, just as the footprints of all animals that walk fit into the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared the foremost among them due to its great size; so too, monks, all wholesome qualities are rooted in heedfulness, converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:3: "Monks, just as all the rafters of a peaked house lean to the peak, slope towards the peak, converge upon the peak, and the peak is declared the foremost among them; so too, monks, all wholesome qualities are rooted in heedfulness, converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:7: "Monks, just as all petty kings are followers of a wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch is declared the foremost among them; so too, monks, ...
translations.an10.15:8: "Monks, just as the radiance of all the stars does not amount to a sixteenth part of the radiance of the moon, and the moon's radiance is declared the foremost among them; so too, monks, ...
translations.an10.15:9: "Monks, just as in the autumn, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, rising in the sky, dispels all darkness from space and shines, beams, and radiates; so too, monks, ...
translations.an10.17:1: "Dwell with a refuge, monks, do not dwell without a refuge. Monks, it is suffering to dwell without a refuge. There are, monks, these ten things that provide a refuge. Which ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. And this, monks, is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.17:2: "Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned, a bearer of the teachings, an accumulator of the teachings. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings are many learned by him, borne in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. And this, monks, is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.17:3: "Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades. And this, monks, is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:10: "Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. 'This monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago'—the senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth alone is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:11: "Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, possessing wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. 'This monk is wise, possessing wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering'—the senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is compassionate towards the seniors ... not decline. This too is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:2: "Dwell with a refuge, monks, do not dwell without a refuge. Monks, it is suffering to dwell without a refuge. There are, monks, these ten things that provide a refuge. Which ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous ... he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. 'This monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains himself by undertaking the training rules'—the senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth alone is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:4: "Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades. 'This monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades'—the senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth alone is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:5: "Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to admonish, possessing qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and respectfully accepting instruction. 'This monk is easy to admonish, possessing qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and respectfully accepting instruction'—the senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth alone is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a thing that provides a refuge.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, a monk is skilled and diligent in the various duties of his fellow practitioners, possessing the means to examine them, capable of doing and arranging them. 'This monk is skilled and diligent in the various duties of his fellow practitioners, possessing the means to examine them, capable of doing and arranging them.' The senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for protection.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, a monk loves the Dhamma, delights in conversation about it, rejoices greatly in the higher Dhamma and discipline. 'This monk loves the Dhamma, delights in conversation about it, rejoices greatly in the higher Dhamma and discipline.' The senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for protection.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, a monk lives with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and acquiring wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility for wholesome qualities. 'This monk lives with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and acquiring wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility for wholesome qualities.' The senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for protection.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines for curing the sick. 'This monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines for curing the sick.' The senior monks think he should be advised and instructed, the middle monks ... the junior monks think he should be advised and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the seniors, the middling, and the juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for protection.
translations.an10.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks ...
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, does a monk have tranquil bodily formations? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. That is how, monks, a monk has tranquil bodily formations.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk well liberated in mind? Here, monks, a monk's mind is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion. That is how, monks, a monk is well liberated in mind.
translations.an10.20:2: "Monks, there are these ten noble abodes in which the noble ones of the past, present, or future dwell. What ten? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has eliminated idiosyncratic truths, has completely given up searching, has unsullied intentions, has tranquil bodily formations, is well liberated in mind, and well liberated by wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, does a monk have abandoned five factors? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. That is how, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, does a monk possess six factors? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear ... Having smelled an odor with the nose ... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue ... Having felt a tactile object with the body ... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. That is how, monks, a monk possesses six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, does a monk have a single guard? Here, monks, a monk possesses a mind guarded by mindfulness. That is how, monks, a monk has a single guard.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, does a monk have four supports? Here, monks, a monk reflects before using something, reflects before enduring something, reflects before avoiding something, reflects before removing something. That is how, monks, a monk has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, does a monk have eliminated idiosyncratic truths? Here, monks, whatever various idiosyncratic truths of various ascetics and brahmins there are—such as 'the world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal'; 'the world is finite' or 'the world is infinite'; 'the soul and the body are the same' or 'the soul and the body are different'; 'the Tathāgata exists after death' or 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death' or 'the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' or 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—all these have been eliminated, removed, given up, relinquished, let go, abandoned, forsaken. That is how, monks, a monk has eliminated idiosyncratic truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, does a monk have completely given up searching? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures, abandoned the search for existence, and quieted the search for the holy life. That is how, monks, a monk has completely given up searching.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, does a monk have unsullied intentions? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned intentions of sensuality, intentions of ill will, and intentions of cruelty. That is how, monks, a monk has unsullied intentions.
translations.an10.24:1: On one occasion the Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: "Friends, monks." "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Mahācunda. The Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Just as, friend, a person who is wealthy might speak of being wealthy, who is rich might speak of being rich, who is affluent might speak of being affluent. When some need for money arises, he would be able to bring forth wealth, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know of him thus: 'This venerable one, being wealthy, speaks of being wealthy; being rich, speaks of being rich; being affluent, speaks of being affluent. For what reason? Because this venerable one, when some need for money arises, is able to bring forth wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:2: "A monk, friend, speaking of knowledge, saying: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma.' If, friend, that monk is overcome and remains under the influence of greed, hatred ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, when one understands thus, greed does not arise; thus this venerable one is overcome and remains under the influence of greed. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, when one understands thus, hatred does not arise ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire does not arise; thus this venerable one is overcome and remains under the influence of wicked desire.'
translations.an10.24:3: A monk, friend, speaking of development, saying: 'I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.' If, friend, that monk is overcome and remains under the influence of greed, hatred ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, when one understands thus, greed does not arise; thus this venerable one is overcome and remains under the influence of greed. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, when one understands thus, hatred does not arise ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire does not arise; thus this venerable one is overcome and remains under the influence of wicked desire.'
translations.an10.24:5: Just as, friend, a person who is poor might speak of being wealthy, who is without wealth might speak of being rich, who is without affluence might speak of being affluent. When some need for money arises, he would not be able to bring forth wealth, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know of him thus: 'This venerable one, being poor, speaks of being wealthy; being without wealth, speaks of being rich; being without affluence, speaks of being affluent. For what reason? Because this venerable one, when some need for money arises, is not able to bring forth wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:9: A monk, friend, speaking of knowledge and development, saying: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma, I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.' If, friend, that monk is not overcome and remains not under the influence of greed, hatred ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire, he should be understood thus: 'This venerable one understands in such a way that, when one understands thus, greed does not arise; thus this venerable one is not overcome and remains not under the influence of greed. This venerable one understands in such a way that, when one understands thus, hatred does not arise ... delusion ... anger ... hostility ... contempt ... insolence ... envy ... stinginess ... wicked jealousy ... wicked desire does not arise; thus this venerable one is not overcome and remains not under the influence of wicked desire.'
translations.an10.29:1: "As far, monks, as the Kosalan realm extends, as far as King Pasenadi of Kosala's dominion reaches, King Pasenadi of Kosala is considered the foremost. Yet, monks, even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, there is change, there is alteration. Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, how much more so toward the inferior.
translations.an10.29:10: Internally perceiving the formless, one sees externally blue forms, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance. Just as, for example, the flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance, or like a cloth from Varanasi, smoothed on both sides, blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance; in the same way, internally perceiving the formless, one sees externally blue forms, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance; thinking, 'Having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the fifth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Internally perceiving the formless, one sees externally yellow forms, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. Just as, for example, the kanikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance, or like a cloth from Varanasi, smoothed on both sides, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance; in the same way, internally perceiving the formless, one sees externally yellow forms, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance; thinking, 'Having mastered them, I know, I see,' one perceives thus. This is the sixth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: One, perceiving nothingness internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, red appearance, and red radiance. Just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, red appearance, and red radiance, or as a cloth from Varanasi, smoothed on both sides, is red, of red color, red appearance, and red radiance; so too, one, perceiving nothingness internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, red appearance, and red radiance; they perceive: 'Having mastered these, I know and see.' This is the seventh base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: One, perceiving nothingness internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white appearance, and white radiance. Just as the morning star is white, of white color, white appearance, and white radiance, or as a cloth from Varanasi, smoothed on both sides, is white, of white color, white appearance, and white radiance; so too, one, perceiving nothingness internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white appearance, and white radiance; they perceive: 'Having mastered these, I know and see.' This is the eighth base of mastery. These, monks, are the eight bases of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: The best of these eight bases of mastery, monks, is when one, perceiving nothingness internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white appearance, and white radiance; they perceive: 'Having mastered these, I know and see.' There are beings, monks, who perceive thus. Even for beings who perceive thus, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are these four ways of practice, monks. What four? The painful way with slow direct knowledge, the painful way with quick direct knowledge, the pleasant way with slow direct knowledge, the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge—these, monks, are the four ways of practice.
translations.an10.29:16: The best of these four ways of practice, monks, is the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge. There are beings, monks, who practice thus. Even for beings who practice thus, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are these four perceptions, monks. What four? One perceives the limited, one perceives the expansive, one perceives the immeasurable, one perceives the base of nothingness, thinking: 'There is nothing'—these, monks, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The best of these four perceptions, monks, is when one perceives the base of nothingness, thinking: 'There is nothing.' There are beings, monks, who perceive thus. Even for beings who perceive thus, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far, monks, as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world system. In that thousandfold world system there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru mountain kings, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand realms of the Four Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Thirty-three gods, a thousand realms of the Yāma gods, a thousand realms of the Tusita gods, a thousand realms of the Nimmānarati gods, a thousand realms of the Paranimmitavasavatti gods, a thousand brahma worlds. As far, monks, as the thousandfold world system extends, Great Brahmā is considered the highest there. Even for Great Brahmā, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim a supreme purity. The best of those who proclaim a supreme purity, monks, is when one, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for the direct knowledge and realization of that. There are beings, monks, who speak thus. Even for beings who speak thus, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, monks, when this world contracts. As the world contracts, monks, most beings are reborn in the Ābhassara realm. There they are mind-made, feeding on joy, self-luminous, moving through the air, dwelling in glory, and they remain thus for a very long time. As the world contracts, monks, the Ābhassara gods are considered the highest. Even for the Ābhassara gods, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are these ten kasiṇa bases, monks. What ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, and immeasurable; one perceives the water kasiṇa ... one perceives the fire kasiṇa ... one perceives the air kasiṇa ... one perceives the blue kasiṇa ... one perceives the yellow kasiṇa ... one perceives the red kasiṇa ... one perceives the white kasiṇa ... one perceives the space kasiṇa ... one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, and immeasurable. These, monks, are the ten kasiṇa bases.
translations.an10.29:5: Monks, among these ten kasina bases, the consciousness kasina is the foremost, wherein one perceives a single consciousness, boundless and non-dual, above, below, and all around. Monks, there are beings with such perception. Even for beings with such perception, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate even toward the foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: Monks, there are these eight bases for mastery. What eight? One, perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly. Having mastered them, one perceives: 'I know, I see.' This is the first basis for mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: One, perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally, limitless, beautiful and ugly. Having mastered them, one perceives: 'I know, I see.' This is the second basis for mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly. Having mastered them, one perceives: 'I know, I see.' This is the third basis for mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally, limitless, beautiful and ugly. Having mastered them, one perceives: 'I know, I see.' This is the fourth basis for mastery.
translations.an10.51:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable sir!" those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, examining their own facial reflection in a clean bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, if they see there any dust or blemish, they strive to remove that dust or blemish. If they do not see there any dust or blemish, they are satisfied, their aspiration fulfilled: 'It is a gain for me, it is well purified for me.' In the same way, monks, self-examination is very helpful for a monk regarding wholesome qualities: 'Do I usually dwell with covetousness or without covetousness? Do I usually dwell with a mind of ill will or without a mind of ill will? Do I usually dwell overcome by sloth and torpor or free from sloth and torpor? Do I usually dwell restless or not restless? Do I usually dwell with doubt or free from doubt? Do I usually dwell angry or not angry? Do I usually dwell with a defiled mind or an undefiled mind? Do I usually dwell with an agitated body or an unagitated body? Do I usually dwell lazy or energetic? Do I usually dwell unconcentrated or concentrated?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, monks, upon examination, a monk knows thus: 'I usually dwell with covetousness, with a mind of ill will, overcome by sloth and torpor, restless, with doubt, angry, with a defiled mind, with an agitated body, lazy, unconcentrated,' then, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil unwholesome states. Just as, monks, if one's clothes or head were on fire, one would apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish that fire on one's clothes or head. In the same way, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil unwholesome states.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, examining their own facial reflection in a clean bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, if they see there any dust or blemish, they strive to remove that dust or blemish. If they do not see there any dust or blemish, they are satisfied, their aspiration fulfilled: 'It is a gain for me, it is well purified for me.' In the same way, monks, self-examination is very helpful for a monk regarding wholesome qualities: 'Am I one who gains internal serenity of mind, or am I not one who gains internal serenity of mind? Am I one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, or am I not one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom?'
translations.an10.54:5: But if, monks, upon examination, a monk knows thus: 'I am not one who gains internal serenity of mind, I am not one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,' then, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very wholesome states. Just as, monks, if one's clothes or head were on fire, one would apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish that fire on one's clothes or head. In the same way, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, striving, exertion, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very wholesome states. Then, after some time, he becomes one who gains internal serenity of mind and one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, monks, upon examination, a monk knows thus: 'I am one who gains internal serenity of mind, I am one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,' then, monks, that monk, established in those very wholesome states, should apply himself further for the destruction of the taints.
translations.an10.58:1: "If, monks, wanderers of other sects were to ask thus: 'What is the root of all phenomena, friends? What is the origin of all phenomena? What is the arising of all phenomena? What is the meeting place of all phenomena? What is the chief of all phenomena? What is the ruler of all phenomena? What is the superior of all phenomena? What is the essence of all phenomena? What is the immersion of all phenomena? What is the conclusion of all phenomena?'—being asked thus, monks, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, venerable sir, guided by the Blessed One, having the Blessed One as refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it."
translations.an10.58:2: "Well then, monks, listen and attend carefully. I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.59:1: "Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our mind will be familiar with the going forth, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not obsess the mind; our mind will be familiar with the perception of impermanence, our mind will be familiar with the perception of non-self, our mind will be familiar with the perception of unattractiveness, our mind will be familiar with the perception of danger, knowing the world's equality and inequality, our mind will be familiar with that perception; knowing the world's existence and non-existence, our mind will be familiar with that perception; knowing the world's arising and passing away, our mind will be familiar with that perception; our mind will be familiar with the perception of abandoning, our mind will be familiar with the perception of dispassion, our mind will be familiar with the perception of cessation.'—thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
translations.an10.60:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. Now at that time the Venerable Girimananda was sick, afflicted, gravely ill. Then the Venerable Ananda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ananda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ananda, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, Nibbana.' This, Ananda, is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ananda, is the perception of non-delight in the entire world? Here, Ananda, a monk dwells abandoning and not clinging to those clingings, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies regarding the world. This, Ananda, is called the perception of non-delight in the entire world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ananda, is the perception of disenchantment with all formations? Here, Ananda, a monk is repelled, humiliated, and disgusted with all formations. This, Ananda, is called the perception of disenchantment with all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ananda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ananda, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: 'I breathe in long'; or breathing out long, he knows: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he knows: 'I breathe in short'; or breathing out short, he knows: 'I breathe out short.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind ... concentrating the mind ... liberating the mind ... contemplating impermanence ... contemplating fading away ... contemplating cessation ... contemplating relinquishment.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.' This, Ananda, is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ananda, were to recite these ten perceptions to the monk Girimananda, it is possible that on hearing these ten perceptions, his illness would immediately subside."
translations.an10.60:2: "Venerable sir, the Venerable Girimananda is sick, afflicted, gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the Venerable Girimananda out of compassion." "If you, Ananda, were to recite ten perceptions to the monk Girimananda, it is possible that on hearing these ten perceptions, his illness would immediately subside.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of unattractiveness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of disenchantment with all formations, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ananda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ananda, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.' Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates subject to clinging. This, Ananda, is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ananda, is perception of non-self? Here, Ananda, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'The eye is non-self, forms are non-self; the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self; the nose is non-self, odors are non-self; the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self; the body is non-self, tangibles are non-self; the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.' Thus he dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ananda, is called perception of non-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ananda, is perception of unattractiveness? Here, Ananda, a monk reviews this very body from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurity: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.' Thus he dwells contemplating unattractiveness in this body. This, Ananda, is called perception of unattractiveness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ananda, is perception of danger? Here, Ananda, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'This body is of much suffering, of much danger. Thus in this body various kinds of illness arise, such as: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, disease of the external ear, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, lip-disease; cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, gripes, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, vitiligo, pustules, psoriasis; scabies, eruptions; bile disorders, phlegm disorders, wind disorders, combined disorders; disorders due to change of climate, disorders due to careless behavior, disorders due to assault; disorders born of kamma; and cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.' Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This, Ananda, is called perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ananda, is perception of abandoning? Here, Ananda, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, abolishes it. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill-will; he abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, abolishes it. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of cruelty; he abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, abolishes it. He does not tolerate any arisen evil unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, terminates them, abolishes them. This, Ananda, is called perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: "Monks, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, such that before that there was no ignorance and afterward it came to be. Yet, monks, it is discerned: 'Ignorance has this as its condition.'
translations.an10.61:2: I say, monks, that ignorance has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? 'The five hindrances' should be said. I say, monks, that the five hindrances have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? 'The three kinds of misconduct' should be said. I say, monks, that the three kinds of misconduct have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of misconduct? 'Lack of restraint of the sense faculties' should be said. I say, monks, that lack of restraint of the sense faculties has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of restraint of the sense faculties? 'Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension' should be said. I say, monks, that lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? 'Unwise attention' should be said. I say, monks, that unwise attention has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for unwise attention? 'Lack of faith' should be said. I say, monks, that lack of faith has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? 'Not listening to the true Dhamma' should be said. I say, monks, that not listening to the true Dhamma has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for not listening to the true Dhamma? 'Association with bad people' should be said.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, monks, association with bad people, when full, fulfills not listening to the true Dhamma; not listening to the true Dhamma, when full, fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith, when full, fulfills unwise attention; unwise attention, when full, fulfills lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension, when full, fulfills lack of restraint of the sense faculties; lack of restraint of the sense faculties, when full, fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; the three kinds of misconduct, when full, fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances, when full, fulfill ignorance. Thus there is nutriment for this ignorance, and thus there is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, monks, when on a mountaintop heavy rain falls, that water, flowing downhill, fills the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies; the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies, when full, fill the small ponds; the small ponds, when full, fill the large ponds; the large ponds, when full, fill the small rivers; the small rivers, when full, fill the large rivers; the large rivers, when full, fill the great ocean, the sea; thus there is nutriment for this great ocean, the sea, and thus there is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, monks, association with good people, when full, fulfills listening to the true Dhamma; listening to the true Dhamma, when full, fulfills faith; faith, when full, fulfills wise attention; wise attention, when full, fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension; mindfulness and clear comprehension, when full, fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; restraint of the sense faculties, when full, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; the three kinds of good conduct, when full, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness, when full, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment, when full, fulfill true knowledge and liberation. Thus there is nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and thus there is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ananda approached the Venerable Sariputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sariputta. When the courteous and friendly conversation was concluded, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ananda said this to the Venerable Sariputta:
translations.an10.7:2: "Friend Sariputta, could there be for a monk such an attainment of concentration that he would not perceive earth in earth, not perceive water in water, not perceive fire in fire, not perceive air in air, not perceive the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, not perceive the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, not perceive the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not perceive this world in this world, not perceive the other world in the other world; and yet he would still be perceiving?"
translations.an10.7:4: "But how, friend Sariputta, could there be for a monk such an attainment of concentration that he would not perceive earth in earth ... and yet he would still be perceiving?" "On one occasion, friend Ananda, I was dwelling right here in Savatthi in the Blind Men's Grove. There I attained such a concentration that I did not perceive earth in earth, I did not perceive water in water, I did not perceive fire in fire, I did not perceive air in air, I did not perceive the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, I did not perceive the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, I did not perceive the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, I did not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I did not perceive this world in this world, I did not perceive the other world in the other world; and yet I was still perceiving."
translations.an3.10:1: "Monks, one endowed with three things, without abandoning three stains, is deposited in hell as if carried off and placed there. With what three? He is immoral, and the stain of immorality is not abandoned by him; he is envious, and the stain of envy is not abandoned by him; he is stingy, and the stain of stinginess is not abandoned by him. Monks, one endowed with these three things, without abandoning these three stains, is deposited in hell as if carried off and placed there."
translations.an3.12:5: "Furthermore, monks, in whatever place a monk understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,' understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' This, monks, is the second thing that is memorable for a monk for life."
translations.an3.15:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Baranasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable sir!" those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an3.15:2: "Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Sacetana. Then, monks, King Sacetana addressed a chariot-maker: 'My good chariot-maker, in six months from now there will be a battle. Will you be able, my good chariot-maker, to make a new pair of wheels for me?' 'I can, lord,' the chariot-maker replied to King Sacetana. Then, monks, the chariot-maker, in six months less six nights, finished one wheel. Then, monks, King Sacetana addressed the chariot-maker: 'My good chariot-maker, in six days from now there will be a battle. Is the new pair of wheels finished?' 'Lord, in these six months less six nights, one wheel is finished.' 'But will you be able, my good chariot-maker, to finish a second wheel in these six days?' 'I can, lord,' monks, the chariot-maker, having finished a second wheel in six days, took the new pair of wheels and approached King Sacetana; having approached, he said to King Sacetana: 'Lord, this new pair of wheels is finished.' 'And what difference is there, my good chariot-maker, between this wheel finished in six months less six nights and this wheel finished in six days? I see no difference at all.' 'There is a difference, lord. Let the lord see the difference.'"
translations.an3.15:3: "Then, monks, the chariot-maker set rolling the wheel that was finished in six days. Rolling along, it went as far as the momentum carried it, then wobbled and fell to the ground. But he set rolling the wheel that was finished in six months less six nights. Rolling along, it went as far as the momentum carried it and then stood still as if fixed on an axle."
translations.an3.15:5: "Monks, it might occur to you: 'Surely, the chariot-maker at that time was someone else.' But it should not be seen thus. I was the chariot-maker at that time. At that time, monks, I was skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of wood. But now, monks, I am an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of the body, skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of speech, skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of the mind. Monks, any monk or nun in whom bodily crookedness is not abandoned, bodily fault, bodily flaw; verbal crookedness is not abandoned, verbal fault, verbal flaw; mental crookedness is not abandoned, mental fault, mental flaw—they have fallen from this Dhamma and Discipline, just like that wheel finished in six days."
translations.an3.15:6: "Monks, any monk or nun in whom bodily crookedness is abandoned, bodily fault, bodily flaw; verbal crookedness is abandoned, verbal fault, verbal flaw; mental crookedness is abandoned, mental fault, mental flaw—they are established in this Dhamma and Discipline, just like that wheel finished in six months less six nights."
translations.an3.1:3: "Thus, monks, the fool is fearful, the wise one is fearless. The fool is beset by calamity, the wise one is free from calamity. The fool is afflicted, the wise one is unafflicted. Monks, there is no fear from the wise one, no calamity from the wise one, no affliction from the wise one."
translations.an3.20:1: "Monks, a merchant endowed with three factors soon attains greatness and abundance in wealth. What three? Here, monks, a merchant is clear-sighted, skilled, and well-supported. And how, monks, is a merchant clear-sighted? Here, monks, a merchant knows a commodity: 'This commodity, bought thus, sold thus, will bring this much profit, this much income.' Thus, monks, a merchant is clear-sighted.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, monks, is a merchant skilled? Here, monks, a merchant is skilled in buying and selling a commodity. Thus, monks, a merchant is skilled.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, monks, is a merchant well-supported? Here, monks, householders or householders' sons who are wealthy, with great wealth and property, know of that merchant: 'This worthy merchant is clear-sighted and skilled, capable of supporting wife and children, and capable of giving to us from time to time.' They bestow wealth upon him: 'Here, good merchant, take this wealth, support your wife and children, and give to us from time to time.' Thus, monks, a merchant is well-supported. Monks, a merchant endowed with these three factors soon attains greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities soon attains greatness and abundance in wholesome qualities. What three? Here, monks, a monk is clear-sighted, energetic, and well-supported. And how, monks, is a monk clear-sighted? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,' 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' Thus, monks, a monk is clear-sighted.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk energetic? Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and acquiring wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility regarding wholesome qualities. Thus, monks, a monk is energetic.
translations.an3.22:1: "Monks, there are these three kinds of sick persons found existing in the world. What three? Here, monks, a certain sick person, whether or not he obtains suitable food, whether or not he obtains suitable medicine, whether or not he obtains a suitable attendant, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: Here, monks, a certain sick person obtains suitable food, not failing to obtain it; obtains suitable medicine, not failing to obtain it; obtains a suitable attendant, not failing to obtain it; and recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Here, monks, regarding that sick person who obtains suitable food, not failing to obtain it; obtains suitable medicine, not failing to obtain it; obtains a suitable attendant, not failing to obtain it; and recovers from that illness—because of this sick person, sick-food is allowed, sick-medicine is allowed, a sick-attendant is allowed. And moreover, monks, because of this sick person, other sick persons should be attended to. These, monks, are the three kinds of sick persons found existing in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: In the same way, monks, there are these three persons similar to the sick found existing in the world. What three? Here, monks, a certain person, whether or not he obtains the opportunity to see the Tathagata, whether or not he obtains the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathagata, does not enter upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: Here, monks, a certain person, whether or not he obtains the opportunity to see the Tathagata, whether or not he obtains the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathagata, enters upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: "Monks, there are these three persons who are helpful to another person. What three? Monks, a person who, because of another person, goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, goes for refuge to the Sangha; this person, monks, is helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, monks, a person who, because of another person, understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,' 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering'; this person, monks, is helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, monks, a person who, because of another person, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters upon and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge; this person, monks, is helpful to that person. These, monks, are the three persons who are helpful to another person.
translations.an3.2:1: "Monks, the fool is characterized by his actions, the wise one is characterized by his actions; wisdom shines forth in behavior. Monks, a fool is to be known by three things. What three? By bodily misconduct, by verbal misconduct, by mental misconduct. Monks, a fool is to be known by these three things.
translations.an3.2:2: Monks, a wise one is to be known by three things. What three? By bodily good conduct, by verbal good conduct, by mental good conduct. Monks, a wise one is to be known by these three things.
translations.an3.30:4: A person with upside-down wisdom, unwise, unskilled, even if he goes frequently to the presence of monks,
translations.an3.30:5: Such a one is unable to grasp the beginning, the middle, or the end of the talk, for wisdom is not found in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A person with wisdom in his lap is said to be better than that; even if he goes frequently to the presence of monks,
translations.an3.30:8: A person with broad wisdom is said to be better than those; even if he goes frequently to the presence of monks,
translations.an3.32:4: "Here, Ananda, a monk thinks: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbana.' Thus, Ananda, a monk might attain such a concentration that there would be no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding this conscious body, and no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding all external signs; and having attained and dwelling in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, the latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit would not be present, and he would dwell having attained that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom."
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sariputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to Venerable Sariputta: "In brief, Sariputta, I would teach the Dhamma; in detail, Sariputta, I would teach the Dhamma; in brief and in detail, Sariputta, I would teach the Dhamma; but those who understand are rare." "Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in brief, to teach the Dhamma in detail, to teach the Dhamma in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma."
translations.an3.33:2: "Therefore, Sariputta, you should train thus: 'There will be no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding this conscious body, and there will be no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding all external signs; and having attained and dwelling in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, the latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit would not be present, and I will dwell having attained that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.' Thus, indeed, Sariputta, you should train."
translations.an3.33:3: "And when, Sariputta, a monk has no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding this conscious body, and has no latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit regarding all external signs; and having attained and dwelling in that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, the latent tendencies of 'I-making', 'mine-making', and conceit are not present, and he dwells having attained that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom; this, Sariputta, is called: 'A monk has cut off craving, removed the fetter, and by rightly breaking through conceit has made an end of suffering.' And this, Sariputta, is what I said with reference to this in the Questions of Udaya in the Parayana:"
translations.an3.33:4: 'The abandoning of perceptions of sensual pleasures, and of both kinds of mental distress; The dispelling of sloth, and the restraining of remorse.'
translations.an3.34:1: "These, monks, are three sources for the arising of kamma. Which three? Greed is a source for the arising of kamma, hatred is a source for the arising of kamma, delusion is a source for the arising of kamma."
translations.an3.34:10: "That kamma, monks, which is done without delusion, born of non-delusion, originating from non-delusion, arisen from non-delusion, when delusion has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no more subject to future arising."
translations.an3.34:11: "Just as, monks, seeds that are unbroken, unspoiled, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, well-stored, a person would burn with fire. Having burned them with fire, he would make them into ashes. Having made them into ashes, he would scatter them in a great wind or sweep them away in a swift-flowing stream. Thus, monks, those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising. In the same way, monks, that kamma which is done without greed, born of non-greed, originating from non-greed, arisen from non-greed, when greed has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no more subject to future arising."
translations.an3.34:13: "Kamma born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion, for the unwise; Whatever kamma is done by that, whether little or much, is to be experienced right here, no other ground is found."
translations.an3.34:2: "That kamma, monks, which is done with greed, born of greed, originating from greed, arisen from greed, wherever that individual is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence."
translations.an3.34:5: "Just as, monks, seeds that are unbroken, unspoiled, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, well-stored, sown in a well-prepared field in good soil, and the rain-god would provide suitable rain. Thus, monks, those seeds would come to growth, increase, and maturity. In the same way, monks, that kamma which is done with greed, born of greed, originating from greed, arisen from greed, wherever that individual is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence."
translations.an3.34:6: "That kamma which is done with hatred... that kamma which is done with delusion, born of delusion, originating from delusion, arisen from delusion, wherever that individual is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence. These, monks, are the three sources for the arising of kamma."
translations.an3.34:9: "That kamma, monks, which is done without hatred, born of non-hatred, originating from non-hatred, arisen from non-hatred, when hatred has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no more subject to future arising."
translations.an3.35:3: "Well then, young man, I will question you on this very point. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, young man? Suppose there is a householder or a householder's son with a mansion house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and shutters closed. Therein is a couch spread with a rug of wool, a coverlet of wool, a spread of wool, an antelope hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends; an oil lamp is burning there; and four wives with pleasing features are attending on him. What do you think, young man, would he sleep happily or not? Or how does it seem to you?" "He would sleep happily, venerable sir. Among those in the world who sleep happily, he would be one."
translations.an3.35:4: "What do you think, young man? Could there arise in that householder or householder's son any fevers of passion, bodily or mental, born of lust, by which, burning with those fevers of passion born of lust, he would lie in suffering?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.an3.35:8: Always indeed sleeps happily, the brahmin who is fully extinguished; Who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, cooled, without acquisitions.
translations.an3.39:10: Thus dwelling, having known the state without acquisitions; The intoxications regarding health, youth, and life.
translations.an3.39:2: I had, monks, three mansions—one for the winter, one for the summer, one for the rains. I, monks, in the rains mansion for the four months of the rains, being entertained by musicians without men, did not descend from the upper mansion. And just as, monks, in other homes, slaves, workers, and servants are given broken rice with sour gruel as food, even so, monks, in my father's home, slaves, workers, and servants were given rice with meat.
translations.an3.39:3: To me, monks, endowed with such power and such delicacy, this occurred: 'An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to old age himself, not beyond old age, seeing another who is old, is distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, overlooking himself. I too am subject to old age, not beyond old age. If I, being subject to old age, not beyond old age, seeing another who is old, were to be distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.' For me, monks, reflecting thus, the intoxication with youth regarding youth was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to illness himself, not beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, is distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, overlooking himself: 'I too am subject to illness, not beyond illness. If I, being subject to illness, not beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, were to be distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.' For me, monks, reflecting thus, the intoxication with health regarding health was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to death himself, not beyond death, seeing another who is dead, is distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, overlooking himself: 'I too am subject to death, not beyond death. If I, being subject to death, not beyond death, seeing another who is dead, were to be distressed, humiliated, and disgusted, that would not be proper for me.' For me, monks, reflecting thus, the intoxication with life regarding life was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: A monk, monks, overcome by intoxication with youth, gives up the training and reverts to the lower life. A monk, monks, overcome by intoxication with health ... A monk, monks, overcome by intoxication with life, gives up the training and reverts to the lower life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death; As they are, so are beings, ordinary people are disgusted.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted by them, beings with such a nature; That would not be proper for me, dwelling thus.
translations.an3.40:1: "There are, monks, these three authorities. Which three? Self as authority, the world as authority, the Dhamma as authority. And what, monks, is self as authority? Here, monks, a monk, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of this or that state of existence did I go forth from the home life into homelessness. But I am sunk in birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; sunk in suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned. If I, having left behind such sensual pleasures, went forth from the home life into homelessness, were to seek such or even worse sensual pleasures, that would not be proper for me.' Reflecting thus: 'My energy shall be aroused, unflagging; mindfulness established, unconfused; body tranquil, unagitated; mind concentrated, one-pointed.' Making self itself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, monks, is called self as authority.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, monks, is the Dhamma as authority? Here, monks, a monk, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of this or that state of existence did I go forth from the home life into homelessness. But I am sunk in birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; sunk in suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves. And there are my fellow monks who dwell knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, were to dwell lazy and heedless, that would not be proper for me.' Reflecting thus: 'My energy shall be aroused, unflagging; mindfulness established, unconfused; body tranquil, unagitated; mind concentrated, one-pointed.' Making the Dhamma itself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, monks, is called the Dhamma as authority. These, monks, are the three authorities.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secrecy in the world, for one doing evil deeds; Yourself, O person, knows, whether it is true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Indeed, O witness, you despise yourself, thinking it good; Who, having evil within oneself, conceals oneself.
translations.an3.40:6: The devas and the Tathāgatas see, In the world a fool walking crookedly; Therefore, one who has self as authority, and one who has the world as authority, the wise and meditator; One who has the Dhamma as authority and lives in accordance with the Dhamma, The sage with true endeavor does not decline.
translations.an3.48:1: "Monks, depending on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, great trees grow by three means of growth. What three? They grow by branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow by bark and shoots; they grow by sapwood and heartwood. Monks, depending on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, great trees grow by these three means of growth."
translations.an3.48:2: "Just so, monks, depending on a faithful householder, the people within grow by three means of growth. What three? They grow by faith; they grow by virtue; they grow by wisdom. Monks, depending on a faithful householder, the people within grow by these three means of growth."
translations.an3.48:3: "Just as a rocky mountain in a vast wild forest, depending on it, the forest trees grow."
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins, aged, old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of their lifespan, a hundred and twenty years old, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged friendly and courteous talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: "We, Master Gotama, are brahmins aged, old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of our lifespan, a hundred and twenty years old; we have not done what is good, not done what is skillful, not made a shelter from fear. Let Master Gotama advise us, instruct us, so that it may be for our long-term welfare and happiness."
translations.an3.51:2: "Indeed, brahmins, you are aged, old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of your lifespan, a hundred and twenty years old; you have not done what is good, not done what is skillful, not made a shelter from fear. This world, brahmins, is led on by aging, sickness, and death. When the world is thus led on by aging, sickness, and death, restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of mind here becomes for one who has passed away a shelter, a refuge, a light, a protection, and a support."
translations.an3.51:3: "Life is led on, of little duration; for one led on by old age there are no shelters. Seeing this danger in death, one should do meritorious deeds that bring happiness."
translations.an3.52:4: "Thus the world is burning, with aging and death; one should extract with giving, what is given is well-extracted."
translations.an3.57:2: "Vaccha, those who say: 'The ascetic Gotama says: "Only to me should gifts be given... not to the disciples of others are gifts of great fruit"' do not speak my words. They misrepresent me falsely and untruthfully. Vaccha, whoever restrains another from giving a gift creates three obstacles, three obstructions. What three? He creates an obstacle to the merit of the donor, an obstacle to the gain of the recipients, and beforehand he has damaged and harmed himself. Vaccha, whoever restrains another from giving a gift creates these three obstacles, three obstructions."
translations.an3.5:1: "Monks, a fool is to be known by three qualities. What three? He asks a question improperly; he answers a question improperly; and when another answers a question properly, with well-rounded, well-arranged, polished words, he does not approve of it. Monks, a fool is to be known by these three qualities."
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Sangarava approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged friendly and courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Sangarava said to the Blessed One: "We, Master Gotama, are called brahmins. We perform sacrifices and have sacrifices performed. There, Master Gotama, both the one who sacrifices and the one who has sacrifices performed all engage in a meritorious practice involving many bodies, namely that concerned with sacrifice. But this one, Master Gotama, who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from some clan or other, tames himself alone, calms himself alone, extinguishes himself alone; thus he engages in a meritorious practice involving a single body, namely that concerned with going forth."
translations.an3.60:10: "But here, brahmin, someone does not declare by means of a sign, but having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or deities, he declares: 'Such is your mind, thus is your mind, such is your thought.' Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise."
translations.an3.60:11: "But here, brahmin, someone does not declare by means of a sign, nor having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or deities, but having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought while thinking and pondering, he declares: 'Such is your mind, thus is your mind, such is your thought.' Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise."
translations.an3.60:12: "But here, brahmin, someone does not declare by means of a sign, nor having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or deities, nor having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought while thinking and pondering, but having attained a concentration without thought and examination, he knows with his mind the mind of another, encompassing it: 'As the mental formations of this venerable one are directed, immediately after this mind, such and such a thought will be thought.' Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of mind-reading."
translations.an3.60:13: "And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus: 'Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, attain this and abide.' This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle do you consider more excellent and sublime?"
translations.an3.60:14: "Therein, Master Gotama, where a miracle is such that someone here experiences various kinds of psychic power... up to having mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world, this, Master Gotama, is a miracle that only the one who performs it experiences, only for the one who performs it does it occur. This, Master Gotama, seems to me like a miracle of illusion."
translations.an3.60:16: And this, Venerable Gotama, is the wonder: someone instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend in this way, do not attend in that way; abandon this, attain and dwell in that.' This, Venerable Gotama, is the wonder that is considered superior and more excellent among these three wonders.
translations.an3.60:17: It is wonderful, Venerable Gotama, it is marvelous, Venerable Gotama. How well this has been spoken by Venerable Gotama, and we consider Venerable Gotama to be endowed with these three wonders. For Venerable Gotama experiences various kinds of psychic power... even up to the Brahma world, he wields mastery with the body. Venerable Gotama, with his mind, knows the mind of one who has attained concentration without thought and examination: 'As this venerable one's mental formations are directed, immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.' Venerable Gotama instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend in this way, do not attend in that way; abandon this, attain and dwell in that.'
translations.an3.60:18: "Certainly, brahmin, you have spoken to me with a challenging and insinuating statement; nevertheless, I will answer you. For I, brahmin, experience various kinds of psychic power... even up to the Brahma world, I wield mastery with the body. I, brahmin, with my mind, know the mind of one who has attained concentration without thought and examination: 'As this venerable one's mental formations are directed, immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.' I, brahmin, instruct thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend in this way, do not attend in that way; abandon this, attain and dwell in that.'"
translations.an3.60:19: "But, Venerable Gotama, is there even one other monk who is endowed with these three wonders, apart from Venerable Gotama?" "Not just one hundred, brahmin, not two hundred, not three hundred, not four hundred, not five hundred, but many more monks are endowed with these three wonders." "But where, Venerable Gotama, do those monks dwell now?" "Right here, brahmin, in this community of monks."
translations.an3.60:2: "Well then, brahmin, I will ask you about this same matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, brahmin? Here a Tathagata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed. He says thus: 'Come, this is the path, this is the practice; having practiced accordingly, I myself have realized the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life and make it known. Come, you too practice accordingly; having practiced accordingly, you too will realize the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life and dwell having attained it.' Thus this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly for that goal, and there are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? In this case, is the practice of merit that has one body or many bodies, namely, the undertaking of the going forth?" "In this case too, Venerable Gotama, the practice of merit has many bodies, namely, the undertaking of the going forth."
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, Venerable Ananda said to the brahmin Sangarava: "Brahmin, of these two practices, which practice do you consider to be less arduous, less troublesome, more fruitful, and more beneficial?" When this was said, the brahmin Sangarava said to Venerable Ananda: "Just as Venerable Gotama and Venerable Ananda. These are my venerable ones, these are my praiseworthy ones."
translations.an3.60:5: A second time, Venerable Ananda said to the brahmin Sangarava: "I am not asking you, brahmin: 'Who are your venerable ones? Who are your praiseworthy ones?' I am asking you thus: 'Brahmin, of these two practices, which practice do you consider to be less arduous, less troublesome, more fruitful, and more beneficial?'" A second time, the brahmin Sangarava said to Venerable Ananda: "Just as Venerable Gotama and Venerable Ananda. These are my venerable ones, these are my praiseworthy ones."
