translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "Even up to the third time, the brahmin Sangarava, when asked a legitimate question by Ananda, evades it and does not answer. Suppose I were to release him." Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Sangarava: "What discussion arose today among the king's officials sitting together in the royal court?" "Today, Venerable Gotama, this discussion arose among the king's officials sitting together in the royal court: 'Formerly, there were fewer monks, and more of them displayed the wonder of psychic power beyond human capability; but now there are more monks, and fewer display the wonder of psychic power beyond human capability.' This, Venerable Gotama, is the discussion that arose today among the king's officials sitting together in the royal court."
translations.an3.60:8: "There are, brahmin, these three wonders. Which three? The wonder of psychic power, the wonder of mind-reading, and the wonder of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the wonder of psychic power? Here, brahmin, someone experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without sinking as if on land; he travels cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; he wields mastery with the body even up to the Brahma world. This, brahmin, is called the wonder of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the wonder of mind-reading? Here, brahmin, someone by means of a sign declares: 'Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, such is your mind.' And even if he declares much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: 'These are the Four Noble Truths'—this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. This has been said. With reference to what was it said? With the descent of the embryo, monks, there is the coming together of the six elements; with the descent, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling. For one who feels, monks, I declare: 'This is suffering,' I declare: 'This is the origin of suffering,' I declare: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' I declare: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But, monks, for one who holds to the view that everything is due to past action, there is no desire or effort regarding what should be done and what should not be done. Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done cannot be found as true and established, the mindful are unprotected, and one living thus cannot have a personal righteous doctrine. This, monks, is my first righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such doctrines.
translations.an3.61:8: These, monks, are the three sectarian grounds which, when wise men cross-examine, interrogate, and press them, even after going far, stand on inaction.
translations.an3.61:9: And this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins? 'These six elements'—this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These six sense bases'—this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These eighteen mental examinations'—this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. 'These Four Noble Truths'—this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, not refuted, undefiled, blameless, not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: "There are these three dangers that separate mother and child," so says the uninstructed ordinary person. What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great conflagration arises. When a great conflagration has arisen, villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. When villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there a mother does not find her child, and a child does not find its mother. This, monks, is the first danger that separates mother and child, so says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:2: Again, monks, there comes a time when a great rain cloud arises. When a great rain cloud has arisen, a great flood is produced. When a great flood is produced, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there a mother does not find her child, and a child does not find its mother. This, monks, is the second danger that separates mother and child, so says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:3: Again, monks, there comes a time when there is danger, a jungle uprising, and people mount their vehicles and travel around. When there is danger, a jungle uprising, and people mount their vehicles and travel around, there a mother does not find her child, and a child does not find its mother. This, monks, is the third danger that separates mother and child, so says the uninstructed ordinary person. These, monks, are the three dangers that separate mother and child, so says the uninstructed ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:4: These, monks, are the three dangers that are shared by mother and child, but the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of them as dangers not shared by mother and child. What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great fire arises. When a great fire has arisen, villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. When villages, towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the first danger that is shared by mother and child, but the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a danger not shared by mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when a great storm arises. When a great storm has arisen, a great flood is produced. When a great flood is produced, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the second danger that is shared by mother and child, but the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a danger not shared by mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when there is danger, a jungle uprising, and people mount their vehicles and travel around the countryside. When there is danger, a jungle uprising, and people mounted on vehicles are traveling around the countryside, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, and a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the third danger that is shared by mother and child, but the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a danger not shared by mother and child. These, monks, are the three dangers that are shared by mother and child, but the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of them as dangers not shared by mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: There are these three dangers, monks, that are not shared by mother and child. What three? The danger of aging, the danger of illness, the danger of death. Monks, a mother does not get her wish for her aging child: 'May I age, but not my child.' Nor does a child get his wish for his aging mother: 'May I age, but not my mother.'
translations.an3.62:8: Monks, a mother does not get her wish for her ill child: 'May I be ill, but not my child.' Nor does a child get his wish for his ill mother: 'May I be ill, but not my mother.'
translations.an3.62:9: Monks, a mother does not get her wish for her dying child: 'May I die, but not my child.' Nor does a child get his wish for his dying mother: 'May I die, but not my mother.' These, monks, are the three dangers that are not shared by mother and child.
translations.an3.63:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Sangha of monks when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Venāgapura. The brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: 'The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan family, has arrived at Venāgapura. Now a good report about that Master Gotama has spread: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' He has realized with his own direct knowledge this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, and he makes it known to others. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a spiritual life that is entirely perfect and pure.' It is good to see such arahants.'
translations.an3.63:11: 'It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is amazing, Master Gotama. Who else could be one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, such a noble high and luxurious bed, except Master Gotama?'
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Venāgapura approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, after an exchange of courteous and memorable talk, sat down to one side; some raised their joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. When they were seated, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: Brahmin, there are these three kinds of high and luxurious beds, of which I am now one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty. What three? The divine high and luxurious bed, the brahmā high and luxurious bed, the noble high and luxurious bed. These, brahmin, are the three kinds of high and luxurious beds, of which I am now one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty.
translations.an4.10:10: Beings wander on in saṁsāra, going to birth and death. But those who have fully understood sensual pleasures and all bonds of existence,
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the yoke of sensual pleasures, and by the yoke of existence, bound by the yoke of views, with ignorance placed foremost.
translations.an4.18:1: Monks, there are these four ways of going of a nāga. What four? He does not go by way of favor, he does not go by way of aversion, he does not go by way of delusion, he does not go by way of fear. These, monks, are the four ways of going of a nāga.
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks!' 'Venerable sir!' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.1:4: Virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation: these things were realized by the illustrious Gotama.
translations.an4.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in the Kāḷakārāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks!' 'Venerable sir!' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.24:2: Whatever in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—that I know.
translations.an4.24:5: If, monks, I were to say, 'I know it and I do not know it,' that would be just the same for him.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, monks, the Tathāgata, having seen what is to be seen, does not conceive of the seen, does not conceive of the unseen, does not conceive of what is to be seen, does not conceive of a seer. Having heard what is to be heard, he does not conceive of the heard, does not conceive of the unheard, does not conceive of what is to be heard, does not conceive of a hearer. Having sensed what is to be sensed, he does not conceive of the sensed, does not conceive of the unsensed, does not conceive of what is to be sensed, does not conceive of a sensor. Having cognized what is to be cognized, he does not conceive of the cognized, does not conceive of the uncognized, does not conceive of what is to be cognized, does not conceive of a cognizer. Thus, monks, the Tathāgata is such in regard to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. And I say, 'From such a one, there is no other such one more excellent or refined.'
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, Clung to as true by others, The such one does not rely on them, Nor would he hold another's truth or falsehood.
translations.an4.28:1: "Monks, these four ancient noble traditions are original, long-standing, traditional, and unadulterated, never adulterated in the past, not being adulterated now, nor will they be adulterated in the future; they are not disparaged by wise ascetics and brahmins. What four? Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of such contentment; and he does not engage in improper search for the sake of robes. Not getting a robe, he is not agitated; getting a robe, he uses it without greed, without infatuation, without attachment, seeing the danger and understanding the escape. And because of this contentment with any kind of robe, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. Whoever is skilled, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful in this is called, monks, a monk who stands in the ancient, original noble tradition.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, monks, a monk delights in development, delights in abandoning; and because of this delight in development and delight in abandoning, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. Whoever is skilled, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful in this is called, monks, a monk who stands in the ancient, original noble tradition. These, monks, are the four ancient noble traditions, original, long-standing, traditional, and unadulterated, never adulterated in the past, not being adulterated now, nor will they be adulterated in the future; they are not disparaged by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an4.28:5: And endowed with these four noble traditions, monks, if a monk lives in the eastern direction, he overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; if he lives in the western direction, he overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; if he lives in the northern direction, he overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him; if he lives in the southern direction, he overcomes discontent, discontent does not overcome him. Why is that? Because, monks, the wise one is a conqueror of discontent.
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not overcome the wise, Nor does the wise overcome discontent; The wise overcomes discontent, For the wise is a conqueror of discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: "Monks, there are these four wheels, endowed with which, the four wheels turn for devas and humans, endowed with which, devas and humans soon attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What four? Living in a suitable region, associating with good people, right self-resolution, and past merit—these, monks, are the four wheels, endowed with which, the four wheels turn for devas and humans, endowed with which, devas and humans soon attain greatness and abundance in wealth."
translations.an4.32:1: "Monks, there are these four bases of sympathy. What four? Giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—these, monks, are the four bases of sympathy."
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kind speech, Beneficial conduct and impartiality in situations, As is appropriate in each case; These are the sympathies in the world, Like linchpins for a moving chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these sympathies were absent, A mother would not receive respect and honor, Nor a father, for the sake of their child.
translations.an4.33:1: "Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his den in the evening. Having emerged from his den, he stretches. Having stretched, he surveys all four directions. Having surveyed all four directions, he roars his lion's roar three times. Having roared his lion's roar three times, he sets out in search of prey. And those animals who hear the sound of the lion, the king of beasts, mostly fall into fear, terror, and alarm. They enter holes if they are hole-dwellers, enter water if they are water-dwellers, enter the forest if they are forest-dwellers; birds take to the air. And those royal elephants in villages, towns, and capital cities, bound by strong leather bonds, even they, breaking and snapping those bonds, frightened, voiding excrement, flee in all directions. So powerful, monks, is the lion, the king of beasts, among animals, so influential, so mighty.
translations.an4.33:2: In the same way, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, blessed, he teaches the Dhamma: 'Such is identity, such is the origin of identity, such is the cessation of identity, such is the way leading to the cessation of identity.' And those devas who are long-lived, beautiful, enjoying much happiness, dwelling in lofty mansions for a long time, hearing the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma, mostly fall into fear, terror, and alarm: 'It seems, friends, that we, though impermanent, thought ourselves permanent; though unstable, thought ourselves stable; though non-eternal, thought ourselves eternal. It seems, friends, that we are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, included within identity.' So powerful, monks, is the Tathāgata in the world with its devas, so influential, so mighty.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, having directly known, Set in motion the wheel of Dhamma; For the world with its devas, The teacher, the matchless one.
translations.an4.33:4: Identity and its cessation, And the origin of identity; The noble eightfold path, Leading to the calming of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: "Monks, there are these four supreme objects of confidence. Which four? Whatever beings there are—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them. Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost. For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:2: Whatever conditioned phenomena there are, the noble eightfold path is declared the foremost among them. Monks, those who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in the foremost. For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:3: Whatever phenomena there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost among them, that is, the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the termination of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbāna. Monks, those who have confidence in the phenomenon of dispassion have confidence in the foremost. For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:4: Whatever assemblies or groups there are, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples is declared the foremost among them, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals—this is the Blessed One's disciple Saṅgha: worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Monks, those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the foremost. For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost. These, monks, are the four supreme objects of confidence."
translations.an4.34:5: For those who have confidence in the foremost, who understand the foremost Dhamma; For those who have confidence in the foremost Buddha, the unsurpassed recipient of offerings.
translations.an4.34:6: For those who have confidence in the foremost Dhamma, in the bliss of dispassion and peace; For those who have confidence in the foremost Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: For one who gives a gift in what is foremost, foremost merit increases; Foremost life and beauty, fame, reputation, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: "Master Gotama, we describe a person of great wisdom, a great man, as endowed with four qualities. With which four? Here, Master Gotama, he is learned, he understands the meaning of various statements thus: 'This is the meaning of this statement, this is the meaning of that statement.' He is mindful, able to recall and recollect what was done and said long ago. And whatever are the duties of a householder, he is skillful and diligent in them, possessing the method of investigation, capable of doing and arranging them. Master Gotama, we describe a person of great wisdom, a great man, as endowed with these four qualities. If, Master Gotama, you approve, may Master Gotama approve of me; but if, Master Gotama, you disapprove, may Master Gotama disapprove of me."
translations.an4.35:6: He who knows the release from the snare of death for all beings; The welfare of devas and humans, he revealed the Dhamma according to the right method; Having seen and heard which, many people gain confidence.
translations.an4.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā. The brahmin Doṇa was also traveling along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā. The brahmin Doṇa saw on the Blessed One's footprints wheels with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in all respects; having seen this, it occurred to him: "It is wonderful, indeed, marvelous, indeed! Surely these are not the footprints of a human being!" Then the Blessed One, having left the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the brahmin Doṇa, following the Blessed One's footprints, saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a tree—graceful, inspiring confidence, with peaceful faculties and mind, attained to the ultimate taming and peace, controlled, guarded, restrained in his faculties, a nāga. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: "Will the venerable one be a deva?" "Brahmin, I will not be a deva." "Will the venerable one be a gandhabba?" "Brahmin, I will not be a gandhabba." "Will the venerable one be a yakkha?" "Brahmin, I will not be a yakkha." "Will the venerable one be a human?" "Brahmin, I will not be a human."
translations.an4.36:4: "Brahmin, those taints by which, if they were not abandoned, I would be a deva—those taints have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising. Those taints by which, if they were not abandoned, I would be a gandhabba … a yakkha … a human—those taints have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising. Just as, brahmin, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water, grown in the water, stands rising above the water, unsmeared by the water; so too, brahmin, I, born in the world, grown in the world, having overcome the world, dwell unsmeared by the world. Remember me, brahmin, as a Buddha."
translations.an4.37:1: "Monks, a monk endowed with four qualities is incapable of decline and is close to Nibbāna. With which four? Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, guards the doors of the sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, monks, is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains by undertaking the training rules. Thus, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue.
translations.an4.37:3: And how, monks, is a monk one with guarded sense doors? Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its sign or its details. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might overwhelm him, he practices restraint over it; he guards the faculty of the eye; he undertakes restraint of the faculty of the eye. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a tactile object with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its sign or its details. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the mind unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might overwhelm him, he practices restraint over it; he guards the faculty of the mind; he undertakes restraint of the faculty of the mind. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one with guarded sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating? Here, monks, a monk reflects wisely on the food he consumes: 'Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but simply for the support and maintenance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: 'Thus I shall destroy old feelings and not give rise to new ones, and I shall be healthy and blameless and dwell in comfort.' It is in this way, monks, that a monk is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness? Here, monks, during the day, a monk purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting; during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting; during the middle watch of the night, he lies down on the right side in the lion's posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, after noting in his mind the time for rising; during the last watch of the night, he rises and purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking and sitting. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is devoted to wakefulness. Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of decline and is close to Nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: A monk established in virtue, restrained in the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Dwelling thus, ardent, untiring day and night, developing wholesome qualities for the attainment of security from bondage.
translations.an4.38:1: "A monk, monks, who has abandoned individual truths, is called 'one who has laid aside his burden, with bodily formations calmed, withdrawn.' And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned individual truths? Here, monks, whatever individual truths are held by various ascetics and brahmins—such as: the world is eternal, or the world is not eternal; the world is finite, or the world is infinite; the soul is the same as the body, or the soul is one thing and the body another; a Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death, or both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death—all these have been abandoned, rejected, discarded, released, given up, relinquished. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has abandoned individual truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, monks, is a monk withdrawn? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the conceit 'I am,' cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is withdrawn. A monk, monks, who has abandoned individual truths, is called 'one who has laid aside his burden, with bodily formations calmed, withdrawn.'
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, the search for a holy life together with it—thus, the adherence to truth, the mass of speculative views.
translations.an4.38:6: For one detached from all lust, liberated through the destruction of craving, the search is relinquished, the mass of speculative views is uprooted.
translations.an4.52:1: "These four, monks, are streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha thus: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' This, monks, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.' This, monks, is the second stream of merit...
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha thus: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' This, monks, is the third stream of merit...
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with virtues that are dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. These, monks, are the four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:5: One whose faith in the Tathāgata is settled, rooted, and firm, and whose virtue is good, praised by the noble ones.
translations.an4.52:6: One who has faith in the Sangha, and whose view is upright, is said to be not poor; their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Also, a number of householders and their wives were traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Blessed One, having left the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The householders and their wives saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree. Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to those householders and their wives:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and generous, restrained, living righteously; they are husband and wife, speaking endearingly to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: Benefits abound for them, happiness arises; enemies are displeased, when both are virtuous.
translations.an4.53:2: "Householders, there are these four kinds of cohabitation. Which four? A wretch cohabits with a wretch, a wretch cohabits with a goddess, a god cohabits with a wretch, a god cohabits with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a wretch cohabit with a wretch? Here, householders, the husband is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, indulges in intoxicants that cause heedlessness; he is immoral, of bad character, with a mind obsessed and overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, he dwells at home abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. And his wife is also one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, indulges in intoxicants that cause heedlessness; she is immoral, of bad character, with a mind obsessed and overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, she dwells at home abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householders, a wretch cohabits with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, stingy, abusive; the wife is virtuous, generous, free from stinginess; she, a goddess, cohabits with a wretch as her husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous, free from stinginess; the wife is immoral, stingy, abusive; she, a wretch, cohabits with a god as her husband.
translations.an4.5:1: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person who is steadfast, and the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on firm ground as a brahmin. And what, monks, is the person who goes with the stream? Here, monks, some person indulges in sensual pleasures and does evil deeds. This is called, monks, the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, monks, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, monks, some person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do evil deeds, but with pain and dejection, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life fully and perfectly. This is called, monks, the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, monks, is the person who is steadfast? Here, monks, some person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously, there to attain final Nibbāna, without returning from that world. This is called, monks, the person who is steadfast.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, monks, is the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on firm ground as a brahmin? Here, monks, some person, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. This is called, monks, the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on firm ground as a brahmin. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."
translations.an4.5:5: Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free from lust, enjoying sensual pleasures here, repeatedly going to birth and old age, overcome by craving, go with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore, let the wise person, established in mindfulness here, not indulging in sensual pleasures and evil, even with pain, abandon sensual pleasures; that person is called one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: One who has abandoned the five defilements, a perfected learner, not subject to decline, attained to mastery of mind, with faculties composed, that man is said to be steadfast.
translations.an4.62:2: "Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness attainable by a householder enjoying sensual pleasures from time to time, when the opportunity arises. Which four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of wealth, the happiness of debtlessness, the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of ownership? Here, householder, a clansman has wealth acquired by his own effort and energy, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. He experiences happiness and joy, thinking, 'I have wealth acquired by my own effort and energy, amassed by the strength of my arms, earned by the sweat of my brow, righteous wealth righteously gained.' This is called, householder, the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of debtlessness? Here, householder, a clansman owes no debt, great or small, to anyone. He experiences happiness and joy, thinking, 'I owe no debt, great or small, to anyone.' This is called, householder, the happiness of debtlessness.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is possessed of blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, blameless mental action. He experiences happiness and joy, thinking, 'I am possessed of blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, blameless mental action.' This is called, householder, the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness attainable by a householder enjoying sensual pleasures from time to time, when the opportunity arises."
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of debtlessness, and then the happiness of ownership, a mortal enjoying the happiness of wealth, from that gains insight with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: "Monks, there are these five corruptions of gold, by which corrupted gold is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant but brittle and does not properly lend itself to work. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver. These, monks, are the five corruptions of gold, by which corrupted gold is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant but brittle and does not properly lend itself to work. But when, monks, gold is freed from these five corruptions, it becomes malleable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and properly lends itself to work. Whatever kind of ornament one wishes—whether a ring, an earring, a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves that purpose."
translations.an5.23:2: "Just so, monks, there are these five corruptions of the mind, by which corrupted mind is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant but brittle and is not properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These, monks, are the five corruptions of the mind, by which corrupted mind is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant but brittle and is not properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, monks, the mind is freed from these five corruptions, it becomes malleable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and is properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. To whatever state realizable by direct knowledge one directs the mind to realize by direct knowledge, one attains the ability to witness it in each and every case when there are suitable conditions."
translations.an5.23:3: "If he wishes: 'May I wield the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I travel through the sky cross-legged like a bird; with my hand may I touch and stroke the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; may I exercise bodily mastery as far as the Brahma-world'—he attains the ability to witness it in each and every case when there are suitable conditions."
translations.an5.23:4: "If he wishes: 'With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near'—he attains the ability to witness it in each and every case when there are suitable conditions."
translations.an5.23:5: "If he wishes: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with my mind: a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind; a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind'—he attains the ability to witness it in each and every case when there are suitable conditions."
translations.an5.25:1: "Monks, right view, supported by five factors, has liberation of mind as its fruit and benefit, and liberation by wisdom as its fruit and benefit."
translations.an5.26:1: "Monks, there are these five bases for liberation where, for a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the undestroyed taints come to destruction, and the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained."
translations.an5.26:3: "Again, monks, neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does a fellow monk in the position of a teacher, but he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it. As he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, he experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma. Experiencing both the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises in him. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure. Being pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the second basis for liberation where, for a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the undestroyed taints come to destruction, and the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained."
translations.an5.26:4: "Again, monks, neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does a fellow monk in the position of a teacher, nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, but he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it. As he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, he experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma. Experiencing both the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises in him. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure. Being pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the third basis for liberation where, for a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the undestroyed taints come to destruction, and the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained."
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk's teacher does not teach the Dhamma, nor does any respected fellow practitioner, nor does he explain the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, nor does he mentally examine, ponder, and reflect on the Dhamma as he has heard and learned it; but rather, a certain sign of concentration is well grasped, well attended to, well taken up, and well penetrated by wisdom. Monks, to the extent that a monk has a certain sign of concentration well grasped, well attended to, well taken up, and well penetrated by wisdom, to that extent he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma in that teaching. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the fifth basis for liberation, wherein for a monk who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, and the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained.
translations.an5.27:1: "Monks, develop immeasurable concentration, mindful and fully aware. Monks, for those who develop immeasurable concentration, mindful and fully aware, five knowledges arise personally. What five? 'This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in pleasantness in the future'—this knowledge arises personally; 'this concentration is noble and spiritual'—this knowledge arises personally; 'this concentration is not practiced by inferior people'—this knowledge arises personally; 'this concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained by tranquility, unified, not forced or restrained by formations'—this knowledge arises personally; 'mindful I enter this concentration, mindful I emerge from it'—this knowledge arises personally.
translations.an5.28:1: "Monks, I will teach the development of the noble right concentration with five factors. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, monks, on level ground at a crossroads, a thoroughbred chariot stands harnessed, with a goad ready. Then a skilled trainer, a horse tamer, mounts it, takes the reins with his left hand, takes the goad with his right hand, and drives it forward and back wherever he wishes. In the same way, monks, when a monk has thus developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with five factors, he directs his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes for the realization by direct knowledge; in each and every case, he is capable of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: 'With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, ... I may understand beings according to their deeds,' he is capable of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:7: When, monks, a monk has thus developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with five factors, he directs his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes for the realization by direct knowledge; in each and every case, he is capable of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:8: Just as, monks, a water pot placed on a stand, full of water up to the brim so a crow could drink, if a strong person were to tip it from any side, would water come out? "Yes, Venerable Sir." "In the same way, monks, when a monk has thus developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with five factors, he directs his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes for the realization by direct knowledge; in each and every case, he is capable of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:9: Just as, monks, on level ground, a lotus pond with embankments on four sides, full of water up to the brim so a crow could drink, if a strong person were to open the embankment from any side, would water come out? "Yes, Venerable Sir." "In the same way, monks, when a monk has thus developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with five factors, he directs his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes for the realization by direct knowledge; ... whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.2:1: "Monks, there are these five powers of a trainee. What five? The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple has faith, believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' This, monks, is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, monks, is the power of moral shame? Here, monks, a noble disciple has moral shame; he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he is ashamed of engaging in evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of moral shame.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, monks, is the power of moral dread? Here, monks, a noble disciple has moral dread; he dreads bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he dreads engaging in evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility of wholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was wandering among the Kosalans with a large community of monks when he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: "Indeed, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala; he is staying in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. And a good report about that venerable Gotama has spread: 'Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, a fully enlightened Buddha, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' He declares this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, having realized it by himself with direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a spiritual life that is entirely perfect and pure. It is good to see such arahants." Then, when the night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala, taking abundant food, both hard and soft, approached the Icchānaṅgala forest grove; having approached, they stood outside the entrance making a loud and noisy commotion.
translations.an5.30:3: "May the Blessed One now consent, venerable sir, may the Fortunate One consent; now is the time for the Blessed One's consent. Wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmin householders, both from town and countryside, will incline to go there. Just as, venerable sir, when rain falls in large drops, the waters flow according to the slope; in the same way, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmin householders, both from town and countryside, will incline to go there. For what reason? Because of the Blessed One's virtue and wisdom."
translations.an5.31:1: At one time ... at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, accompanied by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Princess Sumanā said to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: Similarly, one accomplished in virtue, a faithful individual; Outshines all the miserly in the world, through generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud thundering, adorned with lightning, with a hundred peaks; Fills the highlands and the lowlands, raining down on the earth.
translations.an5.31:12: Thus, one accomplished in vision, a disciple of the fully enlightened Buddha; Overcomes miserliness, in five respects, the wise one.
translations.an5.31:2: "Here, venerable sir, suppose the Blessed One has two disciples equal in faith, equal in virtue, equal in wisdom— one is a giver, one is not a giver. After death, after the breakup of the body, they might be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. But having become devas, venerable sir, would there be any distinction, any difference between them?"
translations.an5.31:3: "There could be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, having become a deva, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: in divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine authority. That giver, Sumanā, having become a deva, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:4: "But if, venerable sir, they fall from there and return to this state, having become humans, venerable sir, would there be any distinction, any difference between them?" "There could be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: in human lifespan, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, and human authority. That giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:5: "But if, venerable sir, both go forth from the household life into homelessness, having gone forth, venerable sir, would there be any distinction, any difference between them?" "There could be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said. "That giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in five respects: he often uses robes that are asked for, seldom without asking; he often uses almsfood that is asked for, seldom without asking; he often uses lodgings that are asked for, seldom without asking; he often uses medicines and requisites for the sick that are asked for, seldom without asking. And with those fellow monastics with whom he lives, they often engage with him in bodily actions that are pleasing, seldom displeasing; they often engage with him in verbal actions that are pleasing, seldom displeasing; they often engage with him in mental actions that are pleasing, seldom displeasing; they often offer him pleasing gifts, seldom displeasing. That giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:6: "But if, venerable sir, both attain arahantship, having attained arahantship, venerable sir, would there be any distinction, any difference between them?" "In this case, Sumanā, I say there is no difference whatsoever, that is, between one liberation and another."
translations.an5.31:9: "Just as the moon, stainless, moving through the sphere of the sky; Outshines all the hosts of stars in the world, with its radiance.
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the hall with the peaked roof. Then General Sīha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, General Sīha said to the Blessed One: "Is it possible, venerable sir, for the Blessed One to point out a visible fruit of giving?"
translations.an5.34:2: "It is possible, Sīha," the Blessed One said. "A giver, a donor, Sīha, is dear and pleasing to many people. That a giver, a donor, Sīha, is dear and pleasing to many people, this is a visible fruit of giving.
translations.an5.34:8: Giving, one becomes dear, many associate with him; He obtains renown and his fame increases; Without timidity, he enters an assembly, The person becomes confident, not miserly.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise give gifts, Having removed the stain of miserliness, desiring happiness; Established for a long time in the heaven of the Thirty-three, They rejoice, having attained the company of the gods.
translations.an5.36:1: "Monks, there are these five timely gifts. What five? One gives a gift to a visitor. One gives a gift to one setting out on a journey. One gives a gift to a sick person. One gives a gift during a famine. One first establishes offerings of the new crops and new fruits among the virtuous. These, monks, are the five timely gifts."
translations.an5.36:2: The wise, generous, free from stinginess, give at the proper time. What is given in due season to the noble ones, to those who are upright and such,
translations.an5.36:3: With a mind clear, the offering becomes vast. Those who rejoice there, or who perform service, are not deprived of that offering; they too share in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: "Monks, a donor giving food gives five things to the recipients. What five? He gives life, beauty, happiness, strength, and clarity of mind. Having given life, he partakes of life, divine or human. Having given beauty, he partakes of beauty, divine or human. Having given happiness, he partakes of happiness, divine or human. Having given strength, he partakes of strength, divine or human. Having given clarity of mind, he partakes of clarity of mind, divine or human. Monks, a donor giving food gives these five things to the recipients."
translations.an5.37:2: The wise giver of life, strength, beauty, and clarity of mind, the giver of happiness, attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as, monks, a great banyan tree growing on level ground at a crossroads is a refuge for birds all around; even so, monks, a faithful son of good family is a refuge for many people: monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers.
translations.an5.38:3: Laden with branches, leaves, and fruit, possessing a trunk, the great tree becomes a resting place for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In its delightful, spacious abode, the birds resort to it; those seeking shade go for shade, those seeking fruit go for fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: So too, a person endowed with virtue, faithful, of peaceful conduct, gentle, amiable, and soft,
translations.an5.38:6: Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, without taints—such a person in the world is a field of merit; people resort to him.
translations.an5.41:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park. Then the householder Anathapindika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the householder Anathapindika: "Householder, there are these five enjoyments of wealth. What five? Here, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, provides for his own pleasure and satisfaction, and properly maintains himself in pleasure; he provides for the pleasure and satisfaction of his mother and father, and properly maintains them in pleasure; he provides for the pleasure and satisfaction of his children, wife, slaves, servants, and workers, and properly maintains them in pleasure. This is the first enjoyment of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, makes the five offerings. Offerings to relatives, offerings to guests, offerings to the departed, offerings to the king, offerings to the deities—this is the fourth enjoyment of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, establishes an uplifting offering, of heavenly fruit, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, among those ascetics and brahmins who are restrained from intoxication and heedlessness, settled in patience and gentleness, taming themselves, calming themselves, and extinguishing themselves. This is the fifth enjoyment of wealth. These, householder, are the five enjoyments of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, while enjoying these five enjoyments of wealth, the wealth of that noble disciple diminishes, he thinks thus: 'I am enjoying the enjoyments of wealth, and my wealth is diminishing.' Thus he has no regret. If, householder, while enjoying these five enjoyments of wealth, the wealth of that noble disciple increases, he thinks thus: 'I am enjoying the enjoyments of wealth, and my wealth is increasing.' Thus he has no regret on both counts."
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth is enjoyed, dependents are supported, dangers are passed through; uplifting offerings are given, and the five offerings are made; virtuous ones, restrained, living the holy life, are supported.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose a wise person dwelling at home might desire wealth for, that purpose of mine is attained, and what is done brings no remorse.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anathapindika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the householder Anathapindika:
translations.an5.43:4: "It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires long life to pray for long life or to delight in it or to do anything for the sake of long life. A noble disciple who desires long life should practice the way that leads to long life. Practicing the way that leads to long life, he achieves the attainment of long life. He obtains long life, divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires beauty to pray for beauty or to delight in it or to do anything for the sake of beauty. A noble disciple who desires beauty should practice the way that leads to beauty. Practicing the way that leads to beauty, he achieves the attainment of beauty. He obtains beauty, divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple who desires happiness to pray for happiness or to delight in it or to do anything for the sake of happiness. A noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the way that leads to happiness. Practicing the way that leads to happiness, he achieves the attainment of happiness. He obtains happiness, divine or human."
translations.an5.43:7: Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should not beg for fame or delight in it, nor should they do so for the sake of fame. Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should practice the path that leads to fame. Practicing the path that leads to fame results in the attainment of fame. They obtain fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Life, beauty, fame, reputation, heaven, and high birth; one who desires these, one after another, excellent pleasures.
translations.an5.49:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallika had passed away. Then a certain man approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he whispered in the king's ear: 'Sire, Queen Mallika has passed away.' When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala, sorrowful and sad, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, sat brooding, unable to speak.
translations.an5.51:3: Indeed, bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles of the mind that weaken wisdom, with weak wisdom, would know his own good, the good of others, or the good of both, or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Suppose, bhikkhus, a river coming down from a mountain, flowing far, swift, carrying everything. A person would open channels on both banks. Thus, bhikkhus, the current in the middle of the river would be dispersed, spread out, scattered; it would not flow far, swiftly, or carry everything. In the same way, bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles of the mind that weaken wisdom, with weak wisdom, would know his own good, the good of others, or the good of both, or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain bhikkhu approached his own preceptor; having approached, he said to his preceptor: 'Now, venerable sir, my body feels as if it has been drugged, I have lost my bearings, the teachings do not appear to me, sloth and torpor overwhelm my mind, I lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and I have doubt about the teachings.'
translations.an5.56:3: 'That is how it is, bhikkhu, for one who does not guard the doors of the senses, who is not moderate in eating, who is not devoted to wakefulness, who does not examine wholesome qualities, who does not devote himself to the development of the factors of enlightenment in the earlier and later parts of the night: the body feels as if drugged, one loses one's bearings, the teachings do not appear, sloth and torpor overwhelm the mind, one leads the spiritual life dissatisfied, and one has doubt about the teachings. Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train thus: 'I will guard the doors of the senses, be moderate in eating, be devoted to wakefulness, examine wholesome qualities, and devote myself to the development of the factors of enlightenment in the earlier and later parts of the night.' That is how you should train.'
translations.an5.56:4: Then that bhikkhu, exhorted by the Blessed One with this exhortation, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side towards him, and departed. Then that bhikkhu, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—that unsurpassed goal of the holy life he realized for himself in this very life, having directly known and attained it. He understood: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to any state of being.' And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: 'It is not only I who am subject to separation from all that is dear and pleasing; but wherever there is coming and going, passing away and reappearing of beings, all beings are subject to separation from what is dear and pleasing.' By frequently reflecting on that fact, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, and makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are destroyed.
translations.an5.57:11: 'It is not only I who am the owner of my kamma, the heir of my kamma, born of my kamma, related to my kamma, and have my kamma as my refuge; whatever kamma I do, good or bad, I will be its heir. But wherever there is coming and going, passing away and reappearing of beings, all beings are the owners of their kamma, the heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, and have their kamma as their refuge; whatever kamma they do, good or bad, they will be its heirs.' By frequently reflecting on that fact, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, and makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are destroyed.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxication, seeing renunciation as safety; that was my exertion, aspiring for Nibbana.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple reflects thus: 'It is not only I who am subject to aging, not free from aging; but wherever there is coming and going, passing away and reappearing of beings, all beings are subject to aging, not free from aging.' By frequently reflecting on that fact, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, and makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are destroyed.
translations.an5.57:8: 'It is not only I who am subject to illness, not free from illness; but wherever there is coming and going, passing away and reappearing of beings, all beings are subject to illness, not free from illness.' By frequently reflecting on that fact, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, and makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are destroyed.
translations.an8.13:1: "Monks, a royal thoroughbred horse endowed with eight factors is worthy of a king, a possession of a king, and reckoned as a factor of a king. What eight? Here, monks, a royal thoroughbred horse is well-born on both sides—from the mother's side and from the father's side. He is born in a region where other thoroughbred horses are born. Whatever food they give him—wet or dry—he eats it carefully, without scattering it. He is disgusted to sit down or lie down on excrement or urine. He is gentle, pleasant to live with, and does not frighten other horses. Whatever deceptions, tricks, frauds, or deceits he has, he reveals them to the charioteer as they really are. The charioteer strives to eliminate them. He is a bearer. He arouses the thought: 'Whether the other horses pull or not, I will pull here.' When going, he goes by the straight path. He is strong, showing strength right up to the end of his life. Monks, a royal thoroughbred horse endowed with these eight factors is worthy of a king, a possession of a king, and reckoned as a factor of a king."
translations.an8.14:1: "And, monks, I will teach you the eight faults of a horse and the eight faults of a person. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: "And what, monks, are the eight faults of a horse? Here, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, steps backward and turns the chariot around from behind. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the first fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, leaps up from behind, strikes the yoke-pole, and breaks the triple rod. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the second fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, throws the thigh out from the chariot-pole and crushes the chariot-pole itself. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the third fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, takes a wrong path and turns the chariot over. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the fourth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, leaps up, lifting the fore-part of the body and raising the forelegs. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the fifth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, disregarding the charioteer, disregarding the goad, with his teeth he breaks the bit in his mouth and goes wherever he wants. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the sixth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, neither goes forward nor backward, but stands right there like a post. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the seventh fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, monks, a certain faulty horse, when told 'Go!' by the charioteer, being prodded and urged, draws in his forelegs and draws in his hindlegs and sits down right there on all four legs. Such, monks, is a certain faulty horse here. This, monks, is the eighth fault of a horse. These, monks, are the eight faults of a horse.
translations.an8.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā at the foot of Naḷeru's Nimba tree. Then Pahārāda, the lord of the Asuras, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Pahārāda, the lord of the Asuras, the Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.22:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you should remember Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma, as endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities." This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: "But if, venerable sir, I were to die before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me thus: 'There is no fetter by which Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma, being bound, would return to this world.' This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: "These, venerable sir, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities found in me. But I do not know: 'Endowed with which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities have I been declared by the Blessed One?'"
translations.an8.22:12: Then that monk, having received almsfood in the house of Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after his meal, on returning from his alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, approached the dwelling of the householder Ugga of Elephant Village; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the householder Ugga of Elephant Village approached that monk; having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Ugga of Elephant Village was addressed by that monk: "Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. What, householder, are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities with which you are endowed, as declared by the Blessed One?"
translations.an8.22:3: "Venerable sir, I do not know: 'With which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities I am declared by the Blessed One to be endowed.' However, venerable sir, listen to the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that are found in me, pay careful attention; I will speak." "Yes, householder," that monk replied to the householder Ugga of Elephant Village. The householder Ugga of Elephant Village said this: "Venerable sir, when I was attending in the elephant forest, I first saw the Blessed One from afar; at the very sight, venerable sir, my mind became clear, and intoxication was abandoned. This, venerable sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:4: Then, venerable sir, with a confident mind, I waited on the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a progressive talk, namely: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
