When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, soft, unobstructed, uplifted, and confident, then he explained the teaching of the Buddhas that is unique: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth free from stains would properly receive dye, so too, right there on that seat, the dust-free, stainless vision of the Dhamma arose in me: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.' Then, venerable sir, I, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, penetrated the Dhamma, crossed over doubt, gone beyond uncertainty, attained self-confidence, independent of others in the Teacher's dispensation, right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, and undertook the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:5: Venerable sir, I had four young wives. Then, venerable sir, I approached those wives; having approached, I said this to those wives: 'Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. Whichever of you wishes, let her enjoy the wealth here and make merit, or go to her own family. Or if there is a man you desire, to whom shall I give you?' When this was said, venerable sir, the eldest wife said to me: 'Give me, master, to such and such a man.' Then, venerable sir, I had that man summoned, and taking the wife with my left hand and the ceremonial bowl with my right hand, I presented her to that man. Venerable sir, while giving away a young wife, I do not recall any alteration of mind. This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:6: And, venerable sir, there are riches in my family. But they are shared with virtuous people of good qualities. This, venerable sir, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:7: And, venerable sir, when I wait on a monk, I wait on him respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This, venerable sir, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:8: And, venerable sir, it is not surprising that when the Sangha is invited, deities approach and announce: 'Householder, such and such a monk is liberated both ways, such and such one is wisdom-liberated, such and such one is a body-witness, such and such one is attained to view, such and such one is faith-liberated, such and such one is a Dhamma-follower, such and such one is a faith-follower, such and such one is virtuous with good qualities, such and such one is immoral with bad qualities.' And, venerable sir, while serving the Sangha, I do not recall generating such a thought: 'I will give a little to this one or a lot to that one.' Rather, venerable sir, I give with an equal mind. This, venerable sir, is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:9: And, venerable sir, it is not surprising that deities approach me and announce: 'Householder, well-proclaimed is the Dhamma by the Blessed One.' When this is said, venerable sir, I say this to those deities: 'Whether you deities say so or not, still the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.' And, venerable sir, I do not recall any elation of mind because of that: 'Deities approach me, or I converse with deities.' This, venerable sir, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.23:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava Shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. With which seven? Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of shame; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has moral dread; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise—with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities, monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed." This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, approached the dwelling of Hatthaka of Āḷavī; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that monk; having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Hatthaka of Āḷavī was addressed by that monk:
translations.an8.23:3: "Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One as possessing seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. Which seven? 'Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is endowed with faith; he is virtuous ... he has a sense of shame ... he has moral dread ... he is learned ... he is generous ... he is wise, monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī.' Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One as possessing these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities." "Venerable sir, were there no laypeople there wearing white?" "Friend, there were no laypeople there wearing white." "Good, venerable sir, that there were no laypeople there wearing white."
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having received almsfood at Hatthaka of Āḷavī's residence, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after his meal, having returned from his alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to Hatthaka of Āḷavī: "Hatthaka, this is a great assembly. How do you, Hatthaka, bring together this great assembly?" "Venerable sir, by these four bases of sympathy that have been taught by the Blessed One, I bring together this great assembly. Venerable sir, I know: 'This one should be brought together by giving,' and I bring him together by giving; I know: 'This one should be brought together by kind speech,' and I bring him together by kind speech; I know: 'This one should be brought together by beneficial conduct,' and I bring him together by beneficial conduct; I know: 'This one should be brought together by impartiality,' and I bring him together by impartiality. And, venerable sir, there are riches in my family. They do not think of listening to a poor man in the same way." "Good, good, Hatthaka. This is indeed the way, Hatthaka, to bring together a great assembly. For all those in the past who brought together a great assembly, all brought together a great assembly by these four bases of sympathy. All those in the future who will bring together a great assembly, all will bring together a great assembly by these four bases of sympathy. All those at present who bring together a great assembly, all bring together a great assembly by these four bases of sympathy."
translations.an8.26:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in Jīvaka's Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, to what extent is one a lay follower?" "Jīvaka, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; to that extent, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower."
translations.an8.26:2: "But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower virtuous?" "Jīvaka, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life ... abstains from intoxicants that cause heedlessness; to that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous."
translations.an8.26:3: "But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own welfare, not for the welfare of others?" "Jīvaka, when a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith, but does not encourage others to accomplish faith ... he himself understands the meaning and the Dhamma and practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. To that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for his own welfare, not for the welfare of others."
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, venerable sir, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed. And since, venerable sir, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed, this too, venerable sir, is a strength of a monk whose taints are destroyed, relying on which strength the monk whose taints are destroyed declares the destruction of the taints: 'Destroyed are my taints.'
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, venerable sir, the four bases of spiritual power have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed ... the five faculties have been developed and well-developed ... the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and well-developed ... the Noble Eightfold Path has been developed and well-developed. And since, venerable sir, the Noble Eightfold Path has been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed, this too, venerable sir, is a strength of a monk whose taints are destroyed, relying on which strength the monk whose taints are destroyed declares the destruction of the taints: 'Destroyed are my taints.'
translations.an8.2:1: "Monks, there are these eight causes, eight conditions that lead to the obtaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been obtained, and to its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment when it has been obtained. Which eight? Here, monks, a monk dwells in dependence on the Teacher or on a fellow monk who is a senior, in whom he has established keen respect and reverence, affection and esteem. This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition that leads to the obtaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been obtained, and to its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment when it has been obtained."
translations.an8.2:11: 'And this venerable one, having heard the Dhamma, withdraws into seclusion twofold: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind. Surely this venerable one knows and sees, knowing and seeing.' This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, concord, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: 'And this venerable one, when in the Saṅgha, does not engage in various kinds of talk, in low talk. He either speaks on the Dhamma himself or invites another to speak, or he maintains noble silence without despising it. Surely this venerable one knows and sees, knowing and seeing.' This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, concord, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: Living in dependence on that teacher or a fellow celibate who is worthy of respect, where strong shame and fear of wrongdoing are established, and there is affection and respect, from time to time they approach and ask questions: 'How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones reveal what is not revealed, clarify what is not clear, and dispel doubt regarding numerous doubtful points. This, bhikkhus, is the second cause, the second condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains by undertaking the training precepts. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth cause, the fourth condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, a bearer of the teachings, an accumulator of the teachings. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings are learned by him, borne in mind, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated by view. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth cause, the fifth condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:6: He dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking the burden of wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth cause, the sixth condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:7: When in the Saṅgha, he does not engage in various kinds of talk, nor in low talk. He either speaks on the Dhamma himself or requests another to speak, and he does not despise noble silence. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh cause, the seventh condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the cessation of feeling; such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.' This, bhikkhus, is the eighth cause, the eighth condition that leads to the acquisition of unattained wisdom pertaining to the higher life, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:9: His fellow celibates esteem him thus: 'This venerable one lives in dependence on the teacher or a fellow celibate who is worthy of respect, where strong shame and fear of wrongdoing are established, and there is affection and respect. Surely this venerable one knows what he knows and sees what he sees.' This quality also leads to affection, respect, development, concord, and unity.
translations.an8.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas on Suṁsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Forest, the deer park. Now at that time the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, the following thought arose in his mind: 'This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires; this Dhamma is for the contented, not for the discontented; this Dhamma is for the secluded, not for one who enjoys company; this Dhamma is for the energetic, not for the lazy; this Dhamma is for one with mindfulness established, not for the unmindful; this Dhamma is for the composed, not for the uncomposed; this Dhamma is for the wise, not for the unwise.'
translations.an8.30:10: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great person and will become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder's son there is a gabled house, plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with bolts fastened and shutters closed, so will your dwelling at the foot of a tree appear to you, dwelling contented, delighting without agitation, for a pleasant dwelling, for entering upon nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:11: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great person and will become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder's son there is a couch spread with rugs, blankets, and covers, with an excellent covering of antelope hide, with a canopy and red cushions at both ends, so will your bed of grass appear to you, dwelling contented, delighting without agitation, for a pleasant dwelling, for entering upon nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:12: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great person and will become one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder's son there are various medicines, that is: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, so will your medicine of putrid urine appear to you, dwelling contented, delighting without agitation, for a pleasant dwelling, for entering upon nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should dwell right here among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park for the coming rains residence as well.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having advised Venerable Anuruddha with this advice—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm—so he disappeared from among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park and reappeared in the Bhagga country, on Crocodile Hill, in the Deer Park at Bhesakalā's Grove. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, I will teach the eight thoughts of a great man. Listen... And what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This teaching, monks, is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires. This teaching is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This teaching is for one who is secluded, not for one who loves company. This teaching is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy. This teaching is for one with established mindfulness, not for one of muddled mindfulness. This teaching is for one who is composed, not for one who is not composed. This teaching is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise. This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in Venerable Anuruddha's mind—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm—so he disappeared from the Bhagga country, on Crocodile Hill, in the Deer Park at Bhesakalā's Grove, and reappeared in front of Venerable Anuruddha among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Venerable Anuruddha also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to Venerable Anuruddha:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha, having spent the next rains residence right there among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life—having realized it for himself with direct knowledge, he attained and dwelled in it. He understood: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the arahants. Then Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, on that occasion spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: 'Knowing my thought, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, came to me by means of a mind-made body, through psychic power.'
translations.an8.30:24: 'As I had thought, he taught further; the Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:3: 'Good, good, Anuruddha. It is good, Anuruddha, that you have thought this thought of a great man: "This teaching is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires. This teaching is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This teaching is for one who is secluded, not for one who loves company. This teaching is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy. This teaching is for one with established mindfulness, not for one of muddled mindfulness. This teaching is for one who is composed, not for one who is not composed. This teaching is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise." Well then, Anuruddha, think also this eighth thought of a great man: "This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation."'
translations.an8.30:4: 'When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as you wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, you will enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.'
translations.an8.30:5: 'When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as you wish, with the stilling of thought and examination, you will enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration.'
translations.an8.30:6: 'When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as you wish, with the fading away of rapture, you will dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, which the noble ones describe: "Equanimous, mindful, one dwells happily." You will enter and dwell in the third jhāna.'
translations.an8.30:7: 'When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as you wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, you will enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.'
translations.an8.39:1: 'Monks, there are these eight streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This, monks, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment for happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.'
translations.an8.39:2: 'Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. This, monks, is the second stream of merit... leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.'
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Sangha for refuge. This, monks, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourisher of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. Monks, these are the five great gifts, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, not to be adulterated, not disparaged by wise ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life. Monks, a noble disciple who abstains from the destruction of life gives fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression to immeasurable beings. Having given fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression to immeasurable beings, he partakes of immeasurable fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression. This, monks, is the first great gift, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, not to be adulterated, not disparaged by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourisher of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.39:7: Having abandoned the basis for heedlessness caused by liquor, wine, and intoxicants, he abstains from the basis for heedlessness caused by liquor, wine, and intoxicants. Monks, a noble disciple who abstains from the basis for heedlessness caused by liquor, wine, and intoxicants gives fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression to immeasurable beings. Having given fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression to immeasurable beings, he partakes of immeasurable fearlessness, non-enmity, and non-oppression. This, monks, is the fifth great gift, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, not to be adulterated, not disparaged by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the eighth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourisher of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.40:1: Monks, the destruction of life, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of the destruction of life for a human being is leading to a short life.
translations.an8.40:2: Monks, taking what is not given, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of taking what is not given for a human being is leading to loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Monks, sexual misconduct, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of sexual misconduct for a human being is leading to having enemies and rivals.
translations.an8.40:4: Monks, false speech, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of false speech for a human being is leading to being falsely accused.
translations.an8.40:5: Monks, divisive speech, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of divisive speech for a human being is leading to the breaking of friendships.
translations.an8.40:6: Monks, harsh speech, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of harsh speech for a human being is leading to unpleasant sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Monks, idle chatter, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of ghosts. The slightest result of idle chatter for a human being is leading to speech that is not accepted.
translations.an8.6:2: Monks, for an unlearned ordinary person, gain arises, loss arises, fame arises, disgrace arises, blame arises, praise arises, pleasure arises, and pain arises. For a learned noble disciple, too, gain arises, loss arises, fame arises, disgrace arises, blame arises, praise arises, pleasure arises, and pain arises. Here, monks, what is the distinction, the difference, the distinguishing factor between a learned noble disciple and an unlearned ordinary person? Our teachings, venerable sir, are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.
translations.an8.6:4: For him, gain obsesses the mind, loss obsesses the mind, fame obsesses the mind, disgrace obsesses the mind, blame obsesses the mind, praise obsesses the mind, pleasure obsesses the mind, and pain obsesses the mind. He welcomes arisen gain and resists arisen loss; he welcomes arisen fame and resists arisen disgrace; he welcomes arisen praise and resists arisen blame; he welcomes arisen pleasure and resists arisen pain. Being thus involved in welcoming and resisting, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain; these conditions among humans are impermanent, impermanent, subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing these, a mindful person of wisdom observes the changing nature; desirable things do not excite his mind, nor is he repelled by the undesirable.
translations.an8.7:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Mount Vulture Peak, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta: “It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own failings. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review the failings of others. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own successes. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review the successes of others. Devadatta, bhikkhus, overcome and mentally obsessed by eight bad qualities, is bound for the plane of misery, bound for hell, for an eon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.7:2: What eight? Overcome and mentally obsessed by gain, bhikkhus, Devadatta is bound for the plane of misery, bound for hell, for an eon, irredeemable. Overcome and mentally obsessed by loss … by fame … by disrepute … by honor … by dishonor … by evil desires … by bad friendship, bhikkhus, Devadatta is bound for the plane of misery, bound for hell, for an eon, irredeemable. These, bhikkhus, are the eight bad qualities overcome and mentally obsessed by which Devadatta is bound for the plane of misery, bound for hell, for an eon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to dwell overcoming again and again any arisen gain, any arisen loss … any arisen fame … any arisen disrepute … any arisen honor … any arisen dishonor … any arisen evil desire … any arisen bad friendship.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the devas, just as a strong man might bend or stretch his arm, so disappeared from among the Tāvatiṁsa devas and appeared in front of the Venerable Uttara on the Sankheyyaka mountain in Mahisavatthu, in the Vaṭajālika. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Venerable Uttara; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Uttara and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, venerable sir, that the Venerable Uttara teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus: ‘It is good, friends, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own failings; it is good, friends, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review the failings of others … his own successes … the successes of others’?” “Yes, lord of the devas.” “But, venerable sir, is this the Venerable Uttara’s own inspiration, or is it the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?” “Well then, lord of the devas, I will give you a simile. For by means of a simile some wise people here understand the meaning of what is said.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of the devas, there were a great heap of grain not far from a village or town. Then a great crowd of people would take grain from it—with baskets, bags, on their shoulders, and in their cupped hands. If someone, lord of the devas, were to approach that great crowd of people and ask: ‘From where are you taking this grain?’ how, lord of the devas, should that great crowd of people answer correctly?” “‘We are taking it from that great heap of grain,’ venerable sir, that great crowd of people would answer correctly.” “Just so, lord of the devas, whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Relying on that, we and others speak.”
translations.an8.8:7: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir, how well spoken this is by the Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Relying on that, we and others speak.’ On one occasion, venerable Uttara, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Mount Vulture Peak, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta:
translations.mn108:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:13: “There are, brahmin, ten inspiring qualities taught by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In whomsoever these qualities are found, him we now honor, respect, revere, and venerate; having honored and respected him, we live in dependence on him. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults, undertaking and training in the training precepts.
translations.mn108:15: He is learned, a bearer of the teachings, an accumulator of the teachings. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has learned much, retained, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view.
translations.mn108:17: He obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life.
translations.mn108:18: He wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels through space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so powerful and mighty; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near.
translations.mn108:2: Now on that occasion King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was having Rājagaha fortified, being apprehensive of King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with their own mind. They understand a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust'; a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust'; a mind with hate as 'a mind with hate'; a mind without hate as 'a mind without hate'; a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion'; a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion'; a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind'; a distracted mind as 'a distracted mind'; an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind'; an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind'; a surpassed mind as 'a surpassed mind'; an unsurpassed mind as 'an unsurpassed mind'; a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind'; an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind'; a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind'; an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind'.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, they enter upon and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring qualities declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In whom these qualities are found, him we now honor, respect, revere, and venerate; and having honored and respected him, we live in dependence on him.
translations.mn108:25: Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Venerable Ānanda: "And where, Venerable Ānanda, are you living now?" "I am living now in the Bamboo Grove, brahmin." "I hope, Venerable Ānanda, that the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for seclusion?" "Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for seclusion, as is fitting for such guardians and protectors as yourselves." "Indeed, Venerable Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of solitude, remote from people, suitable for seclusion, as is fitting for such meditators, devoted to meditation, as yourselves. For you, Venerable Sirs, are meditators, devoted to meditation. I recall, Venerable Ānanda, one occasion when that Blessed One Gotama was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then, Venerable Ānanda, I approached the Great Wood, the Hall with the Peaked Roof, and approached that Blessed One Gotama. And there that Blessed One Gotama spoke in many ways about meditation. That Blessed One Gotama was a meditator and devoted to meditation. And that Blessed One Gotama praised all meditation."
translations.mn108:28: "So, Venerable Ānanda, that Blessed One Gotama criticized blameworthy meditation and praised praiseworthy meditation. Well then, Venerable Ānanda, we must go now; we have much work, many duties." "Now is the time, brahmin, as you see fit." Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, having delighted in and rejoiced in the Venerable Ānanda's words, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "It is still too early to walk for alms in Rājagaha. Suppose I were to go to the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna's workplace, to where the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna is."
translations.mn108:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna's workplace, to where the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna was. The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna saw the Venerable Ānanda coming in the distance. Seeing him, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Venerable Ānanda. Welcome, Venerable Ānanda. It has been a long time since Venerable Ānanda found an opportunity to come here. Let Venerable Ānanda be seated; this seat is prepared." The Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna also took a low seat and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna said to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: "Is there, Venerable Ānanda, even one monk who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with all those qualities with which that Blessed One Gotama was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?" "There is not, brahmin, even one monk who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with all those qualities with which that Blessed One was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For, brahmin, the Blessed One was the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert on the path. And his disciples now dwell following that path and become possessed of it afterwards."
translations.mn108:7: "Is there, Venerable Ānanda, even one monk appointed by that Blessed Gotama thus: 'He will be your refuge after I am gone,' whom you now follow?" "There is not, brahmin, even one monk appointed by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One thus: 'He will be your refuge after I am gone,' whom we now follow."
translations.mn108:9: "But, Venerable Ānanda, being without a refuge, what is the cause for your harmony?" "We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; the Dhamma is our refuge."
translations.mn117:10: Here, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as 'wrong intention' and right intention as 'right intention': this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong intention? Intention of sensual pleasure, intention of ill will, intention of harming: this, bhikkhus, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, monks, is right intention? I say, monks, that right intention is twofold: there is, monks, right intention that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment; and there is, monks, right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, monks, is right intention that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-cruelty: this, monks, is right intention that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment.
translations.mn117:14: And what, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever thinking, pondering, intention, mental fixation, mental application, mental directing, verbal formation of one who has a noble mind, a taintless mind, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path—this, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: They strive to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention; this is their right effort. Mindfully they abandon wrong intention, mindfully they enter upon and abide in right intention; this is their right mindfulness. Thus these three states run and circle around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Herein, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong speech as wrong speech and right speech as right speech; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, monks, is right speech? I say, monks, that right speech is twofold: there is, monks, right speech that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment; and there is, monks, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, monks, is right speech that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter: this, monks, is right speech that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment.
translations.mn117:2: "Monks, I will teach you noble right concentration with its supports and requisites. Listen and attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The desisting, refraining, abstinence, avoidance of the four kinds of verbal misconduct by one who has a noble mind, a taintless mind, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path—this, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Herein, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong action as wrong action and right action as right action; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, monks, is right action? I say, monks, that right action is twofold: there is, monks, right action that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment; and there is, monks, right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, monks, is right action that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct: this, monks, is right action that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment.
translations.mn117:28: Herein, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood and right livelihood as right livelihood; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, monks, is wrong livelihood? Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain: this, monks, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, monks, is right livelihood? I say, monks, that right livelihood is twofold: there is, monks, right livelihood that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment; and there is, monks, right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, monks, is right livelihood that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood: this, monks, is right livelihood that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in attachment.
translations.mn117:34: Herein, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? For one with right view, monks, right intention arises; for one with right intention, right speech arises; for one with right speech, right action arises; for one with right action, right livelihood arises; for one with right livelihood, right effort arises; for one with right effort, right mindfulness arises; for one with right mindfulness, right concentration arises; for one with right concentration, right knowledge arises; for one with right knowledge, right liberation arises. Thus, monks, one endowed with eight factors is a trainee; one endowed with ten factors is an arahant. Herein too, by right knowledge many evil unwholesome states are abandoned and come to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:35: Herein, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? For one with right view, monks, wrong view is destroyed. And whatever evil unwholesome states arise dependent on wrong view, these too are destroyed. Dependent on right view, many wholesome states come to fulfillment by development. For one with right intention, monks, wrong intention is destroyed ... for one with right speech, monks, wrong speech is destroyed ... for one with right action, monks, wrong action is destroyed ... for one with right livelihood, monks, wrong livelihood is destroyed ... for one with right effort, monks, wrong effort is destroyed ... for one with right mindfulness, monks, wrong mindfulness is destroyed ... for one with right concentration, monks, wrong concentration is destroyed ... for one with right knowledge, monks, wrong knowledge is destroyed ... for one with right liberation, monks, wrong liberation is destroyed. And whatever evil unwholesome states arise dependent on wrong liberation, these too are destroyed. Dependent on right liberation, many wholesome states come to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:36: Thus, bhikkhus, there are twenty factors on the side of the wholesome and twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome. This exposition of the Dhamma on the Great Forty has been rolled forth, not to be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or by anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Here, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as wrong view and right view as right view: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong view? 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no spontaneously reborn beings; no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.' This, bhikkhus, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Right view, I say, is of two kinds, bhikkhus: there is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are spontaneously reborn beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.' This, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the right view as a path factor of one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path. This, bhikkhus, is called right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One makes an effort to abandon wrong view and to enter upon right view: this is one's right effort. Mindfully one abandons wrong view, mindfully one enters upon and abides in right view: this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three states run and circle around right view, that is, right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Palace of Migāra's Mother, together with many very well-known elder disciples—with the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, the Venerable Mahākappina, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Ānanda, and with other very well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Bhikkhus, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit. Bhikkhus, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. When the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven enlightenment factors. When the seven enlightenment factors are developed and cultivated, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he understands: 'I breathe in long'; or breathing out long, he understands: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he understands: 'I breathe in short'; or breathing out short, he understands: 'I breathe out short.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.'
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formation.'
translations.mn118:2: Now on that occasion the elder bhikkhus were advising and instructing the newly ordained bhikkhus. Some elder bhikkhus were advising and instructing ten bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were advising and instructing twenty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were advising and instructing thirty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were advising and instructing forty bhikkhus. And those newly ordained bhikkhus, being advised and instructed by the elder bhikkhus, came to know successive stages of distinction.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out gladdening the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in concentrating the mind'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in liberating the mind'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out liberating the mind.'
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating fading away'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out contemplating fading away.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating cessation'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out contemplating cessation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.'
translations.mn118:23: And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: At that time, monks, a monk breathing in long knows 'I breathe in long'; breathing out long knows 'I breathe out long'; breathing in short knows 'I breathe in short'; breathing out short knows 'I breathe out short'; he trains 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body'; he trains 'I will breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he trains 'I will breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Monks, I say that this is a certain body among the bodies, namely, in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:25: At that time, monks, a monk trains 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture'; he trains 'I will breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains 'I will breathe out experiencing pleasure'; he trains 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; he trains 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation'; he trains 'I will breathe in tranquilizing the mental formation'; he trains 'I will breathe out tranquilizing the mental formation'; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Monks, I say that this is a certain feeling among the feelings, namely, the careful attention to in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:26: At that time, monks, a monk trains 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe out gladdening the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe in concentrating the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe out concentrating the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe in liberating the mind'; he trains 'I will breathe out liberating the mind'; he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Monks, I do not say that there is mindfulness of breathing for one who is forgetful and not clearly comprehending. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:27: At that time, monks, a monk trains 'I will breathe in contemplating impermanence'; he trains 'I will breathe out contemplating impermanence'; he trains 'I will breathe in contemplating fading away'; he trains 'I will breathe out contemplating fading away'; he trains 'I will breathe in contemplating cessation'; he trains 'I will breathe out contemplating cessation'; he trains 'I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains 'I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment'; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, he closely looks on with equanimity. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:28: Thus developed, monks, mindfulness of breathing thus practiced fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: And how developed, monks, how practiced do the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: Now at that time the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the Sangha of monks on the fifteenth day, the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā. Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent Sangha of monks, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: At that time, monks, when a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, his mindfulness is established and unconfused. At that time, monks, when a monk's mindfulness is established and unconfused, the mindfulness enlightenment factor is aroused in him. At that time the monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor; the mindfulness enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in him.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that phenomenon, examines it, and makes a thorough inquiry. At that time, monks, when a monk dwelling thus mindful investigates that phenomenon, examines it, and makes a thorough inquiry, the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is aroused in him. At that time the monk develops the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor; the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in him.
translations.mn118:33: For one with aroused energy, non-sensual rapture arises. At that time, monks, when non-sensual rapture arises in a monk with aroused energy, the rapture enlightenment factor is aroused in him. At that time the monk develops the rapture enlightenment factor; the rapture enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in him.
translations.mn118:34: For one with rapture, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil. At that time, monks, when for a monk with rapture the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil, the tranquility enlightenment factor is aroused in him. At that time the monk develops the tranquility enlightenment factor; the tranquility enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in him.
translations.mn118:35: For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. At that time, monks, when for a monk whose body is tranquil and who is happy the mind becomes concentrated, the concentration enlightenment factor is aroused in him. At that time the monk develops the concentration enlightenment factor; the concentration enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in him.
translations.mn118:36: He closely observes that well-concentrated mind. At that time, monks, when a monk closely observes that well-concentrated mind, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused in that monk at that time; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity at that time; the enlightenment factor of equanimity comes to fulfillment by development in that monk.
translations.mn118:4: "I have entered upon this path, monks; my mind is intent upon this path. Therefore, monks, arouse even more energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized. I will remain right here in Savatthi for the Komudi full moon of the fourth month."
translations.mn118:40: Thus developed, monks, thus frequently practiced, the four foundations of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.mn118:41: And how developed, monks, how frequently practiced, do the seven factors of enlightenment fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those senior monks instruct and advise the new monks even more. Some senior monks instruct and advise ten monks, some senior monks instruct and advise twenty monks, some senior monks instruct and advise thirty monks, some senior monks instruct and advise forty monks. And those new monks, being instructed and advised by the senior monks, know a supreme distinction between what came before and what came after.
translations.mn118:9: There are, monks, in this community of monks, arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—such monks, too, are present in this community of monks.
translations.mn11:13: In such a Dhamma and Discipline, monks, confidence in the Teacher is said to be not rightly directed; confidence in the Dhamma is said to be not rightly directed; fulfillment in virtues is said to be not rightly directed; affection for companions in the holy life is said to be not rightly directed. For what reason? Because, monks, it is a Dhamma and Discipline poorly proclaimed, poorly expounded, not emancipating, not conducive to peace, proclaimed by one not fully enlightened.
translations.mn11:14: But the Tathagata, monks, an arahant, fully enlightened, claiming to teach the full understanding of all clinging, rightly proclaims the full understanding of all clinging—he proclaims the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures, proclaims the full understanding of clinging to views, proclaims the full understanding of clinging to rules and observances, proclaims the full understanding of clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn11:15: In such a Dhamma and Discipline, monks, confidence in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed; confidence in the Dhamma is said to be rightly directed; fulfillment in virtues is said to be rightly directed; affection for companions in the holy life is said to be rightly directed. For what reason? Because, monks, it is a Dhamma and Discipline well proclaimed, well expounded, emancipating, conducive to peace, proclaimed by one fully enlightened.
translations.mn11:2: "Here only, monks, is there a recluse; here a second recluse; here a third recluse; here a fourth recluse. The doctrines of others are empty of recluses." Thus, monks, you should rightly roar your lion's roar.
translations.mn11:6: There are these two views, monks: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, are attached to the view of existence, have adopted the view of existence, have embraced the view of existence, they are opposed to the view of non-existence. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, are attached to the view of non-existence, have adopted the view of non-existence, have embraced the view of non-existence, they are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape from these two views, they are with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with craving, with clinging, unwise, adherents, opponents, delighting in and devoted to proliferation; they are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; they are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn11:9: There are these four kinds of clinging, monks. What four? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesali in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sariputta, the Tathagata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. And because the Tathagata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, this too is a Tathagata's power of the Tathagata on account of which he claims the place of the chief, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of Brahma.
translations.mn12:19: Again, Sariputta, with the destruction of the taints, the Tathagata has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it. And because the Tathagata, with the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it, this too is a Tathagata's power of the Tathagata on account of which he claims the place of the chief, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of Brahma.
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, had recently left this Dhamma and Discipline. He was speaking thus in the Vesali assembly: "The ascetic Gotama does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him, and when he teaches the Dhamma to anyone, it leads him when he practices it to the complete destruction of suffering."
translations.mn12:20: These, Sariputta, are the ten Tathagata's powers of the Tathagata. Possessing these powers, the Tathagata claims the place of the chief, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of Brahma.
translations.mn12:22: There are these four kinds of self-confidence of the Tathagata, Sariputta. Possessing these kinds of self-confidence, the Tathagata claims the place of the chief, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of Brahma. What four?
translations.mn12:23: 'You claim to be fully enlightened, but these things have not been fully understood by you.' In that case, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightfully refute me. Not seeing such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:24: 'You claim to be one with taints destroyed, but these taints have not been fully destroyed by you.' In that case, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightfully refute me. Not seeing such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:25: 'Those things that are said to be obstructive, when practiced, are not sufficient to cause obstruction.' In that case, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightfully refute me. Not seeing such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:26: 'The purpose for which the Dhamma is taught, that does not lead one who practices accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.' In that case, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightfully refute me. Not seeing such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:32: There are, Sāriputta, these four modes of generation. What four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of an eggshell—this is called, Sāriputta, egg-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of a membrane—this is called, Sāriputta, womb-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born in rotten fish or in a rotten corpse or in rotten dough or in a cesspool or in a sewer—this is called, Sāriputta, moisture-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? Gods, hell-beings, some human beings, and some beings in the lower worlds—this is called, Sāriputta, spontaneous generation. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of generation.
translations.mn12:35: There are, Sāriputta, these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, human beings, and gods.
translations.mn12:36: And I understand, Sāriputta, hell, and the path leading to hell, and the way of practice leading to hell; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. And I understand, Sāriputta, the animal realm, and the path leading to the animal realm, and the way of practice leading to the animal realm; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in the animal realm. And I understand, Sāriputta, the realm of ghosts, and the path leading to the realm of ghosts, and the way of practice leading to the realm of ghosts; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in the realm of ghosts. And I understand, Sāriputta, human beings, and the path leading to the human world, and the way of practice leading to the human world; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappears among human beings. And I understand, Sāriputta, gods, and the path leading to the heavenly world, and the way of practice leading to the heavenly world; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. And I understand, Sāriputta, Nibbāna, and the path leading to Nibbāna, and the way of practice leading to Nibbāna; and I understand how one who practices accordingly, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn12:4: For Sunakkhatta, Sāriputta, is an angry man, a worthless man. And this speech of his was spoken out of anger. Intending to speak dispraise, Sāriputta, Sunakkhatta, that worthless man, actually spoke praise of the Tathāgata. For this, Sāriputta, is praise of the Tathāgata when one says: 'The purpose for which the Dhamma is taught, that leads one who practices accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.'
translations.mn12:43: Whoever, Sāriputta, knowing me thus, seeing me thus, would say: 'The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him'—without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, Sāriputta, he is as if deposited in hell. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might here and now realize final knowledge; even so, Sāriputta, do I say that without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is as if deposited in hell.
translations.mn12:44: I recall, Sāriputta, having lived a spiritual life possessing four factors: I was an austere ascetic, the utmost austere ascetic; I was a coarse ascetic, the utmost coarse ascetic; I was a scrupulous ascetic, the utmost scrupulous ascetic; I was a secluded ascetic, the utmost secluded ascetic.
translations.mn12:46: In that connection, Sāriputta, this was my coarseness: the dust and dirt accumulated on my body over many years became like a bark crust. Just as, Sāriputta, a tinduka stump accumulates a bark crust over many years, even so, Sāriputta, the dust and dirt accumulated on my body over many years became like a bark crust. It never occurred to me, Sāriputta: 'Oh, let me rub off this dust and dirt with my hand, or let others rub off this dust and dirt with their hands.' Such a thing never occurred to me. This, Sāriputta, was my coarseness.
translations.mn12:47: In that connection, Sāriputta, this was my scrupulousness: mindful, I would step forward; mindful, I would step back. Compassion was established in me even towards a drop of water: 'May I not harm the tiny creatures in the wrong place.' This, Sāriputta, was my scrupulousness.
translations.mn12:49: So, Sariputta, I approached the cow pens where the cows were tethered and the cowherds had left, and there I ate the cow dung of the calves, the young, and the suckling calves. And, Sariputta, as long as my own urine and feces were not yet putrid, I ate my own urine and feces. This, Sariputta, was my great and terrible food.
translations.mn12:5: For indeed, Sariputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have the right view of me: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.'
translations.mn12:50: So, Sariputta, I entered and dwelt in a terrifying forest grove. And there, Sariputta, in that terrifying forest grove, it was so terrifying that anyone with lingering desire who entered that forest grove would have their hair stand on end. And, Sariputta, on those nights that were cold in the winter, during the snow-fall, I dwelt in the open air by night and in the forest grove by day; in the last month of the hot season, I dwelt in the open air by day and in the forest grove by night. And then, Sariputta, this unprecedented verse occurred to me, never heard before: 'Scorched and frozen, alone in the terrifying forest; naked, not sitting by a fire, the sage intent on his quest.'
translations.mn12:51: So, Sariputta, I made my bed in a charnel ground, using bones as a pillow. And then, Sariputta, village boys would come up to me and spit on me, urinate on me, throw dirt on me, and poke sticks in my ears. But, Sariputta, I do not recall that I ever aroused an evil mind towards them. This, Sariputta, was my dwelling in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: 'Purity comes through food.' They say: 'Let us live on jujube fruits.' They eat jujube fruits, jujube fruit powder, drink jujube water—they consume various preparations of jujube. I recall, Sariputta, having taken only a single jujube fruit as food. You might think, Sariputta: 'Surely the jujube fruit at that time was large.' But, Sariputta, it should not be seen thus. At that time too, the jujube fruit was just as it is now. And, Sariputta, as I took only a single jujube fruit as food, my body reached an extreme state of emaciation. Just like the joints of a bamboo or a reed, so were my limbs because of that little food. Just like a camel's hoof, so was my seat because of that little food. Just like a string of beads, so was my spine, protruding and sunken because of that little food. Just like the rafters of an old house, so were my ribs, loose and dangling because of that little food. Just like the reflection of stars in a deep well, so were my eyes, sunk deep in their sockets because of that little food. Just like a bitter gourd cut while still raw and shriveled by wind and sun, so was the skin of my head, shriveled and withered because of that little food. So, Sariputta, when I thought: 'I will touch the skin of my belly,' I actually grasped my spine; when I thought: 'I will touch my spine,' I actually grasped the skin of my belly—so much, Sariputta, had the skin of my belly clung to my spine because of that little food. So, Sariputta, when I thought: 'I will defecate or urinate,' I would fall face down right there because of that little food. So, Sariputta, to relieve my body, I would massage my limbs with my hand. And, Sariputta, as I massaged my limbs with my hand, the rotten roots of my hair fell from my body because of that little food.
translations.mn12:56: But, Sariputta, by that conduct, by that practice, by that severe austerity, I did not attain any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why is that? Because I had not attained that noble wisdom which, when attained, is noble and leads to emancipation, and leads one who practices rightly to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: 'Purity comes through transmigration.' But, Sariputta, there is no realm of transmigration that I have not transmigrated through in this long course, except for the pure abodes. And if I were to transmigrate among the pure abode gods, Sariputta, I would not return to this world.
