translations.mn12:6: For indeed, Sariputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have the right view of me: 'Indeed, the Blessed One wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though in water; he walks on water without sinking as though on earth; he travels cross-legged in the sky like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma-world.'
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: 'Purity comes through sacrifice.' But, Sariputta, there is no sacrifice that I have not offered in this long course, whether by a king, an anointed khattiya, or a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: 'Purity comes through fire-worship.' But, Sariputta, there is no fire that I have not worshipped in this long course, whether by a king, an anointed khattiya, or a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus: 'As long as this worthy person is young, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the prime of youth, in the first stage of life, so long is he endowed with the highest wisdom. But when this worthy person is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, having reached the last stage, being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, then he declines from that highest wisdom.' But, Sāriputta, this should not be seen in that way. I, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, having reached the last stage; my years have turned eighty. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples with a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, endowed with the highest mindfulness, alertness, resolution, and the highest wisdom. Just as, Sāriputta, a skilled archer, trained, dexterous, practiced, could easily shoot a light arrow through the shadow of a palm tree, so are they endowed with supreme mindfulness, supreme alertness, supreme resolution, and supreme wisdom. They would question me again and again on the four foundations of mindfulness, and being questioned, I would answer them, and they would remember what was answered, and they would not ask me a second question further. Except for the time spent eating, drinking, consuming, tasting, except for the time spent attending to the calls of nature, except for the time spent sleeping to dispel fatigue, the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata's words and phrases of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata's readiness in answering questions would not be exhausted. Then those four disciples of mine with a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, would die at the end of a hundred years. Even if you were to carry me around on a bed, Sāriputta, there would be no change in the Tathāgata's wisdom.
translations.mn12:7: For this too, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not find any conformity with the Dhamma in me: 'Indeed, the Blessed One, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near.'
translations.mn12:8: For this too, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not find any conformity with the Dhamma in me: 'Indeed, the Blessed One understands the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind. He understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust. He understands a mind with hate as a mind with hate; a mind without hate as a mind without hate. He understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion. He understands a contracted mind as a contracted mind; a distracted mind as a distracted mind. He understands an exalted mind as an exalted mind; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind. He understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind. He understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind. He understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.'
translations.mn12:9: There are, Sāriputta, these ten Tathāgata's powers that the Tathāgata has, possessing which he claims the place of the chief bull, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of Brahma. What are the ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is not a giver to ascetics or brahmins: of food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, scents, and unguents; bedding, lodging, and lighting. Having performed and undertaken such kamma, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. If they do not reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell, but instead return to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are poor. This is the way, young man, that leads to poverty, namely, not being a giver to ascetics or brahmins: of food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, scents, and unguents; bedding, lodging, and lighting.
translations.mn135:2: Then the young man Subha, Todeyya's son, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the young man Subha, Todeyya's son, said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their kamma, young man, heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, supported by their kamma. Kamma divides beings, that is, into inferior and superior.
translations.mn135:3: "What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why among human beings, who are themselves human, inferiority and superiority are seen? For, Master Gotama, human beings are seen to be short-lived and long-lived; sickly and healthy; ugly and beautiful; uninfluential and influential; poor and wealthy; low-born and high-born; foolish and wise. What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why among human beings, who are themselves human, inferiority and superiority are seen?"
translations.mn135:4: "Beings are owners of their kamma, young man, heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, supported by their kamma. Kamma divides beings, that is, into inferior and superiority." "I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken by Master Gotama in brief without detailed explanation. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief without detailed explanation." "Then, young man, listen and attend closely; I will speak." "Yes, sir," the young man Subha, Todeyya's son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: "Here, student, some woman or man is one who kills living beings, is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. Due to that action, thus undertaken, thus performed, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. If, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of misery... but instead come to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This, student, is the course of conduct that leads to short life, namely: being one who kills living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings."
translations.mn135:6: "But here, student, some woman or man, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious, compassionate, they dwell sympathetic for the welfare of all living beings. Due to that action, thus undertaken, thus performed, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. If, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a happy destination... but instead come to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This, student, is the course of conduct that leads to long life, namely: having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstaining from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious, compassionate, dwelling sympathetic for the welfare of all living beings."
translations.mn13:10: "If, bhikkhus, for that clansman thus striving and exerting himself, wealth comes to him. He experiences pain and grief in protecting those possessions: 'How shall neither kings take my wealth, nor thieves take it, nor fire burn it, nor water carry it away, nor unloved heirs take it?' And while he is thus guarding and protecting, kings take his wealth, or thieves take it, or fire burns it, or water carries it away, or unloved heirs take it. He sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps beating his breast and becomes distraught, thinking: 'What I had, I have no longer.' This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason."
translations.mn13:11: "Again, bhikkhus, having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; mother quarrels with child, child with mother; father quarrels with child, child with father; brother quarrels with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother; friend quarrels with friend. And when they have fallen into quarrels, disputes, and arguments, they attack each other with fists, clods, sticks, or knives. There they meet death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason."
translations.mn13:12: "Again, bhikkhus, having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason, taking up sword and shield, buckling on bow and quiver, they charge into battle massed on both sides, with arrows and spears flying, with swords flashing. There they are pierced with arrows and spears, and their heads are cut off with swords. There they meet death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason."
translations.mn13:13: "Again, bhikkhus, having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason, taking up sword and shield, buckling on bow and quiver, they charge against slippery bastions, with arrows and spears flying, with swords flashing. There they are pierced with arrows and spears, they are splashed with boiling dung, they are crushed under heavy weights, and their heads are cut off with swords. There they meet death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason."
translations.mn13:15: "Again, bhikkhus, having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason, they engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures pertaining to the future life, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, sensual pleasures as the reason."
translations.mn13:16: "And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from sensual pleasures? It is the removal of desire and lust for sensual pleasures, the abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures. This is the escape from sensual pleasures."
translations.mn13:17: "Those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, who do not understand as it really is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, cannot themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, he will fully understand sensual pleasures—such a thing is impossible. But those ascetics or brahmins who understand as it really is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, can themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, he will fully understand sensual pleasures—such a thing is possible."
translations.mn13:18: "And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in forms? Suppose, bhikkhus, there is a maiden of the noble class, or a brahmin class, or a householder class, fifteen or sixteen years old, not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair—is she not at that time at the height of her beauty and loveliness? 'Yes, venerable sir.' The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on that beauty and loveliness—this is the gratification in forms."
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the danger in forms? Here, monks, one might see that same sister at another time, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, crooked as a rafter, bent, leaning on a staff, tottering, frail, youth gone, with broken teeth, gray hair, scanty, bald, wrinkled, with limbs all blotchy. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty and complexion vanished, and the danger become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then, in the morning, a number of monks dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Savatthi for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is too early to walk for alms in Savatthi; let us go to the park of the wanderers of other sects.' Then those monks went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects; having exchanged courteous and friendly conversation, they sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to those monks:
translations.mn13:20: Again, monks, one might see that same sister afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own excrement and urine, being lifted up by others, being laid down by others. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty and complexion vanished, and the danger become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Again, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh, smeared with blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews; bones disconnected, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth, here a skull. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty and complexion vanished, and the danger become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:29: Again, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown in a charnel ground—bones white, resembling sea-shells; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones rotted, crumbled to dust. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty and complexion vanished, and the danger become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:3: "Friend, the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures, and we too teach the full understanding of sensual pleasures; the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of forms, and we too teach the full understanding of forms; the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of feelings, and we too teach the full understanding of feelings; so, friend, what is the distinction, the difference, the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, in teaching the Dhamma or in instruction?"
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from forms? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for forms—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the gratification in feelings? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. At that time, monks, a monk does not intend for his own affliction, or for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both; he feels a feeling that is pleasant and free from affliction. I say, monks, that the highest gratification in feelings is freedom from affliction.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the danger in feelings? That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither approved nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects; without approving or rejecting, they rose from their seats and left, thinking: 'We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: "Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be spoken to thus: 'But, friends, what is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, what is the escape?' When asked thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects will not be able to reply, and will furthermore fall into distress. Why is that? Because, monks, that is outside their domain. I do not see, monks, anyone in this world with its gods, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathagata or a disciple of the Tathagata, or one who has heard it from here."
translations.mn13:8: And what, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, monks, a clansman makes a living by some craft—whether by accounting, calculation, farming, trade, cattle-herding, archery, royal service, or some other craft—exposed to cold and heat, suffering from the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, dying from hunger and thirst. This, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures, visible in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:9: If, monks, that clansman, striving and exerting himself in this way, does not acquire wealth, he grieves, sorrows, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught, thinking: 'My striving is in vain, my effort is fruitless!' This too, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures, visible in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and eventually arrived at Rājagaha; he went to the potter Bhaggava and said to him:
translations.mn140:12: 'He should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate relinquishment, and should train for peace'—so it is said. With reference to what is this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, monk, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to, such as head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to—this is called, monk, the internal earth element. Both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, monk, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to, such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to—this is called, monk, the internal water element. Both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and detaches the mind from the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to, such as that by which one is warmed, ages, and is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted is properly digested, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to—this is called, monk, the internal fire element. Both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and detaches the mind from the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to, such as up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to—this is called, monk, the internal air element. Both the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal space element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, and clung-to, such as the ear-hole, the nostrils, the mouth-opening, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted is swallowed, where it is stored, and by which it is excreted below, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, a cavity, hollow, and not contacted by flesh and blood, and clung-to—this is called, monk, the internal space element. Both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and detaches the mind from the space element.
translations.mn140:2: "If it is not inconvenient for you, Bhaggava, I would like to stay in your dwelling for one night." "It is not inconvenient for me, venerable sir. But there is a monk who has already taken up residence here. If he gives permission, you may stay, venerable sir, as you wish."
translations.mn140:20: Then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant. Just as, monk, a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice would prepare a furnace, prepare the furnace and clean the crucible, clean the crucible and take gold with tongs and put it in the crucible, from time to time he would blow on it, from time to time he would sprinkle water on it, from time to time he would just watch it, that gold becomes well-purified, well-refined, flawless, rid of dross, malleable, wieldy, and radiant, and whatever kind of ornament he wishes—whether a belt, or an earring, or a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves that purpose; just so, monk, then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: 'It is impermanent'; he understands: 'It is not clung to'; he understands: 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: 'It is impermanent'; he understands: 'It is not clung to'; he understands: 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: 'It is impermanent'; he understands: 'It is not clung to'; he understands: 'It is not delighted in.'
translations.mn140:29: 'He should not neglect wisdom, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace'—this is what was said. With reference to this it was said.
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness out of devotion to the Blessed One. He had taken up residence first in that potter's shed. Then the Blessed One approached where Venerable Pukkusāti was; having approached, he said to Venerable Pukkusāti: "If it is not inconvenient for you, monk, we will dwell in the shed for one night." "The potter's shed is spacious, friend. Let the venerable one dwell as he likes."
translations.mn140:30: 'Where the streams of conceiving do not flow, and when the streams of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—this is what was said. With reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: 'I am,' monk, this is a conceiving; 'I am this,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall not be,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be with form,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be formless,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be percipient,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be non-percipient,' this is a conceiving; 'I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,' this is a conceiving. Conceiving, monk, is a disease, conceiving is a tumor, conceiving is a dart. By overcoming all conceivings, monk, one is called a sage at peace. And the sage, monk, being at peace, is not born, does not age, does not die, is not agitated, and does not yearn. For him, monk, there is nothing by which he might be born; not being born, how could he age? Not aging, how could he die? Not dying, how could he be agitated? Not being agitated, for what would he yearn?
translations.mn140:32: 'Where the streams of conceiving do not flow, and when the streams of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—this is what was said. With reference to this it was said. You should remember this exposition of the six elements in brief from me, monk."
translations.mn140:33: Then Venerable Pukkusāti thought: "My Teacher has indeed come, the Fortunate One has indeed come, the Fully Enlightened One has indeed come." Rising from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: "I have transgressed, venerable sir, I have erred in that I was foolish, confused, and unskillful, in that I thought I should address the Blessed One as 'friend.' May the Blessed One forgive my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint." "Indeed, monk, you transgressed, you erred in that you were foolish, confused, and unskillful, in that you thought you should address me as 'friend.' But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends as is proper, we forgive you. For it is growth in the Noble One's discipline when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends as is proper, and undertakes restraint for the future."
translations.mn140:34: "May I receive the full admission, venerable sir, in the Blessed One's presence?" "But is your bowl and robe complete, monk?" "My bowl and robe are not complete, venerable sir." "The Tathāgatas do not give full admission to one whose bowl and robe are not complete."
translations.mn140:35: Then Venerable Pukkusāti, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side towards him, and set out to search for a bowl and robe. Then while Venerable Pukkusāti was searching for a bowl and robe, a stray cow deprived him of life.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter's shed, prepared a spread of grass on one side, sat down cross-legged, set his body straight, and established mindfulness in front of him. Then the Blessed One spent most of the night sitting. Venerable Pukkusāti also spent most of the night sitting. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "This clansman conducts himself in an inspiring way. Suppose I were to question him." Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: "Under whom, monk, have you gone forth? Or who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you profess?" "There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, gone forth from a Sakyan family. Concerning that Blessed One Gotama, such a glorious report has spread: 'Indeed, that Blessed One is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' I have gone forth out of devotion to that Blessed One. That Blessed One is my teacher. And I profess the Dhamma of that Blessed One." "But where, monk, does that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, now reside?" "There is, friend, in the northern countries a city called Sāvatthī. There that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, now resides." "But have you ever seen that Blessed One before? And having seen him, would you recognize him?" "I have never seen that Blessed One before, friend; and having seen him, I would not recognize him."
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'This clansman has gone forth on account of me. Suppose I were to teach him the Dhamma.' Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: 'I will teach you the Dhamma, bhikkhu. Listen and attend closely; I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: 'This person, bhikkhu, consists of six elements, six bases of contact, and eighteen mental examinations, and has four determinations. Where these stand, the streams of conceiving do not flow. When the streams of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace. One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate relinquishment, and should train for peace.' This is the synopsis of the analysis of the elements.
translations.mn146:12: 'Sisters, this simile was made by me to convey the meaning. This is the meaning: 'the inner mass of flesh' is a designation for the six internal sense bases; 'the outer hide' is a designation for the six external sense bases; 'the inner sinews, inner tendons, inner bindings' is a designation for delight and lust; 'the sharp butcher's knife' is a designation for noble wisdom; that noble wisdom cuts, severs, and sunders the inner defilements, fetters, and bonds.
translations.mn146:13: Sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment, which when developed and cultivated, lead to a bhikkhu dwelling having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom. What seven? Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and matures in relinquishment. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena ... energy ... rapture ... tranquility ... concentration ... equanimity, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and matures in relinquishment. These, sisters, are the seven factors of enlightenment, which when developed and cultivated, lead to a bhikkhu dwelling having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having advised those bhikkhunīs with this advice, dismissed them: 'Go, sisters; it is time.' Then those bhikkhunīs, having delighted and rejoiced in Venerable Nandaka's words, rose from their seats, paid homage to him, circumambulated him, and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhunīs: 'Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.' Then those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed.
translations.mn146:3: Now on that occasion the senior bhikkhus were advising the bhikkhunīs in turn. Venerable Nandaka did not wish to advise the bhikkhunīs in turn. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, whose turn is it today to advise the bhikkhunīs in turn?' 'Venerable sir, all have taken their turn to advise the bhikkhunīs. Venerable sir, this Venerable Nandaka does not wish to advise the bhikkhunīs in turn.'
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Nandaka: 'Advise, Nandaka, the bhikkhunīs; instruct, Nandaka, the bhikkhunīs; give, brahmin, a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhunīs.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Then in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he went to the royal park accompanied by a companion. Those bhikkhunīs saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he washed his feet. Those bhikkhunīs paid homage to Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Nandaka said to those bhikkhunīs:
translations.mn146:5: 'Sisters, there will be a question-and-answer talk. There, those who know should say: 'We know,' and those who do not know should say: 'We do not know.' And if anyone has doubt or perplexity, she should question me about it: 'How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?'' 'Venerable sir, we are pleased and satisfied with Venerable Nandaka even to this extent, that he invites us to ask.'
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'The qualities that ripen in liberation have ripened in Rāhula. Suppose I were to lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints.' Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: 'Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Blind Men's Grove for the day's abiding.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One. Taking his sitting cloth, he followed close behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities followed the Blessed One, thinking: "Today the Blessed One will lead Venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints." Then the Blessed One, having entered the Dark Forest, sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of a tree. Venerable Rāhula, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Venerable Rāhula: "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir." "Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir." "Is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.mn148:16: And this, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the origin of identity: one regards the eye thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'
translations.mn148:2: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal a holy life that is entirely perfect and pure, that is, the six sextets. Listen to it, attend carefully, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: And this, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of identity: one regards the eye thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.mn148:3: "The six internal sense bases should be known, the six external sense bases should be known, the six classes of consciousness should be known, the six classes of contact should be known, the six classes of feeling should be known, the six classes of craving should be known.
translations.mn148:34: Bhikkhus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When one is touched by a pleasant feeling, if one does not delight in it, welcome it, or remain holding to it, then the underlying tendency to lust does not lie within one. When touched by a painful feeling, if one does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat one's breast, or become distraught, then the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie within one. When touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands as it really is the origin and passing away, the gratification, danger, and escape in regard to that feeling. Then the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie within one. Bhikkhus, it is possible that by abandoning the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling, by removing the underlying tendency to aversion for painful feeling, by uprooting the underlying tendency to ignorance for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, by abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, one here and now makes an end of suffering."
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with craving.
translations.mn149:11: "And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge? 'The five aggregates subject to clinging' is the answer. That is: form as an aggregate subject to clinging, feeling as an aggregate subject to clinging, perception as an aggregate subject to clinging, volitional formations as an aggregate subject to clinging, consciousness as an aggregate subject to clinging. These things should be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence. These things should be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight. These things should be developed by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be realized by direct knowledge? True knowledge and liberation. These things should be realized by direct knowledge."
translations.mn149:2: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Great Six Sense-base discourse. Listen to it, attend carefully, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: "Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, not knowing and not seeing whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it really is, one is infatuated with the eye, infatuated with forms, infatuated with eye-consciousness, infatuated with eye-contact, infatuated with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For one who lives thus, infatuated, attached, confused, contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging in the future increase. One's craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting in this and that, increases. One's bodily troubles increase, one's mental troubles increase; one's bodily torments increase, one's mental torments increase; one's bodily fevers increase, one's mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering."
translations.mn149:8: For one who lives thus, infatuated, attached, confused, contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging in the future increase. One's craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting in this and that, increases. One's bodily troubles increase, one's mental troubles increase; one's bodily torments increase, one's mental torments increase; one's bodily fevers increase, one's mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: Monks, knowing and seeing the eye as it really is, knowing and seeing forms as they really are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it really is, and knowing and seeing whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it really is, one is not infatuated with the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For one who dwells thus, not infatuated, unattached, unconfused, contemplating danger, the five aggregates subject to clinging in the future undergo diminution. And that craving which is repetitive, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there—that is abandoned. For him, bodily disturbances are abandoned, mental disturbances are abandoned; bodily torments are abandoned, mental torments are abandoned; bodily fevers are abandoned, mental fevers are abandoned. He experiences bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks upon and ponders, that will become the inclination of his mind. If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of renunciation, he abandons thoughts of sensuality, makes thoughts of renunciation abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation. If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of non-ill will... If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of non-cruelty, he abandons thoughts of cruelty, makes thoughts of non-cruelty abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of non-cruelty.
translations.mn19:12: Monks, just as in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been gathered into the village, a cowherd would guard the cows; while resting at the foot of a tree or in the open, he simply needs to be mindful: 'These are the cows.' In the same way, monks, I simply needed to be mindful: 'These are phenomena.'
translations.mn19:13: And my energy, monks, was aroused and unremitting; my mindfulness was established and unconfused; my body was tranquil and undisturbed; my mind was concentrated and unified.
translations.mn19:14: Then, monks, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This, monks, was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Monks, suppose in a forest wilderness there is a great low-lying marsh. A great herd of deer would dwell dependent on it. Then a certain person might appear who desires their harm, injury, and bondage. He would close off the safe, good, delightful path, open up a wrong path, set up a decoy and a dummy. Then, monks, that great herd of deer would in time come to calamity and disaster. But then, monks, a certain person might appear who desires their welfare, benefit, and safety. He would open up the safe, good, delightful path, close off the wrong path, remove the decoy and destroy the dummy. Then, monks, that great herd of deer would in time come to growth, increase, and abundance.
translations.mn19:26: Monks, this simile was made by me to convey the meaning. And this is the meaning: 'The great low-lying marsh' is a term for sensual pleasures. 'The great herd of deer' is a term for beings. 'The person who desires harm, injury, and bondage' is a term for Māra the Evil One. 'The wrong path' is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. 'The decoy' is a term for delight and lust. 'The dummy' is a term for ignorance. 'The person who desires welfare, benefit, and safety' is a term for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'The safe, good, delightful path' is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, monks, I have opened up the safe, good, delightful path, closed off the wrong path, removed the decoy, and destroyed the dummy.
translations.mn19:3: Monks, while I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of sensuality arose in me. I understood thus: 'This thought of sensuality has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to others' affliction, and to the affliction of both; it is destructive of wisdom, conducive to vexation, and does not lead to Nibbāna.' As I reflected, 'It leads to my own affliction,' it subsided. As I reflected, 'It leads to others' affliction,' it subsided. As I reflected, 'It leads to the affliction of both,' it subsided. As I reflected, 'It is destructive of wisdom, conducive to vexation, and does not lead to Nibbāna,' it subsided. Thus, monks, I abandoned, dispelled, and eliminated each arisen thought of sensuality.
translations.mn19:6: Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks upon and ponders, that will become the inclination of his mind. If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of sensuality, he abandons thoughts of renunciation, makes thoughts of sensuality abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of sensuality. If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of ill will... If he frequently thinks upon and ponders thoughts of cruelty, he abandons thoughts of non-cruelty, makes thoughts of cruelty abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of cruelty.
translations.mn19:7: Just as, monks, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the crops are thick, a cowherd would guard his cows. He would strike and drive them back with a stick here and there, restrain and confine them. For what reason? He sees that if he does not, it could lead to killing, imprisonment, a fine, or blame. Even so, monks, I saw the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation, the aspect of purification in wholesome states.
translations.mn19:8: As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute, monks, a thought of renunciation arose in me. I understood thus: 'This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It does not lead to affliction of self, affliction of others, or affliction of both; it is wisdom-fostering, not troublesome, leading to Nibbāna.' If I were to think and ponder upon it night after night, day after day, or night and day, I see no danger from that cause. However, if I were to think and ponder upon it too long, my body would become tired. When the body is tired, the mind becomes disturbed. When the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. Therefore, monks, I steadied my mind internally, composed it, unified it, and concentrated it. For what reason? 'So that my mind may not be disturbed.'
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the root of a Sal tree. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: They perceive Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, they conceive Brahmā, conceive in Brahmā, conceive from Brahmā, conceive 'Brahmā is mine,' they delight in Brahmā. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the Radiant Gods as the Radiant Gods; having perceived the Radiant Gods as the Radiant Gods, they conceive the Radiant Gods, conceive in the Radiant Gods, conceive from the Radiant Gods, conceive 'the Radiant Gods are mine,' they delight in the Radiant Gods. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:123: And that monk, monks, who is an Arahant, with taints destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of being, completely liberated through final knowledge— he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, does not conceive in earth, does not conceive from earth, does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. For what reason? Because, with the destruction of delusion, he is free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the Gods of Great Fruit as the Gods of Great Fruit; having perceived the Gods of Great Fruit as the Gods of Great Fruit, they conceive the Gods of Great Fruit, conceive in the Gods of Great Fruit, conceive from the Gods of Great Fruit, conceive 'the Gods of Great Fruit are mine,' they delight in the Gods of Great Fruit. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Conqueror as the Conqueror; having perceived the Conqueror as the Conqueror, they conceive the Conqueror, conceive in the Conqueror, conceive from the Conqueror, conceive 'the Conqueror is mine,' they delight in the Conqueror. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:147: The Tathāgata too, monks, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, does not conceive in earth, does not conceive from earth, does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. For what reason? I say it is because it is fully understood by the Tathāgata.
translations.mn1:171: The Tathāgata too, monks, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, does not conceive in earth, does not conceive from earth, does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. For what reason? Having understood that 'delight is the root of suffering,' and that 'from being there is birth, for one who has been born there is aging and death.' Therefore, monks, I say: 'The Tathāgata, through the destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment of all cravings, has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.'
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as the seen; having perceived the seen as the seen, they conceive the seen, conceive in the seen, conceive from the seen, conceive 'the seen is mine,' they delight in the seen. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:2: "I will teach you, monks, the exposition of the root of all phenomena. Listen to it, attend carefully, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as the heard; having perceived the heard as the heard, they conceive the heard, conceive in the heard, conceive from the heard, conceive 'the heard is mine,' they delight in the heard. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the cognized as the cognized; having perceived the cognized as the cognized, they conceive the cognized, conceive in the cognized, conceive from the cognized, conceive 'the cognized is mine,' they delight in the cognized. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:23: They perceive unity as unity; having perceived unity as unity, they conceive unity, conceive in unity, conceive from unity, conceive 'unity is mine,' they delight in unity. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive diversity, conceive in diversity, conceive from diversity, conceive 'diversity is mine,' they delight in diversity. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:25: They perceive the all as the all; having perceived the all as the all, they conceive the all, conceive in the all, conceive from the all, conceive 'the all is mine,' they delight in the all. For what reason? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:27: And that monk, monks, who is a trainee, who has not attained his mind's goal, dwelling aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage— he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he should not conceive earth, should not conceive in earth, should not conceive from earth, should not conceive 'earth is mine,' he should not delight in earth. For what reason? I say it is because it should be fully understood.
translations.mn1:3: Here, monks, an unlearned ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma, untrained in the noble Dhamma; who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of good persons—perceives earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth, he conceives in earth, he conceives from earth, he conceives 'earth is mine,' he delights in earth. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water. Having perceived water as water, he conceives water, he conceives in water, he conceives from water, he conceives 'water is mine,' he delights in water. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, he conceives fire, he conceives in fire, he conceives from fire, he conceives 'fire is mine,' he delights in fire. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:51: And that monk, monks, who is an arahant with taints destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine,' he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because, I say, it is fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives beings as beings. Having perceived beings as beings, he conceives beings, he conceives in beings, he conceives from beings, he conceives 'beings are mine,' he delights in beings. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives gods as gods. Having perceived gods as gods, he conceives gods, he conceives in gods, he conceives from gods, he conceives 'gods are mine,' he delights in gods. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives Pajāpati as Pajāpati. Having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, he conceives Pajāpati, he conceives in Pajāpati, he conceives from Pajāpati, he conceives 'Pajāpati is mine,' he delights in Pajāpati. Why is that? Because, I say, it is not fully understood by him.
translations.mn20:2: Monks, a monk who is devoted to higher mind should from time to time attend to five signs. What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, monks, if you understand the meaning of what I have said, remember it accordingly. But if you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, then you should question me about it further, or those monks who are wise.
translations.mn22:14: Monks, I have taught the Dhamma with the simile of the raft, for crossing over, not for holding onto. Understanding this, you should even let go of Dhammas, how much more so non-Dhammas.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Could there be agitation, venerable sir, when there is no external [possession]?" "There could be, monks," the Blessed One said. "Here, monks, someone thinks thus: 'I had it, but I do not have it; I might have it, but I do not obtain it.' He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. Thus, monks, there is agitation when there is no external [possession]."
translations.mn22:19: "But could there be non-agitation, venerable sir, when there is no external [possession]?" "There could be, monks," the Blessed One said. "Here, monks, someone does not think thus: 'I had it, but I do not have it; I might have it, but I do not obtain it.' He does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or become distraught. Thus, monks, there is non-agitation when there is no external [possession]."
translations.mn22:20: "Could there be agitation, venerable sir, when there is no internal [self]?" "There could be, monks," the Blessed One said. "Here, monks, someone holds such a view: 'This world is self, I will be after death, permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will stand like this for ever and ever.' He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all standpoints, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies regarding all views, for the calming of all formations, for the relinquishing of all acquisitions, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. He thinks thus: 'I will be annihilated, I will perish, I will be no more.' He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. Thus, monks, there is agitation when there is no internal [self]."
translations.mn22:23: "Monks, would you grasp at a doctrine of self, such that by grasping at that doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise? Do you see, monks, any doctrine of self such that by grasping at that doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?" "No, venerable sir." "Good, monks. I too do not see any doctrine of self such that by grasping at that doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise."
translations.mn22:24: "Monks, would you rely on a view as a basis, such that by relying on that view as a basis, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise? Do you see, monks, any view as a basis such that by relying on that view as a basis, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?" "No, venerable sir." "Good, monks. I too do not see any view as a basis such that by relying on that view as a basis, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise."
translations.mn22:25: "Monks, if there were a self, would there be 'what belongs to self'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "If there were what belongs to self, would there be 'my self'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, since self and what belongs to self are not found as true and established, then this standpoint for views: 'This world is self, I will be after death, permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will stand like this for ever and ever'—isn't this, monks, a completely foolish doctrine?" "What else could it be, venerable sir? It is indeed, venerable sir, a completely foolish doctrine."
translations.mn22:27: Therefore, monks, whatever form—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling… Whatever perception… Whatever volitional formations… Whatever consciousness—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; in liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: This is called, monks, a monk who has lifted the crossbar, filled in the moat, pulled up the pillar, unfastened the bolt; a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered.
translations.mn22:31: And how, monks, is a monk one who has lifted the crossbar? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has lifted the crossbar.
translations.mn22:32: And how, monks, is a monk one who has filled in the moat? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the round of rebirths leading to renewed existence, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has filled in the moat.
translations.mn22:33: And how, monks, is a monk one who has pulled up the pillar? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has pulled up the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how, monks, is a monk one who has unfastened the bolt? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the five lower fetters, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no more subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has unfastened the bolt.
translations.mn22:35: And how, monks, is a monk a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the conceit ‘I am,’ cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. Thus, monks, a monk is a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered.
translations.mn22:38: If, monks, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata for that, the Tathāgata has no joy, no delight, no elation of mind. If, monks, others do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata for that, the Tathāgata has no sorrow, no regret, no mental displeasure. If, monks, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata for that, the Tathāgata thinks: ‘They perform such actions toward what was already fully understood before.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, monks, if others abuse, revile, scold, or harass you, for that you should not harbor resentment, displeasure, or mental animosity. Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate you, for that you should not feel joy, delight, or elation of mind. Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate you, for that you should think: ‘They perform such actions toward what was already fully understood before.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, monks, abandon what is not yours. Having abandoned it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed. In this Dhamma, well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed, those monks who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—for them there is no round to be described.
translations.mn22:43: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed. In this Dhamma, well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed, those monks who have abandoned the five lower fetters are all spontaneously reborn [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without returning from that world.
translations.mn22:44: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed. In this Dhamma, well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed, those monks who have abandoned three fetters and have weakened lust, hatred, and delusion are all once-returners, who will come back to this world only once and then make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed. In this Dhamma, well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed, those monks who have abandoned three fetters are all stream-enterers, no longer subject to [rebirth in] the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.
translations.mn22:46: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed. In this Dhamma, well proclaimed by me, made clear, revealed, unveiled, with the patchwork removed, those monks who are Dhamma-followers or faith-followers are all headed for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: "Foolish man, to whom do you think I taught such a doctrine? Have I not, foolish man, in many ways spoken of obstructive things as obstructive? And yet for you, indulging in them, they are obstructive. I have said that sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, of much suffering, of much despair, and that the danger in them is greater. I have said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton... like a piece of meat... like a grass torch... like a pit of coals... like a dream... like borrowed goods... like fruits on a tree... like a butcher's knife and block... like a stake... like a snake's head, of much suffering, of much despair, and that the danger in them is greater. And yet you, foolish man, by your own wrong grasp, misrepresent us, harm yourself, and produce much demerit. That, foolish man, will be for your long-lasting harm and suffering."
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "What do you think, monks, has this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, ever kindled even a spark in this Dhamma-Vinaya?" "How could that be, venerable sir? It is not so, venerable sir." When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to respond. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, was silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to respond, said to him: "You will be known, foolish man, by this evil view of yours. Here I will question the monks."
translations.mn22:9: Indeed, monks, that one would indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual desires, apart from perceptions of sensuality, apart from thoughts of sensuality—this is not possible.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, do you call a thing of sorrow? Wives and children, monks, are a thing of sorrow; male and female slaves are a thing of sorrow; goats and sheep are a thing of sorrow; fowl and pigs are a thing of sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are a thing of sorrow. These, monks, are acquisitions that are things of sorrow. Here, one who is tied, infatuated, and attached, being oneself a thing of sorrow, seeks only what is a thing of sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, do you call a thing of defilement? Wives and children, monks, are a thing of defilement; male and female slaves are a thing of defilement; goats and sheep are a thing of defilement; fowl and pigs are a thing of defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are a thing of defilement; gold and silver are a thing of defilement. These, monks, are acquisitions that are things of defilement. Here, one who is tied, infatuated, and attached, being oneself a thing of defilement, seeks only what is a thing of defilement. This, monks, is ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: I too, monks, before my enlightenment, while still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, being myself subject to birth, sought only what is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, sought only what is subject to aging; being myself subject to illness, sought only what is subject to illness; being myself subject to death, sought only what is subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, sought only what is subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, sought only what is subject to defilement. Then, monks, it occurred to me: 'Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek only what is subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging... illness... death... sorrow... being myself subject to defilement, do I seek only what is subject to defilement? What if I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seek the unborn, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna? Being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seek the unaging, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna? Being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, seek the unailing, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna? Being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, seek the deathless, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna? Being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, seek the sorrowless, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna? Being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seek the undefiled, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna?'
translations.mn26:14: Then, monks, at a later time, while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my parents wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: I, monks, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, wandering by stages in the Magadhan country, eventually arrived at Uruvelā, the army town. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a lovely woodland grove, and a river flowing clear with pleasant fords, delightful, and with villages all around for alms. Then, monks, it occurred to me: 'Indeed, this is a delightful stretch of land, a lovely woodland grove, the river flows clear with pleasant fords, delightful, and there are villages all around for alms. This is suitable for a clansman who is intent on striving.' So, monks, I sat down right there, thinking: 'This is suitable for striving.'
translations.mn26:21: Then, monks, having understood Brahma's request and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and difficult to teach, some living seeing the danger in blame and the next world, some not living seeing the danger in blame and the next world. Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or a pond of red lotuses, or a pond of white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged in the water, thriving underwater; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand at an even level with the water; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, standing unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and difficult to teach, some living seeing the danger in blame and the next world, some not living seeing the danger in blame and the next world. Then, monks, I replied to Brahma Sahampati in verse: 'Open are the doors to the Deathless, let those with ears release faith. Perceiving trouble, I did not speak the refined Dhamma among humans, O Brahma.' Then, monks, Brahma Sahampati, thinking, 'The Blessed One has given me the opportunity for teaching the Dhamma,' paid homage to me, circumambulated me, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Then, monks, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw me traveling along the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said: 'Your faculties, friend, are clear, the color of your skin is pure and bright. Under whom, friend, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?' When this was said, monks, I replied to the Ājīvaka Upaka in verses: 'I am the all-conqueror, the all-knower, unstained among all things. I have abandoned all, freed in the destruction of craving. Having known directly, whom should I point to? I have no teacher; one like me does not exist. In the world with its gods, I have no counterpart. For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher; I alone am fully enlightened, cooled, extinguished. To set rolling the wheel of Dhamma, I go to the city of Kāsi. In this world that has become blind, I beat the drum of the Deathless.' 'According to your claim, friend, you ought to be the infinite victor.' 'Like me are the victors who have attained the destruction of the taints. I have conquered evil states, therefore, Upaka, I am a victor.' When this was said, monks, the Ājīvaka Upaka said, 'May it be so, friend,' shook his head, took a wrong path, and left.
translations.mn26:26: Then, monks, traveling gradually, I approached the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi where the group of five monks were. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they agreed among themselves: 'Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming, one who lives luxuriously, who strayed from the struggle, who reverted to luxury. He is not to be greeted, not to be stood up for; his bowl and robe are not to be received. But a seat may be prepared; if he wishes, he may sit down.' However, monks, as I approached, the group of five monks were unable to maintain their agreement. Some came to meet me and received my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some set out water for washing the feet. Still, they addressed me by name and as 'friend.'
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, monks, I said to the group of five monks: 'Do you recall, monks, that I have spoken like this before?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'I am the Arahant, monks, the Tathāgata, fully enlightened. Give ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon realize for yourselves, in this very life, and enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.'
translations.mn26:29: I was able, monks, to convince the group of five monks. I would instruct two monks, while three monks went for alms. What the three monks brought back from almsround would sustain the six of us. Then I would instruct three monks, while two monks went for alms. What the two monks brought back from almsround would sustain the six of us.
