translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, the group of five monks, being thus instructed and taught by me, themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; themselves subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seeking the unaging supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the unaging supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; themselves subject to illness... themselves subject to death... themselves subject to sorrow... themselves subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. And the knowledge and vision arose in them: 'Our liberation is unshakable; this is our last birth; now there is no renewed existence.'
translations.mn26:31: Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing; sounds cognizable by the ear ... smells cognizable by the nose ... tastes cognizable by the tongue ... touches cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn26:34: Monks, suppose a jungle deer wandering in a jungle forest walks, stands, sits, and lies down confidently. Why is that? Because it has not gone into the range of the hunter. In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, made him sightless, gone beyond Māra's range, and become invisible to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:35: Again, monks, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:36: Again, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body. He enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:37: Again, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:38: Again, monks, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking: 'Infinite is space.' This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:39: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking: 'Infinite is consciousness.' This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. At that time, several monks were sitting together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka engaged in Dhamma discussion. Then the Blessed One stood outside the door waiting for the discussion to end. Knowing the discussion had ended, he cleared his throat and knocked on the door. The monks opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'What discussion were you sitting together for just now, monks? And what discussion was left unfinished?' 'Venerable sir, our Dhamma discussion concerning the Blessed One was left unfinished, and then the Blessed One arrived.' 'Good, monks. It is fitting for you clansmen who have gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness to sit together for Dhamma discussion. When you have gathered, monks, you should do one of two things: engage in Dhamma discussion or maintain noble silence.'
translations.mn26:40: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, a monk enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, thinking: 'There is nothing.' This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:41: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, a monk enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, monks, is called ... the Evil One.
translations.mn26:5: Monks, there are these two quests: the noble quest and the ignoble quest. And what, monks, is the ignoble quest? Here, monks, someone who is subject to birth seeks what is also subject to birth; who is subject to aging seeks what is also subject to aging; who is subject to illness seeks what is also subject to illness; who is subject to death seeks what is also subject to death; who is subject to sorrow seeks what is also subject to sorrow; who is subject to defilement seeks what is also subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, monks, do you say is subject to birth? Wives and children, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; fowl and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These acquisitions are subject to birth. And this person, attached, infatuated, committed, being himself subject to birth, seeks what is also subject to birth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder or a householder's son or one born in some family hears that Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, he reflects thus: 'Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.' Then, after some time, having abandoned a small or large fortune, having abandoned a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the ochre robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth in this way, he, undertaking the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, abstains from killing living beings; he has laid aside the rod and the sword, is conscientious, full of compassion, and dwells with kindness and sympathy for the welfare of all living beings. He abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with honesty and purity of heart. He abstains from sexual misconduct; he lives a celibate life, living apart, abstaining from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse. He abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, reliable, trustworthy, and not a deceiver of the world. He abstains from malicious speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here to cause division, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere to cause division. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of friendships; he delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. He abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, loving, going to the heart, courteous, agreeable, and pleasing to many. He abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks on the good, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; his speech is like a treasure, uttered at the right time, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal. He abstains from injuring seeds and plants. He eats only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and outside the proper time. He abstains from dancing, singing, music, and watching shows. He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying himself with cosmetics. He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting male and female slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting fowl and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and lands. He abstains from going on errands and running messages. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from dealing with false weights, false metals, and false measures. He abstains from bribery, deception, fraud, and crooked practices. He abstains from mutilating, executing, imprisoning, robbery, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to satisfy his stomach. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden, so too, the bhikkhu is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to satisfy his stomach. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him. Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the bliss of blamelessness.
translations.mn27:15: On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he were to dwell without restraint over the faculty of the eye, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him, he practices restraint, guards the faculty of the eye, and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye. On hearing a sound with the ear... On smelling an odor with the nose... On tasting a flavor with the tongue... On touching a tangible with the body... On cognizing a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he were to dwell without restraint over the faculty of the mind, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him, he practices restraint, guards the faculty of the mind, and achieves restraint over the faculty of the mind. Possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an unblemished bliss.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when flexing and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, consuming food, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, possessing this noble contentment, possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, and possessing this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded dwelling: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: After his meal, returning from his alms round, he sits down, crosses his legs, holds his body erect, and establishes mindfulness in front of him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells undisturbed, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, unperplexed about wholesome qualities; he purifies his mind from doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, something followed by the Tathāgata, something delighted in by the Tathāgata. Yet even at this point, the noble disciple has not yet come to the definite conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out of Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares. He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming in the distance. Seeing him, he said to the wanderer Pilotika: 'So, Master Vacchāyana, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?' 'Just now, sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.' 'What does Master Vacchāyana think of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and discernment? He seems to me to be wise.' 'Who am I, sir, to know the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and discernment? One would have to be like him to know his wisdom and discernment.' 'Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with high praise indeed.' 'Who am I, sir, to praise the ascetic Gotama? He is praised by the praiseworthy, the best of gods and humans.' 'But for what reason does Master Vacchāyana have such confidence in the ascetic Gotama?'
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This too is called, brahmin... 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' This too is called, brahmin... 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This too is called, brahmin, the footprint of the Tathāgata, frequented by the Tathāgata, delighted in by the Tathāgata. Yet a noble disciple does not yet come to the definite conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:3: 'Just as, sir, a skilled elephant-tracker might enter an elephant wood and see there a large elephant's footprint, long in length and broad in width. He would come to the conclusion: 'Indeed, this is a large bull elephant.' In the same way, sir, when I saw four footprints in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:4: What four? Here, sir, I see some learned nobles who are subtle, skilled in debating, like hair-splitting marksmen, who wander about, as it were, shattering the views of others with their wisdom. They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama will come to such and such a village or town.' They formulate a question: 'We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers thus when asked, we will refute his doctrine thus. And if he answers thus when asked, we will refute his doctrine thus.' They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama has come to such and such a village or town.' They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. Having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question, so how could they refute his doctrine? Indeed, they become the ascetic Gotama's disciples. When, sir, I saw this first footprint in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: 'The simile of the elephant's footprint is not yet complete in detail to that extent, brahmin. But listen, brahmin, to how the simile of the elephant's footprint is complete in detail. Pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friend,' those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friend, while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in that monk, he is stirred by that, feels a sense of urgency: 'It is truly a loss for me, not a gain; ill-gotten for me, not well-gotten, that while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in me.' Just as, friend, a daughter-in-law, upon seeing her father-in-law, is stirred, feels a sense of urgency; even so, friend, if while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in that monk, he is stirred by that, feels a sense of urgency: 'It is truly a loss for me, not a gain; ill-gotten for me, not well-gotten, that while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in me.' If, friend, while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in that monk, he is pleased by that. To this extent also, friend, much has been done by that monk.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element is disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friend, when the waters in the great ocean recede a hundred leagues, two hundred leagues, three hundred leagues, four hundred leagues, five hundred leagues, six hundred leagues, seven hundred leagues. There comes a time, friend, when the water in the great ocean stands at seven palm-trees deep, six palm-trees deep, five palm-trees deep, four palm-trees deep, three palm-trees deep, two palm-trees deep, a palm-tree deep. There comes a time, friend, when the water in the great ocean stands seven fathoms deep, six fathoms deep, five fathoms deep, four fathoms deep, three fathoms deep, two fathoms deep, a fathom deep. There comes a time, friend, when the water in the great ocean stands half a fathom deep, waist-deep, knee-deep, ankle-deep. There comes a time, friend, when there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet the tip of a finger. Thus, friend, the impermanence of the external water element, so ancient, will become apparent; its nature to vanish, to perish, to change will become apparent.
translations.mn28:13: Then what of this body, which is clung to through craving, of limited duration? Could there be in regard to it 'I am' or 'This is mine' or 'I am'? Surely, for him there is not...
translations.mn28:14: If, friend, while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in that monk, he is pleased by that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friend, when the external fire element is disturbed. It burns up villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. It reaches a green area, a road, a rock, water, or a delightful tract of land, and having no fuel, it is extinguished. There comes a time, friend, when people seek fire even with a cock's feather or a tendon-splitter. Thus, friend, the impermanence of the external fire element, so ancient, will become apparent; its nature to vanish, to perish, to change will become apparent. Then what of this body, which is clung to through craving, of limited duration? Could there be in regard to it 'I am' or 'This is mine' or 'I am'?
translations.mn28:18-20: Surely, for him there is not... If, friend, while recollecting the Buddha thus, recollecting the Dhamma thus, recollecting the Sangha thus, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in that monk, he is pleased by that. To this extent also, friend, much has been done by that monk.
translations.mn28:2: "Just as, friend, whatever footprints there are of animals that walk the forest, all are included within the elephant's footprint; the elephant's footprint is declared the chief among them because of its great size; even so, friend, all wholesome qualities are included within the Four Noble Truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friend, when the external air element is disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friend, when in the last month of the hot season people seek wind even with a palm-leaf fan or a winnowing basket, and the grasses on the threshing floor do not stir. Thus, friend, the impermanence of the external air element, so ancient, will become apparent; its nature to vanish, to perish, to change will become apparent. Then what of this body, which is clung to through craving, of limited duration? Could there be in regard to it 'I am' or 'This is mine' or 'I am'? Surely, for him there is not.
translations.mn28:23: If others abuse, revile, annoy, and harass that monk, he understands thus: 'This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me. That is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.' He sees that contact is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. His mind, having that element as its object, leaps forward, becomes serene, settles, and becomes liberated.
translations.mn28:24: If, friend, other people treat that monk in ways that are undesirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable—with contact of fists, stones, sticks, or knives—he understands thus: 'This body is of such a nature that contacts of fists, stones, sticks, and knives occur to it. For it was said by the Blessed One in the simile of the saw: "Even if, monks, bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, he who entertained hate in his mind on that account would not be carrying out my teaching." My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and unagitated, my mind concentrated and unified. Let now contacts of fists, stones, sticks, and knives occur to this body; for this is how the teaching of the Buddhas is to be followed.'
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friend, when space is enclosed by timber, creepers, grass, and clay, it comes to be called 'house'; so too, friend, when space is enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, it comes to be called 'form.'
translations.mn28:27: If, friend, the internal eye is intact but external forms do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding kind of consciousness. If the internal eye is intact and external forms come into its range, but there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding kind of consciousness. But when, friend, the internal eye is intact, external forms come into its range, and there is corresponding attention, then there is manifestation of the corresponding kind of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: The form of one thus arisen is included in the form aggregate affected by clinging. The feeling of one thus arisen is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging. The perception of one thus arisen is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging. The formations of one thus arisen are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging. The consciousness of one thus arisen is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging. He understands thus: 'Indeed, this is how there comes to be the inclusion, gathering, and amassing of these five aggregates affected by clinging. And it was said by the Blessed One: "One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination." And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen. Any desire, attachment, fondness, and craving for these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering. The removal and abandonment of desire and attachment for these five aggregates affected by clinging is the cessation of suffering.' At this point too, friend, much has been done by that monk.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering. And what, friend, are the five aggregates affected by clinging? They are: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, and the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.
translations.mn28:37: If the internal mind is intact but external mental phenomena do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding kind of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element is disturbed. Then the external earth element disappears. For even this external earth element, so vast, is seen to be impermanent, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to change. How much more this short-lived body, which is clung to through craving, with the notion 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am'? But for him, there is no such thing.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Mount Vulture Peak not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, a clansman goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am beset by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am beset by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering. Perhaps an ending of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.' Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor does he become complacent. He does not exalt himself or disparage others because of that gain, honor, and renown. He does not become intoxicated, negligent, or fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he achieves accomplishment in virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment in virtue and becomes complacent. He exalts himself and disparages others because of that accomplishment in virtue: 'I am virtuous, of good character, but these other monks are immoral, of bad character.' He becomes intoxicated, negligent, and falls into heedlessness because of that accomplishment in virtue. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. Suppose, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass over the heartwood of a great standing tree that has heartwood, would pass over the sapwood, would pass over the inner bark, would cut off the outer bark, and taking that, would depart thinking it is heartwood. A man with good sight, seeing him, might say: 'This good man does not know the heartwood, the sapwood, the inner bark, the outer bark, or the twigs and leaves. Thus this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passes over the heartwood of a great standing tree that has heartwood, passes over the sapwood, passes over the inner bark, cuts off the outer bark, and taking that, departs thinking it is heartwood. Whatever he needs to do with heartwood, that purpose will not be served for him.'
translations.mn2:10: And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should not be attended to, which one does not attend to? Bhikkhus, when one attends to certain things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases; the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen taint of existence increases; the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen taint of ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, which one does not attend to. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be attended to, which one attends to? Bhikkhus, when one attends to certain things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned; the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned; the unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, which one attends to. By not attending to things that should not be attended to and by attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He wisely attends: 'This is suffering'; he wisely attends: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he wisely attends: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he wisely attends: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering'. When he wisely attends thus, three fetters are abandoned: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances. These are called, bhikkhus, the taints to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint. And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty. For, bhikkhus, if he dwells without restraint of the eye faculty, taints of distress and fever might arise; but if he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, such taints of distress and fever do not arise. Reflecting wisely, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty ... the nose faculty ... the tongue faculty ... the body faculty ... the mind faculty. For, bhikkhus, if he dwells without restraint of the mind faculty, taints of distress and fever might arise; but if he dwells restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, such taints of distress and fever do not arise. For, bhikkhus, if he dwells without restraint, taints of distress and fever might arise; but if he dwells restrained, such taints of distress and fever do not arise. These are called, bhikkhus, the taints to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood: 'Not for fun, not for indulgence, not for adornment, not for embellishment, but only for the support and maintenance of this body, for keeping it healthy, for assisting the holy life, thinking: 'Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and dwell in comfort.'
translations.mn2:16: Reflecting wisely, he uses medicines and requisites for the sick: 'Only for the relief of arisen afflictive feelings, for the utmost freedom from disease.'
translations.mn2:17: For, bhikkhus, if he does not use them, taints of distress and fever might arise; but if he uses them, such taints of distress and fever do not arise. These are called, bhikkhus, the taints to be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: "Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And what, bhikkhus, does one know and see for the destruction of the taints? Wise attention and unwise attention. Bhikkhus, when one attends unwisely, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase; but when one attends wisely, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned."
translations.mn2:6: And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should not be attended to, which one attends to? Bhikkhus, when one attends to certain things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases; the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen taint of existence increases; the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen taint of ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, which one attends to. And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be attended to, which one does not attend to? Bhikkhus, when one attends to certain things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned; the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned; the unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, which one does not attend to.
translations.mn2:7: By attending to things that should not be attended to and by not attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase. He attends unwisely thus: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I exist in the future? Shall I not exist in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?' Or else he is inwardly perplexed about the present thus: 'Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?'
translations.mn2:8: When they attend unwisely in this way, one of the six views arises in them. The view 'I have a self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I have no self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive non-self with self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with non-self' arises in them as true and established; or else they have such a view: 'This self of mine that speaks and feels, that experiences the results of good and bad actions here and there, this self of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever.' This is called, bhikkhus, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views. Fettered by the fetter of views, the untaught ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; they are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn2:9: But, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones and is skilled in the noble Dhamma, well trained in the noble Dhamma; who has seen good persons and is skilled in the good Dhamma, well trained in the good Dhamma—understands things that should be attended to and things that should not be attended to. Understanding things that should be attended to and things that should not be attended to, they do not attend to things that should not be attended to, and they attend to things that should be attended to.
translations.mn31:10: "Good, good, Anuruddha. But, Anuruddha, while you dwell thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?" "Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as we wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, venerable sir, is a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, attained by us while dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute."
translations.mn31:11-13: "Good, good, Anuruddha. But, Anuruddha, by transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?" "Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as we wish, with the subsiding of thought and examination, we enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. By transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, attained by us."
translations.mn31:14: "Good, good, Anuruddha. But, Anuruddha, by transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?" "Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as we wish, with the fading away of rapture, we dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, we enter and dwell in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'One dwells happily with equanimity and mindfulness.' By transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, attained by us."
translations.mn31:15: "Good, good, Anuruddha. But, Anuruddha, by transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?" "Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as we wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, we enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. By transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, attained by us."
translations.mn31:16: "Good, good, Anuruddha. But, Anuruddha, by transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, have you attained any other superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?" "Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as we wish, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' we enter and dwell in the base of infinite space. By transcending that abiding and by the subsiding of that abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, attained by us."
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: Now at that time the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood.
translations.mn31:3: Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood. The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming in the distance. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: "Do not, ascetic, enter this park. There are three clansmen dwelling here who are fond of themselves. Do not disturb them."
translations.mn31:4: The venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said to the park keeper: "Do not, friend park keeper, prevent the Blessed One. Our teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived." Then the venerable Anuruddha approached the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila; having approached, he said to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila: "Come forth, venerable ones, come forth! Our teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived."
translations.mn31:5: Then the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One. One received the Blessed One's bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerable ones paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the venerable Anuruddha: "I hope, Anuruddha, that you are keeping well, I hope you are comfortable, I hope you are not having trouble getting almsfood?" "We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are comfortable, Blessed One; and we are not having trouble getting almsfood, venerable sir."
translations.mn31:6: "But I hope, Anuruddha, that you are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?" "Surely, venerable sir, we are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes." "But how, Anuruddha, do you live in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?"
translations.mn31:9: "Surely, venerable sir, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute." "But how, Anuruddha, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?" "Here, venerable sir, whichever of us returns first from the village with almsfood prepares the seats, sets out drinking water and food for cleaning, and sets out the refuse bowl. Whichever returns last from the village with almsfood, if there is leftover food and he wishes, he eats it; if he does not wish, he discards it where there is little greenery or drops it into water where there are no living beings. He puts away the seats, puts away the drinking water and food for cleaning, puts away the refuse bowl, and sweeps the eating place. Whoever sees that the water pot for drinking, or the water pot for cleaning, or the water pot for the lavatory is empty or low, he fills it. If it is too heavy for one, he calls a second by a gesture of the hand, and we lift it together by the hand; but we do not, venerable sir, break into speech because of that. And every five days we sit together the whole night discussing the Dhamma. Thus, venerable sir, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute."
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: "I have such confidence in Master Gotama. For Master Gotama is one whose body is developed and whose mind is developed." "Certainly, Aggivessana, this statement of yours is invasive and presumptuous, but I will answer you. Since I, Aggivessana, shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, it is impossible that any arisen pleasant feeling would invade my mind and remain, or that any arisen painful feeling would invade my mind and remain."
translations.mn36:12: "Why shouldn't it be, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: 'Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn36:2: Now on that occasion the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and outer robe, was wanting to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: Then, Aggivessana, the thought occurred to me: 'Suppose I, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind.' So I, Aggivessana, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind. While I did so, sweat poured from my armpits. Just as if a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain him, and crush him; so too, Aggivessana, while I, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind, sweat poured from my armpits. But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful striving. Yet such painful feeling that arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:26: And, Aggivessana, some deities seeing me said: 'The ascetic Gotama is dead.' Other deities said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead, he is dying.' And other deities said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead nor dying; he is an arahant, for such is the way of life of the arahants.'
translations.mn36:27: Then, Aggivessana, the thought occurred to me: 'Suppose I practice entirely cutting off food.' Then, Aggivessana, deities approached me and said: 'Good sir, do not practice entirely cutting off food. If you, good sir, practice entirely cutting off food, we will infuse divine nourishment into your pores, and you will sustain yourself on that.' Then, Aggivessana, the thought occurred to me: 'If I claim to be completely abstaining from food, and these deities infuse divine nourishment into my pores and I sustain myself on that, that would be a falsehood on my part.' So, Aggivessana, I refused those deities, saying, 'Enough.'
translations.mn36:28: Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: 'Suppose I were to take a little food, a small amount, whether it be mung bean soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup.' So, Aggivessana, I took a little food, a small amount, whether it be mung bean soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. As I, Aggivessana, took a little food, a small amount, whether it be mung bean soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup, my body reached an extreme state of emaciation. Just like the joints of a withered reed or a black bamboo, so too did my limbs become because of that little food. Just like a camel's hoof, so too did my seat become because of that little food. Just like a string of beads, so too did my spine, protruding and bent, become because of that little food. Just like the rafters of an old house, loose and dangling, so too did my ribs become, loose and dangling, because of that little food. Just like in a deep well, the water stars, deep-set and sunken, are seen, so too in my eye sockets, the eye stars, deep-set and sunken, were seen because of that little food. Just like a bitter gourd, cut while raw, shrivels and withers from wind and sun, so too did the skin of my head shrivel and wither because of that little food. When I, Aggivessana, thought to touch the skin of my belly, I actually grasped the spine; when I thought to touch the spine, I actually grasped the skin of my belly, so much, Aggivessana, had the skin of my belly clung to the spine because of that little food. When I, Aggivessana, thought to defecate or urinate, I would fall right there face down because of that little food. Then I, Aggivessana, to relieve this body, would massage my limbs with my hand. As I, Aggivessana, massaged my limbs with my hand, the rotten roots of the hairs fell from my body because of that little food.
translations.mn36:29: And then, Aggivessana, people seeing me would say: 'The ascetic Gotama is black.' Some people would say: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is dark brown.' Some people would say: 'The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor dark brown, he has a golden skin.' So much, Aggivessana, was my naturally clear and bright complexion ruined because of that little food.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, this Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son is coming, a debater, a clever speaker, regarded as holy by many people. He, venerable sir, desires to disparage the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would sit for a moment out of compassion." The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, harsh, and severe feelings due to self-mortification, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, harsh, and severe feelings due to self-mortification, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present experience painful, harsh, and severe feelings due to self-mortification, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. But by this severe and difficult practice I do not attain any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to enlightenment?'
translations.mn36:32: Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: 'Why should I fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?' Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: 'I do not fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.'
translations.mn36:34: Then I, Aggivessana, having taken solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Even such pleasant feelings that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not overwhelm my mind.
translations.mn36:38: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus with details and particulars, I recollected my manifold past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first knowledge I attained in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Even such pleasant feelings that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not overwhelm my mind.
translations.mn36:4: "There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the development of the body, not to the development of the mind. They experience, Master Gotama, bodily painful feeling. In the past, Master Gotama, when one was touched by bodily painful feeling, one's thighs would cramp, one's heart would burst, hot blood would gush from one's mouth, and one would reach madness and mental derangement. That mind, Master Gotama, is dependent on the body, it proceeds under the body's control. Why is that? Because the mind is undeveloped. But there are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the development of the mind, not to the development of the body. They experience, Master Gotama, mental painful feeling. In the past, Master Gotama, when one was touched by mental painful feeling, one's thighs would cramp, one's heart would burst, hot blood would gush from one's mouth, and one would reach madness and mental derangement. That body, Master Gotama, is dependent on the mind, it proceeds under the mind's control. Why is that? Because the body is undeveloped. It occurs to me, Master Gotama: 'Surely Master Gotama's disciples dwell devoted to the development of the mind, not to the development of the body.'"
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions...
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I truly understood: 'This is suffering'; I truly understood: 'This is the origin of suffering'; I truly understood: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; I truly understood: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' I truly understood: 'These are the taints'; I truly understood: 'This is the origin of the taints'; I truly understood: 'This is the cessation of the taints'; I truly understood: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.'
translations.mn36:43: As I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of being, my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there arose the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' I understood: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.mn36:45: I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. And each one thinks: 'The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma especially for me.' But that, Aggivessana, should not be seen in that way; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others merely for the purpose of giving instruction. At the end of that talk, Aggivessana, I steady my mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness, and concentrate it on that same sign of concentration as before, in which I constantly abide." "This is credible for Master Gotama, as is fitting for one who is an Arahant, a fully enlightened Buddha. But does Master Gotama recall sleeping during the day?"
translations.mn36:46: "I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after the meal, returning from almsround, having spread my outer robe folded in four, lying down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, I fell asleep." "This, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins call dwelling in delusion." "Not by this alone, Aggivessana, is one deluded or undeluded. But, Aggivessana, listen to how one is deluded and how one is undeluded, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, sir," Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn36:47: "Whoever, Aggivessana, has not abandoned the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, ripening in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—him I call 'deluded.' For, Aggivessana, not having abandoned the taints, one is deluded. Whoever, Aggivessana, has abandoned the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, ripening in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—him I call 'undeluded.' For, Aggivessana, having abandoned the taints, one is undeluded. In the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, ripening in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of growing again, so too, Aggivessana, in the Tathāgata the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, ripening in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising."
translations.mn36:5: "But how, Aggivessana, have you heard about the development of the body?" "Such as Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these, Master Gotama, are naked ascetics, living without restraints, licking their hands, not accepting food brought, not accepting food specially prepared, not accepting an invitation, not accepting food from a pot, not accepting food from a bowl, not accepting food across a threshold, not accepting food across a stick, not accepting food across a pestle, not from two eating together, not from a pregnant woman, not from a nursing woman, not from a woman living with a man, not from food collected in times of famine, not from where a dog is standing, not from where flies are swarming; they do not accept fish or meat, they do not drink liquor, wine, or fermented drinks. They maintain themselves on one house, one morsel; or on two houses, two morsels... up to seven houses, seven morsels. They subsist on one alms-giving, on two... up to seven. They take food once a day, once every two days... up to once every seven days. Thus they dwell devoted to the practice of eating food at stated intervals even up to half a month."
translations.mn36:6: "But, Aggivessana, do you sustain yourselves with just that much?" "No, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, we eat excellent solid foods, we eat excellent meals, we eat excellent delicacies, we drink excellent drinks. They strengthen this body, they build it up, they fatten it." "What you, Aggivessana, give up earlier and later accumulate, thus there is accumulation and depletion for this body. But, Aggivessana, have you heard of mental development?" When asked by the Blessed One about mental development, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son was unable to answer.
translations.mn36:8: "And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in an unlearned ordinary person. Touched by that pleasant feeling, they become lustful for pleasure and fall into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, they sorrow, grieve, lament, beat their breast, and become distraught. For them, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling that has arisen obsesses the mind due to the body being undeveloped; a painful feeling that has arisen obsesses the mind due to the mind being undeveloped. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom it is thus on both sides—a pleasant feeling that has arisen obsesses the mind due to the body being undeveloped; a painful feeling that has arisen obsesses the mind due to the mind being undeveloped—thus, Aggivessana, one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn36:9: "And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in a learned noble disciple. Touched by that pleasant feeling, they do not become lustful for pleasure and do not fall into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, they do not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat their breast, or become distraught. For them, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling that has arisen does not obsess the mind due to the body being developed; a painful feeling that has arisen does not obsess the mind due to the mind being developed. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom it is thus on both sides—a pleasant feeling that has arisen does not obsess the mind due to the body being developed; a painful feeling that has arisen does not obsess the mind due to the mind being developed—thus, Aggivessana, one is developed in body and developed in mind."
translations.mn38:10: "Monks, for one who doubts, does doubt arise: 'Does this exist?'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, for one who doubts, does doubt arise: 'Does it originate from nutriment?'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, for one who doubts, does doubt arise: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, does that which exists cease?'?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:11: "Monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This exists,' is that doubt abandoned?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'It originates from nutriment,' is that doubt abandoned?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, that which exists ceases,' is that doubt abandoned?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:12: "Monks, 'This exists'—are you thus free from doubt about this?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, 'It originates from nutriment'—are you thus free from doubt about this?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, 'With the cessation of that nutriment, that which exists ceases'—are you thus free from doubt about this?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:13: "Monks, 'This exists'—is this well seen by right wisdom as it really is?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, 'It originates from nutriment'—is this well seen by right wisdom as it really is?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, 'With the cessation of that nutriment, that which exists ceases'—is this well seen by right wisdom as it really is?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:14: "Monks, if you were to cling to this view, hold to it, treasure it, regard it as 'mine,' thus purified and cleansed, would you then understand that I have taught the Dhamma as a simile of a raft, for crossing over, not for holding onto?" "No, venerable sir." "Monks, if you do not cling to this view, do not hold to it, do not treasure it, do not regard it as 'mine,' thus purified and cleansed, would you then understand that I have taught the Dhamma as a simile of a raft, for crossing over, not for holding onto?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:15: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? Physical food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: "Good, monks. Thus, monks, you should also speak thus, and I also speak thus—when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time a monk named Sāti, the fisherman's son, had such a wrong view arise: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that runs and wanders on, not another."
translations.mn38:20: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: "Good, bhikkhus. So, bhikkhus, you too should speak thus, and I also speak thus: 'When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' That is: with the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering."
translations.mn38:23: "Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing thus, would you run back to the past thus: 'Were we in the past? Were we not in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?'?" "No, venerable sir." "Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing thus, would you run forward to the future thus: 'Shall we be in the future? Shall we not be in the future? What shall we be in the future? How shall we be in the future? Having been what, what shall we become in the future?'?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:25: "Good, bhikkhus. You have been led by me, bhikkhus, to this Dhamma which is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves. For this Dhamma, bhikkhus, is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves—so that what was said, was said with reference to this."
translations.mn38:26: "Bhikkhus, the descent of the embryo takes place through the union of three things. Here, the mother and father come together, but the mother is not in season, and the gandhabba is not present—in that case no descent of an embryo takes place. Here, the mother and father come together, and the mother is in season, but the gandhabba is not present—in that case no descent of an embryo takes place. But when, bhikkhus, the mother and father come together, the mother is in season, and the gandhabba is present—through the union of these three things the descent of an embryo takes place."
translations.mn38:27: "Then, bhikkhus, the mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months with great anxiety, a heavy burden. Then, bhikkhus, the mother gives birth after nine or ten months with great anxiety, a heavy burden. Then, when the child is born, she nourishes it with her own blood. For, bhikkhus, mother's milk is called blood in the Noble One's discipline."
translations.mn38:28: "Then, bhikkhus, as the boy grows up and his faculties mature, he plays with those playthings of boys, such as toy plows, tipcats, somersaults, pinwheels, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows."
translations.mn38:39: "Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Again, bhikkhus, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna."
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "What do you think, bhikkhus, has this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, even kindled a spark of wisdom in this Dhamma and Discipline?" "How could that be, venerable sir? No, venerable sir." When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum, and without response. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the bhikkhu Sāti was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum, and without response, said to him: "You will be recognized, foolish man, by your own pernicious view. I will question the bhikkhus about this."
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Do you too, bhikkhus, understand the Dhamma taught by me as this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, does when, through his own wrong grasp, he both misrepresents us and injures himself and produces much demerit?" "No, venerable sir. For in many ways, venerable sir, the Blessed One has stated that consciousness is dependently arisen; without a condition there is no origination of consciousness." "Good, good, bhikkhus. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me thus. For in many ways, bhikkhus, I have stated that consciousness is dependently arisen; without a condition there is no origination of consciousness. Yet this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, through his own wrong grasp, both misrepresents us and injures himself and produces much demerit. That will lead to the harm and suffering of that foolish man for a long time."
translations.mn38:9: "Do you see, monks, that this is conditioned?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Do you see, monks, that it originates from nutriment?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Do you see, monks, that with the cessation of that nutriment, what is conditioned is subject to cessation?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of monks when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold misconduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous; he covets the wealth and property of others thus: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' He has a mind of ill will and intentions of hate thus: 'May these beings be killed, slaughtered, annihilated, destroyed, or may they not exist at all!' He holds wrong view, distorted vision thus: 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no spontaneously reborn beings; no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.' That, householders, is how there is threefold misconduct by mind. It is because of such misconduct, householders, that some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct by body? Here, householders, someone, abandoning the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious, merciful, he dwells compassionate to all living beings. Abandoning taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he does not take by way of theft the wealth and property of others in village or forest. Abandoning sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, by their clan, by Dhamma, who have a husband, whose use entails punishment, or even with one garlanded by a man. That, householders, is how there is threefold good conduct by body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold good conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone, abandoning false speech, abstains from false speech; when summoned to a council, to an assembly, to his relatives' presence, to his guild, or to the court, and questioned as a witness thus: 'So, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, he says, 'I do not know,' or knowing, he says, 'I know'; not seeing, he says, 'I do not see,' or seeing, he says, 'I see'; he does not in full awareness speak falsehood for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trivial worldly gain. Abandoning divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech; having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere to create conflict, or having heard something elsewhere, he does not repeat it here to create conflict. Thus he reconciles those who are divided and promotes unity among those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that promote concord. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, loving, going to the heart, courteous, agreeable to many people, and delightful to many people. Abandoning idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks on the good, on the Dhamma and the Discipline; his speech is like a treasure, uttered at the right time, accompanied by reason, measured, and connected with the goal. That, householders, is how there is fourfold good conduct by speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is not covetous; he does not covet the wealth and property of others thus: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' His mind is without ill will and intentions of hate thus: 'May these beings live happily, free from enmity, affliction, and anxiety!' He holds right view, undistorted vision thus: 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are spontaneously reborn beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.' That, householders, is how there is threefold good conduct by mind. It is because of such good conduct, householders, that some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If, householders, one who lives righteously and equitably should wish: 'Oh, that on the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas!' it is possible that on the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas. For what reason? Because he lives righteously and equitably.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, after an exchange of friendly and courteous greetings, sat down to one side; some extended their joined palms in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One's presence and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. Sitting to one side, the brahmin householders of Sālā said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn41:4: "What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason, why some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason, why some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world?"
translations.mn41:43: If, householders, one who lives righteously and equally should wish: 'Oh, that I, with the destruction of the taints, might in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for myself with direct knowledge'; it is possible that he, with the destruction of the taints, might in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge. For what reason? Because he lives righteously and equally.
translations.mn41:5: Householders, it is because of unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct that some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell.
