It is because of righteous conduct and equal conduct that some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:6: We do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken briefly by Master Gotama, without it being explained in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach us the Dhamma in such a way that we might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken briefly by Master Gotama, without it being explained in detail. "Then, householders, listen and attend closely; I will speak." "Yes, sir," the brahmin householders of Sālā replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct by body? Here, householders, someone kills living beings; he is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. He takes what is not given; he takes by way of theft the wealth and property of others in village or forest. He engages in sexual misconduct; he has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, by their clan, by their Dhamma, who have a husband, who are protected by law, even those garlanded in token of betrothal. Thus, householders, there is threefold unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct by body.
translations.mn41:9: And how, householders, is there fourfold unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone speaks falsehood. When summoned to a court, or to a meeting, or to his relatives' presence, or to his guild, or to the royal family's presence, and questioned as a witness thus: 'So, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, he says, 'I know,' or knowing, he says, 'I do not know'; not seeing, he says, 'I see,' or seeing, he says, 'I do not see'; thus he consciously speaks falsehood for his own sake, or for another's sake, or for some trifling worldly end. He speaks divisively; repeating here what he heard there to break those people apart from these, or repeating there what he heard here to break these people apart from those; thus he is a divider of the united, a promoter of divisions, enjoying factions, rejoicing in factions, delighting in factions, he speaks words that cause factions. He speaks harshly; he utters such words as are rough, hard, hurtful, offensive, bordering on anger, unconducive to concentration. He engages in idle chatter; he speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is unbeneficial, speaks contrary to the Dhamma and the Discipline; his speech is not worth treasuring, untimely, unreasonable, rambling, not connected with the goal. Thus, householders, there is fourfold unrighteous conduct and unequal conduct by speech.
translations.mn4:20: Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: 'Suppose that on those nights which are reckoned as auspicious—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—I were to dwell in such awe-inspiring and hair-raising abodes as forest shrines, woodland shrines, tree shrines, perhaps I might see that fear and terror.' So, brahmin, later on, on those nights which are reckoned as auspicious—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—I dwelt in such awe-inspiring and hair-raising abodes as forest shrines, woodland shrines, tree shrines. While I dwelt there, a deer would approach, or a peacock would knock down a branch, or the wind would rustle a heap of leaves. Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: 'Surely this is that fear and terror coming.' Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: 'Why do I dwell always expecting fear? Suppose I subdue that fear and terror in the very posture in which it comes.' While I was walking, that fear and terror came upon me. I neither stood still, nor sat down, nor lay down until I had subdued that fear and terror while walking. While I was standing, that fear and terror came upon me. I neither walked, nor sat down, nor lay down until I had subdued that fear and terror while standing. While I was sitting, that fear and terror came upon me. I neither lay down, nor stood up, nor walked until I had subdued that fear and terror while sitting. While I was lying down, that fear and terror came upon me. I neither sat up, nor stood up, nor walked until I had subdued that fear and terror while lying down.
translations.mn4:22-26: And then, brahmin, my energy was aroused and unrelenting, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, my mind was concentrated and unified. Then, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus I recollected my manifold past lives in their modes and details.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was the first knowledge I attained in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. But these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: And I too, brahmin, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, thought: 'Remote jungle thickets are hard to endure, seclusion is difficult to practice, and it is not easy to enjoy solitude. The forests, I think, rob the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration.'
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was the second knowledge I attained in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: It might occur to you, brahmin: 'Perhaps the ascetic Gotama is still not free from lust, hate, and delusion; that is why he resorts to remote jungle thickets.' But you should not regard it thus, brahmin. I see two benefits in resorting to remote jungle thickets: seeing my own pleasant dwelling in this very life, and having compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins with impure bodily conduct resort to remote jungle thickets, because of the defect of impure bodily conduct, those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invoke unwholesome fear and terror. But I do not resort to remote jungle thickets with impure bodily conduct; I have pure bodily conduct. I am one of those noble ones with pure bodily conduct who resort to remote jungle thickets.' Seeing this purity of bodily conduct in myself, brahmin, I gained even more confidence for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins with impure verbal conduct ... with impure mental conduct ... with impure livelihood resort to remote jungle thickets, because of the defect of impure livelihood, those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invoke unwholesome fear and terror.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not resort to remote jungle thickets with impure livelihood; I have pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those noble ones with pure livelihood who resort to remote jungle thickets.' Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself, brahmin, I gained even more confidence for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the Beluvagāmaka village. Now at that time the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a monk, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking: 'Space is infinite.' He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of infinite space is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He understands this. Established in that, he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a monk, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, thinking: 'There is nothing.' He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He understands this. Established in that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is spontaneously reborn and attains final Nibbāna there, not returning from that world. This too, householder, is one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet liberated, it becomes liberated; if his taints are not yet destroyed, they go to destruction; and if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda: "Just as, Venerable Ānanda, a man seeking one treasure trove might at once find eleven treasure troves; so too, Venerable, seeking one door to the Deathless, I have at once found eleven doors to the Deathless for development. Just as, Venerable, a man's house with eleven doors, if that house were on fire, could save himself safely through any one of those doors; so too, Venerable, I can save myself safely through any one of these eleven doors to the Deathless. These followers of other sects, Venerable, seek a teacher's fee for their teacher; why should I not make an offering to Venerable Ānanda?"
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka approached the Kukkuṭārāma and approached a certain monk; having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to that monk: "Where, Venerable, is Venerable Ānanda staying now? For we wish to see that Venerable Ānanda." "That Venerable Ānanda, householder, is staying at Vesālī in the Beluvagāmaka village."
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka, having completed his business at Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to the Beluvagāmaka village, to Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda: "Is there, Venerable Ānanda, one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet liberated, it becomes liberated; if his taints are not yet destroyed, they go to destruction; and if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it?" "There is, householder, one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet liberated, it becomes liberated; if his taints are not yet destroyed, they go to destruction; and if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it." "But what, Venerable Ānanda, is that one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet liberated, it becomes liberated; if his taints are not yet destroyed, they go to destruction; and if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it?"
translations.mn52:4: "Here, householder, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He understands this. Established in that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is spontaneously reborn and attains final Nibbāna there, not returning from that world. This too, householder, is one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet liberated, it becomes liberated; if his taints are not yet destroyed, they go to destruction; and if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, all-encompassing, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects thus: 'This liberation of mind through loving-kindness is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He understands this. Established in that, he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there were a pit of glowing coals deeper than a man's height, full of coals that were blazing, without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. Then two strong men would grab him by both arms and drag him toward that pit of glowing coals. What do you think, householder? Wouldn't that man twist his body this way and that?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Why is that?" "Because he knows, venerable sir: 'If I fall into this pit of glowing coals, I will meet death or deadly suffering because of that.'" "In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals, full of much suffering, much distress, and with greater danger here.' Seeing this as it really is with right wisdom... he develops that very equanimity.
translations.mn54:23: That noble disciple, householder, based on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness and equanimity, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate... and he understands how beings fare according to their actions.
translations.mn54:24: That noble disciple, householder, based on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness and equanimity, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn60:10: In this case, householders, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and such a doctrine: 'There is what is given... and who proclaim this world and the next world after having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge'—it is to be expected of them that, having abandoned these three unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct—and having undertaken these three wholesome states—bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct—they will behave accordingly. Why is that? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome states, and they see the benefit of renunciation and the cleansing aspect in wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: In this case, householders, a wise person reflects thus: 'If there is an afterlife, then this venerable person, after death, with the breakup of the body, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Even if there is no afterlife, still, let the statement of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; still, in this very life, this venerable person is praised by the wise as a virtuous person, one with right view, who holds the doctrine of a hereafter.' If there is indeed an afterlife, then this venerable person achieves success on both counts: he is praised by the wise in this very life, and after death, with the breakup of the body, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this safe-bet teaching, undertaken well, covers both sides and stands rejecting unwholesome states.
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and such a doctrine: 'For one who acts or makes others act, who mutilates or makes others mutilate, who tortures or makes others torture, who grieves or makes others grieve, who torments or makes others torment, who agitates or makes others agitate, who kills living beings, who takes what is not given, who breaks into houses, who plunders, who commits burglary, who ambushes, who commits adultery, who speaks falsehood—for one who does such things, no evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, no evil would come from that cause, no evil would follow. Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing, slaughtering, mutilating, making others mutilate, torturing, making others torture, no evil would come from that cause, no evil would follow. Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving gifts, making others give gifts, making offerings, making others make offerings, no merit would come from that cause, no merit would follow. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, no merit follows.'
translations.mn60:14: But, householders, regarding those very ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins directly contradict them, saying: 'For one who acts or makes others act... who speaks falsehood—for one who does such things, evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, evil would come from that cause, evil would follow. Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing, slaughtering, mutilating, making others mutilate, torturing, making others torture, evil would come from that cause, evil would follow. Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving gifts, making others give gifts, making offerings, making others make offerings, merit would come from that cause, merit would follow. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is merit, merit follows.' What do you think, householders? Don't these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines that directly contradict each other?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn60:16: When there actually is action, the view 'there is no action' arises in him; that is his wrong view. When there actually is action, he intends 'there is no action'; that is his wrong intention. When there actually is action, he speaks the words 'there is no action'; that is his wrong speech. When there actually is action, he says 'there is no action'; he thereby contradicts those arahants who hold the doctrine of action. When there actually is action, he persuades another 'there is no action'; that is his persuasion in a false doctrine. And because of that persuasion in a false doctrine, he exalts himself and disparages others. Thus, previously his good conduct is abandoned and bad conduct is established—and this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, contradiction of the noble ones, persuasion in a false doctrine, self-exaltation, and disparagement of others. Thus, these many evil, unwholesome states come into being with wrong view as condition.
translations.mn60:17: Here, householders, a wise person reflects thus: 'If there is no action, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, will make himself safe. But if there is action, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of loss, an unhappy destination, the plane of misery, hell. Now, even if there is no action, let the statement of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; still, this venerable person is censured by the wise in this very life as an immoral person, one of wrong view, a non-doer.' If there really is action, then this venerable person has met with misfortune on both counts: he is censured by the wise in this very life, and with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of loss, an unhappy destination, the plane of misery, hell. Thus, this safe-bet teaching has been undertaken poorly by him, it is one-sided and excludes the wholesome state.
translations.mn60:19: But when there really is action, the view 'there is action' occurs to him; that is his right view. When there really is action, he resolves 'there is action'; that is his right intention. When there really is action, he speaks the words 'there is action'; that is his right speech. When there really is action, he says 'there is action'; he does not contradict those arahants who teach action. When there really is action, he persuades another of 'there is action'; that is his declaration of the true Dhamma. And by that declaration of the true Dhamma, he does not praise himself or disparage others. Thus, his previous bad conduct is abandoned and good conduct is established—and this right view, right intention, right speech, non-contradiction of the noble ones, declaration of the true Dhamma, non-self-praise, and non-disparagement of others. In this way, many wholesome qualities come into being with right view as condition.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition. There is no power, no energy, no human strength, no human effort; all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without strength, without energy, and are developed by destiny, circumstance, and nature, and experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.'
translations.mn60:22: But, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins. They say: 'There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause, with condition. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause, with condition. There is power, there is energy, there is human strength, there is human effort; not all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without strength, without energy, and developed by destiny, circumstance, and nature, and experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.' What do you think, householders, aren't these ascetics and brahmins directly opposed to each other?
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: 'There is no immaterial state at all.'
translations.mn60:30: But, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins. They say: 'There is an immaterial state at all.' What do you think, householders, aren't these ascetics and brahmins directly opposed to each other?
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: 'There is no cessation of existence at all.'
translations.mn60:35: There are, householders, these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, householders, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself. Here, householders, a certain person torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, a certain person does not torment himself or devote himself to the practice of tormenting himself, and does not torment others or devote himself to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself or others, in this very life is free from craving, extinguished, cooled, and experiences bliss, having himself become divine.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself? Here, householders, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions... and so on... and dwells devoted to the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body in various ways. This, householders, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs... or one who follows any other such bloody occupation. This, householders, is called the person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person is a king or a royal minister... and so on... and they, terrified by punishment, terrified by fear, with tearful faces and crying, perform their duties. This, householders, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who does not torment himself or devote himself to the practice of tormenting himself, and does not torment others or devote himself to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself or others, in this very life is free from craving, extinguished, cooled, and experiences bliss, having himself become divine?
translations.mn60:4: 'But, householders, is there any teacher agreeable to you in whom you have acquired reasoned faith?' 'No, venerable sir, there is no teacher agreeable to us in whom we have acquired reasoned faith.' 'Since you have not found an agreeable teacher, householders, you should undertake this safe-bet teaching. For, householders, a safe-bet teaching, when undertaken properly, will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. And what, householders, is the safe-bet teaching?'
translations.mn60:5: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus: 'There is no giving, no sacrifice, no offering; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously born beings; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who have attained, who have practiced rightly, and who proclaim this world and the other world after having directly known and realized it for themselves.'
translations.mn60:6: Householders, there are other ascetics and brahmins who directly contradict those ascetics and brahmins. They say: 'There is giving, there is sacrifice, there is offering; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously born beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have attained, who have practiced rightly, and who proclaim this world and the other world after having directly known and realized it for themselves.' What do you think, householders? Don't these ascetics and brahmins directly contradict each other?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn63:8: And why, Maluṅkyaputta, have I not declared that? Because, Maluṅkyaputta, it is not beneficial, it is not connected with the fundamentals of the holy life, it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore I have not declared it.
translations.mn64:13: Again, Ānanda, a monk, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' attains and dwells in the base of infinite space. He regards whatever phenomena there that are included in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, suffering, a disease, a boil, a dart, a misery, an affliction, alien, disintegrating, empty, and not-self. He turns his mind away from those phenomena and directs it to the deathless element thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' If he is firm in that, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very dhamma-delight and dhamma-pleasure, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain final Nibbāna there without returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, a way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Again, Ānanda, a monk, with the complete transcendence of the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' attains and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. He regards whatever phenomena there that are included in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, suffering, a disease, a boil, a dart, a misery, an affliction, alien, disintegrating, empty, and not-self. He turns his mind away from those phenomena and directs it to the deathless element thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' If he is firm in that, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very dhamma-delight and dhamma-pleasure, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain final Nibbāna there without returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, a way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: "Monks, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?" When this was said, the Venerable Maluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One." "But how, Maluṅkyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?" "Venerable sir, I remember identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; clinging to rules and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. That is how I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One."
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it." "Then listen, Ānanda, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: But, Ānanda, there is a path, a way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters; by following that path, that way, one may know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters—this is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He regards whatever phenomena there that are included in form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, suffering, a disease, a boil, a dart, a misery, an affliction, alien, disintegrating, empty, and not-self. He turns his mind away from those phenomena. Having turned his mind away from those phenomena, he directs his mind to the deathless element thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' If he is firm in that, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very dhamma-delight and dhamma-pleasure, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain final Nibbāna there without returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, a way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I wield the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I travel through the sky like a bird while seated cross-legged; may I touch and stroke with my hand the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; may I exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world,' he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be possessed of insight, and dwell in empty huts.
translations.mn6:15: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near'—he should fulfill the precepts... and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:16: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with my mind—may I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate, a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind, an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassed mind as a surpassed mind, an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind'—he should fulfill the precepts... and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:2: "Dwell, monks, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken them, train in the training rules."
translations.mn6:3: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow monks, respected and esteemed'—he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:6: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May my relatives and kin who have passed away, with confident minds recollecting me, have great fruit and great benefit'—he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:7: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be a conqueror of discontent, and may discontent not conquer me; dwelling, may I overcome discontent whenever it arises'—he should fulfill the precepts... and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:8: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be a conqueror of fear and terror, and may fear and terror not conquer me; dwelling, may I overcome fear and terror whenever they arise'—he should fulfill the precepts... and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: If, monks, a monk should wish: 'May I be one who obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that are higher mind and pleasant abidings in this very life'—he should fulfill the precepts... and cultivate the empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kāsīs together with a large Saṅgha of monks. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.mn70:11: "And because, monks, I have known, seen, understood, realized, and penetrated with wisdom: 'In this case, for one feeling such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase'—therefore I say: 'Enter and dwell in such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.'"
translations.mn70:12: I do not say, monks, that all monks should act with heedfulness; nor do I say, monks, that all monks should not act with heedfulness. Those monks, monks, who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—such monks, monks, I say should not act with heedfulness. Why is that? They have done what should be done with heedfulness. They are incapable of negligence.
translations.mn70:13: But those monks, monks, who are trainees who have not attained their mind's ideal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—such monks, monks, I say should act with heedfulness. Why is that? Perhaps these venerable ones, frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, balancing the faculties, might realize for themselves with direct knowledge, and having realized, might enter and dwell in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for these monks, monks, I say: 'One should act with heedfulness.'"
translations.mn70:14: These seven persons, monks, are found existing in the world. Which seven? One liberated both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a bodily witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, a faith-follower.
translations.mn70:15: And what, monks, is the person liberated both ways? Here, monks, a certain person contacts with the body and dwells in those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed. This, monks, is called the person liberated both ways. I say, monks, that this monk should not act with heedfulness. Why is that? He has done what should be done with heedfulness. He is incapable of negligence.
translations.mn70:17: And what, monks, is the person who is a bodily witness? Here, monks, a certain person contacts with the body and dwells in those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This, monks, is called the person who is a bodily witness. I say, monks, that this monk should act with heedfulness. Why is that? Perhaps this venerable one, frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, balancing the faculties, might realize for himself with direct knowledge, and having realized, might enter and dwell in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for this monk, monks, I say: 'One should act with heedfulness.'
translations.mn70:2: "Monks, I eat only one meal a day. And while eating only one meal a day, I perceive little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling. Come, monks, you too eat only one meal a day. And while eating only one meal a day, you too will perceive little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: And what, monks, is a person who is a Dhamma-follower? Here, monks, some person does not dwell having contacted with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms, but having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed, and the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata is accepted by him after reflecting on it with wisdom. And these qualities are present in him: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom. This, monks, is called a person who is a Dhamma-follower. And I say of this monk too, monks, that he has something to be done by diligence. Why is that? Because it is possible that this venerable one, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, balancing his faculties, might in this very life realize for himself with direct knowledge, and having entered upon it, dwell in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, monks, I say that he has something to be done by diligence.
translations.mn70:22: Monks, I do not say that final knowledge is achieved all at once; rather, final knowledge is achieved by gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, is final knowledge achieved by gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress? Here, monks, one who has faith approaches; having approached, he attends; having attended, he lends ear; having lent ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he memorizes it; having memorized the Dhamma, he examines the meaning of the teachings; having examined the meaning, he gains a reflective acceptance of those teachings; having gained a reflective acceptance of the teachings, desire arises; when desire has arisen, he makes an effort; having made an effort, he scrutinizes; having scrutinized, he strives; being resolute, he realizes with the body the ultimate truth and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: Monks, there is no faith; there is no approaching; there is no attending; there is no lending ear; there is no hearing of the Dhamma; there is no memorizing of the Dhamma; there is no examining of the meaning; there is no reflective acceptance of the Dhamma; there is no desire; there is no effort; there is no scrutinizing; there is no striving. You have gone astray, monks, you have taken a wrong path. How far, monks, have these misguided persons strayed from this Dhamma and Discipline!
translations.mn70:25: Monks, there is a four-line exposition, having learned which, a wise person would soon understand the meaning. Shall I recite it to you, monks? Will you understand its meaning?" "Who are we, venerable sir, and who are the knowers of the Dhamma?"
translations.mn70:26: "Monks, even for that teacher who is fond of material gains, devoted to material gains, and lives mixed up with material gains, such a thought does not occur: 'May it be thus for us, and may we do this; may it not be thus for us, and may we not do this.' How much more so for the Tathāgata, who lives completely unmixed with material gains.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, traveling by stages in the Kāsi country, arrived at a market town of the Kāsis named Kīṭāgiri. There the Blessed One dwelled in the market town of the Kāsis, Kīṭāgiri.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka were residing in Kīṭāgiri. Then several monks approached the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka; having approached, they said to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka: "Friends, the Blessed One eats only one meal a day, and so does the Sangha of monks. And while eating only one meal a day, they perceive little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling. Come, friends, you too eat only one meal a day. And while eating only one meal a day, you too will perceive little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling." When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka said to those monks: "Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, and at the wrong time. And while eating in the evening, in the morning, and at the wrong time, we perceive little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable dwelling. Why should we give up what is visible here and now and pursue what is time-consuming? We will eat in the evening, in the morning, and at the wrong time."
translations.mn70:7: "Monks, do you not understand that I have taught the Dhamma thus: For one person, while experiencing a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; for another person, while experiencing a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. For one person, while experiencing a painful feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; for another person, while experiencing a painful feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. For one person, while experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; for another person, while experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma, in the brahmin Bhāradvāja's fire chamber, which was spread with grass.
translations.mn75:10: "But I, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly being a householder, endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing; with sounds cognizable by the ear ... with odors cognizable by the nose ... with tastes cognizable by the tongue ... with tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing. I had three palaces, Māgaṇḍiya: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, one for the summer. In the rainy-season palace, Māgaṇḍiya, I was entertained by female musicians for the four months of the rainy season, and I did not descend from the palace. Then later, having understood as they really are the origin and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed fever for sensual pleasures, and dwelled with a mind free from thirst, inwardly peaceful. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is this delight that is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—having attained a divine pleasure—abiding in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that."
translations.mn75:12: "Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, I formerly being a householder, endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing; with sounds cognizable by the ear ... with odors cognizable by the nose ... with tastes cognizable by the tongue ... with tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensual, and arousing. Then later, having understood as they really are the origin and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed fever for sensual pleasures, and dwelled with a mind free from thirst, inwardly peaceful. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is this delight that is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—having attained a divine pleasure—abiding in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that."
translations.mn75:13: "Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a man with leprosy, with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching his sore openings with his nails, were to cauterize his body with a charcoal pit. His friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen would bring a physician-surgeon. The physician-surgeon would prepare medicine for him. Through that medicine he would be cured of the leprosy and become well, happy, independent, master of himself, able to go where he likes. Then he would see another man with leprosy, with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching his sore openings with his nails, cauterizing his body with a charcoal pit. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that man envy that leprous man for the charcoal pit or for taking the medicine?" "No, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because, Master Gotama, when there is disease, medicine is to be used; when there is no disease, medicine is not to be used."
translations.mn75:16: "Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, sensual pleasures in the past were of painful contact and great affliction and great fever; sensual pleasures in the future will be of painful contact and great affliction and great fever; sensual pleasures in the present are of painful contact and great affliction and great fever. But these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, with impaired faculties, perceive what is actually painful contact in sensual pleasures as pleasant."
translations.mn75:17: "Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a man with leprosy, with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching his sore openings with his nails, cauterizes his body with a charcoal pit. The more, Māgaṇḍiya, that leprous man cauterizes his body with a charcoal pit, the more foul, more stinking, more putrid his sore openings become, and yet he gets a certain amount of gratification and enjoyment—that is, from the scratching of the sores; just so, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures and burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures and burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures increases and the more they burn with fever for sensual pleasures, and yet they get a certain amount of gratification and enjoyment—that is, dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure."
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or a royal minister, endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, who, without abandoning sensual craving, without dispelling the fever of sensuality, could dwell or is dwelling or will dwell with thirst abandoned, with a mind inwardly pacified?" "No, indeed, Venerable Gotama." "Good, Māgaṇḍiya. I too, Māgaṇḍiya, have never seen or heard of a king or a royal minister, endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, who, without abandoning sensual craving, without dispelling the fever of sensuality, could dwell or is dwelling or will dwell with thirst abandoned, with a mind inwardly pacified. But, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt or are dwelling or will dwell with thirst abandoned, with a mind inwardly pacified, all of them, having truly understood the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures, having abandoned sensual craving, having dispelled the fever of sensuality, have dwelt or are dwelling or will dwell with thirst abandoned, with a mind inwardly pacified."
translations.mn75:2: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he approached a certain grove for the day's abiding. Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn75:22: "I have such faith in Venerable Gotama. Venerable Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna." "Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man blind from birth; he would not see dark and light forms, would not see blue forms, would not see yellow forms, would not see red forms, would not see crimson forms, would not see the even and uneven, would not see the stars, would not see the sun and moon. His friends, companions, and relatives would provide him with a physician, a surgeon. That physician, a surgeon, would make a medicine. But by using that medicine, he would not produce eyesight, would not purify his vision. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, wouldn't that physician just get weariness and vexation?" "Yes, Venerable Gotama." "In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would not know health, would not see Nibbāna. That would be weariness for me, that would be vexation for me."
translations.mn75:24: "In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would know health, would see Nibbāna. With the arising of your vision, the desire and lust for the five aggregates subject to clinging would be abandoned; and it would occur to you: 'For a long time, indeed, have I been cheated, deceived, and defrauded by this mind. For I have been clinging only to form, clinging only to feeling, clinging only to perception, clinging only to formations, clinging only to consciousness. With clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.mn75:25: "I have such faith in Venerable Gotama. Venerable Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind." "Then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with good people. When you associate with good people, Māgaṇḍiya, you will hear the true Dhamma; when you hear the true Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will know for yourself, see for yourself: 'These are diseases, tumors, darts; here these diseases, tumors, darts cease without remainder. With the cessation of my clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, reveal what was hidden, show the way to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Venerable Gotama. I go for refuge to Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth in the presence of Venerable Gotama, may I receive the full ordination."
translations.mn75:27: "Māgaṇḍiya, one who was formerly a follower of another teaching and desires the going forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, desires the full ordination, lives on probation for four months; at the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, they give the going forth, give the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu. However, I allow for individual differences in this matter." "Venerable sir, if those who were formerly followers of other teachings, desiring the going forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, desiring the full ordination, live on probation for four months, and at the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, they give the going forth, give the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu, then I will live on probation for four years, and at the end of the four years, let the bhikkhus, if satisfied, give me the going forth, give me the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu."
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvāja. Māgaṇḍiya saw a grass mat prepared in the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvāja. Having seen it, he said to the brahmin Bhāradvāja: 'For whom, sir Bhāradvāja, is this grass mat prepared in your fire chamber? It seems suitable for an ascetic's lodging.'
translations.mn75:6: The Blessed One heard with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, this conversation between the brahmin Bhāradvāja and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya. Then in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, the Blessed One approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvāja; having approached, he sat down on the prepared grass mat. Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Bhāradvāja: 'Was there, Bhāradvāja, some conversation between you and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning this very grass mat?' When this was said, the brahmin Bhāradvāja, astonished and with hair standing on end, said to the Blessed One: 'Indeed, we wanted to tell this to Master Gotama. Yet Master Gotama has spoken of what was unspoken.'
translations.mn75:7: And this conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin Bhāradvāja was left unfinished. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvāja where the Blessed One was; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyi, another five qualities by which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and having honored and respected, dwell in dependence. What five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for higher virtue: 'The ascetic Gotama is endowed with the highest aggregate of virtue.'
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples; practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four foundations of mindfulness. Here, Udāyi, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings ... mind in mind ... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples; practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyi, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples; practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four bases for spiritual power. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations; that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations; that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations; that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples; practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the faculty of faith that leads to peace, leads to enlightenment; he develops the faculty of energy ... the faculty of mindfulness ... the faculty of concentration ... the faculty of wisdom that leads to peace, leads to enlightenment. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: Now at that time several well-known wanderers were dwelling in the wanderers' park at the Peacocks' Sanctuary, namely: Annabhāra, Varadhara, and the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples; practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and matures in release; he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena ... the enlightenment factor of energy ... the enlightenment factor of rapture ... the enlightenment factor of tranquility ... the enlightenment factor of concentration ... the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and matures in release. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the eight liberations. One with form sees forms; this is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. One is resolved only upon the beautiful; this is the third liberation. With the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation. By completely transcending the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. By completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the ten kasina bases. One perceives the earth kasina above, below, across, undivided, measureless. One perceives the water kasina ... One perceives the fire kasina ... One perceives the air kasina ... One perceives the blue kasina ... One perceives the yellow kasina ... One perceives the red kasina ... One perceives the white kasina ... One perceives the space kasina ... One perceives the consciousness kasina above, below, across, undivided, measureless. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyi, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Just as a skilled bath attendant or his apprentice, having kneaded soap-powder in a metal basin, sprinkles it again and again with water, so that the ball of soap-powder becomes saturated, soaked, permeated within and without, yet does not ooze; so too, Udāyi, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is filled with rapture and happiness born of concentration. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration. Just as a deep lake with spring-water welling up from within, having no inflow from east, west, north, or south, and with the heavens not supplying showers from time to time, would have a cool spring welling up from within the lake and drenching, steeping, filling, and pervading the lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of the whole lake untouched by cool water; so too, Udāyi, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness free from rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the happiness free from rapture. Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or white lotuses, or red lotuses, some lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, remain submerged in the water and flourish, drenched, steeped, filled, and pervaded with cool water from their tips to their roots, so that there is no part of those lotuses untouched by cool water; so too, Udāyi, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness free from rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the happiness free from rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. He sits pervading this body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the pure, bright mind. Just as a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his whole body untouched by the white cloth; so too, Udāyi, a monk sits pervading this body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body untouched by the pure, bright mind. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rajagaha for alms. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "It is too early to walk for alms in Rajagaha. Why don't I go to the wanderers' park at the peacocks' feeding ground, to where the wanderer Sakuludayi is?"
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. Just as, Udāyi, a strong conch-blower could easily make himself heard in the four directions; so too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, recollect their manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus they recollect their manifold past lives in their modes and details. Just as, Udāyi, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and then from that village return to his own village. He might think: 'I went from my own village to that village, and there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, remained silent thus; from that village I went to that other village, and there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, remained silent thus; and from that village I have returned to my own village.' So too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, recollect their manifold past lives... in their modes and details. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their kamma: 'These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, hell; but these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their kamma. Just as, Udāyi, if there were two houses with doors, and a man with good eyesight standing between them would see people entering and leaving a house, walking about and wandering around; so too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn... and understand how beings fare according to their kamma... And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, through the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge. Just as, Udāyi, in a mountain glen there might be a lake that is clear, serene, and undisturbed, and a man with good eyesight standing on the bank would see oysters and shells, gravel and pebbles, and schools of fish swimming about and resting. He would think: 'This lake is clear, serene, and undisturbed, and here are these oysters and shells, gravel and pebbles, and schools of fish swimming about and resting.' So too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a practice whereby my disciples, practicing accordingly, through the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge. And there, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One went to where the wanderer Sakuludayi was. Then the wanderer Sakuludayi said to the Blessed One: "Come, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is welcome. It has been a long time, Venerable Sir, since the Blessed One took the opportunity to come here. Let the Blessed One sit down; this seat is prepared." The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The wanderer Sakuludayi also took a low seat and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sakuludayi: "Udāyi, on what topic are you now sitting together, and what conversation was left unfinished?"
translations.mn77:7: "But, Udāyi, how many qualities do you see in me because of which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me?"
