translations.mn77:9: "If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama eats little; he is one who praises eating little,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, there are, Udāyī, disciples of mine who eat only once a day, or once every two days, or once every three days, or once every four days. But I, Udāyī, sometimes eat from this bowl just enough to fill the hollow of my hand, or even more. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama eats little; he is one who praises eating little,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, then those disciples of mine who eat only once a day, or once every two days, or once every three days, or once every four days would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of this quality. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of robe,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, there are, Udāyī, disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing coarse robes; they collect rags from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or shop streets, make them into a patchwork cloak, and wear it. But I, Udāyī, sometimes wear householder's robes that are strong, thick, and soft. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of robe,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, then those disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing coarse robes; who collect rags from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or shop streets, make them into a patchwork cloak, and wear it, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of this quality. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, there are, Udāyī, disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters, who practice continuous walking for alms, delighting in the practice of gleaning; when they have entered a village, even if invited to a seat, they do not accept. But I, Udāyī, sometimes eat when invited, eating fine rice with various curries and sauces. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, then those disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters, who practice continuous walking for alms, delighting in the practice of gleaning; when they have entered a village, even if invited to a seat, they do not accept, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of this quality. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of lodging,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, there are, Udāyī, disciples of mine who dwell at the foot of trees, in the open air; they do not use a roof for eight months of the year. But I, Udāyī, sometimes dwell in gabled houses, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolted doors and closed windows. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging; he is one who praises contentment with any kind of lodging,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, then those disciples of mine who dwell at the foot of trees, in the open air; who do not use a roof for eight months of the year, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of this quality. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded; he is one who praises seclusion,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, there are, Udāyī, disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, living in remote lodgings, who have plunged into remote forest and jungle lodgings; they come into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyī, sometimes dwell crowded by monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and sectarian disciples. If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded; he is one who praises seclusion,' and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on that, then those disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, living in remote lodgings, who have plunged into remote forest and jungle lodgings; who come into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of this quality. Thus, Udāyī, my disciples do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, nor live in dependence on me, because of these five qualities."
translations.mn7:11: And when he obtains the meaning and the Dhamma, and obtains the joy connected with the Dhamma, then joy arises in the joyful one; being joyful, the body becomes tranquil; with the body tranquil, he feels pleasure; being pleased, the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: 'There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and there is an escape beyond this realm of perception.'
translations.mn7:18: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensuality, liberated from the taint of existence, liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' This is called, monks, 'a monk who has bathed with an inner bathing.'
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: 'Does Master Gotama go to the Bāhukā river to bathe?' 'Why, brahmin, the Bāhukā river? What can the Bāhukā river do?' 'Master Gotama, the Bāhukā river is considered auspicious by many people, considered meritorious by many people; and many people wash away their evil deeds in the Bāhukā river.'
translations.mn7:2: Just as, monks, a cloth that is stained and soiled, when a dyer applies to it any dye—whether blue, yellow, red, or pink—it will appear of a bad color, of an impure color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth. So too, monks, when the mind is defiled, a bad destination is to be expected. Just as, monks, a cloth that is clean and bright, when a dyer applies to it any dye—whether blue, yellow, red, or pink—it will appear of a good color, of a pure color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth. So too, monks, when the mind is undefiled, a good destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja in verse: 'Bāhukā and Adhikakkā, and the Gaya and Sundarikā, Sarassatī and Payāga, and the Bāhumatī river too—a fool may plunge into them constantly, but his evil deeds are not cleansed. What will Sundarikā do? What will Payāga do? What will the Bāhukā river do? They do not cleanse a man of his evil deeds, one who has done cruel actions. For one who is pure it is always the holy day; for one who is pure it is always the observance day; for one who is pure, with pure actions, the vow is always fulfilled. Bathe here, brahmin, make yourself safe for all beings. If you speak no falsehood, if you harm no living being, if you take nothing not given, if you are faithful and not greedy, what need have you to go to Gaya? Your well is Gaya itself.'
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed are a defilement of the mind; ill will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind; hostility is a defilement of the mind; denigration is a defilement of the mind; domineering is a defilement of the mind; envy is a defilement of the mind; stinginess is a defilement of the mind; deceit is a defilement of the mind; fraud is a defilement of the mind; obstinacy is a defilement of the mind; presumption is a defilement of the mind; conceit is a defilement of the mind; arrogance is a defilement of the mind; vanity is a defilement of the mind; negligence is a defilement of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He is possessed of verified confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.'
translations.mn7:7: He is possessed of verified confidence in the Sangha thus: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering among the Kurus with a large Sangha of monks when he arrived at a town of the Kurus named Thullakoṭṭhita.
translations.mn82:11: Then Raṭṭhapāla's friends approached Raṭṭhapāla's parents and said: 'Mother and father, Raṭṭhapāla is lying there on the bare ground saying: "Here I shall die or receive the going forth." If you do not permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, he will die right there. But if you permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, you will see him after he has gone forth. And if Raṭṭhapāla does not enjoy going forth from the home life into homelessness, what other course will he take? He will return right here. Permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness.' 'We permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, but after he has gone forth he must visit his parents.' Then Raṭṭhapāla's friends approached Raṭṭhapāla and said: 'Get up, friend Raṭṭhapāla, you are permitted by your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. And after you have gone forth you must visit your parents.'
translations.mn82:12: Then Raṭṭhapāla rose up, regained his strength, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, I am permitted by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Let the Blessed One give me the going forth.'
translations.mn82:13: The clansman Raṭṭhapāla received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the full ordination. Then, not long after the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was fully ordained, half a month later, the Blessed One, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he wished, set out on tour towards Sāvatthī. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One stayed in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park.
translations.mn82:14: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—having realized for himself with direct knowledge that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—having attained it, he dwelled. He directly knew: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being." And the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having risen from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, put his lodging in order, and taking his bowl and robe, set out on tour towards Thullakoṭṭhika. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla stayed in the deer park of King Korabya. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Walking for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father's house.
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having his hair combed in the middle hall of the entrance porch. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming in the distance. Seeing him, he said: "These shaven-headed ascetics have made our only son, dear and beloved, go forth." Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla received neither alms nor a refusal at his own father's house; on the contrary, he received abuse.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time a slave woman belonging to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relatives was about to throw away some old porridge. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that slave woman: "If that, sister, is to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl." Then that slave woman of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relatives, pouring that old porridge into the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, recognized the features of his hands, feet, and voice. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's slave woman approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother; having approached, she said to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother: "Please know, madam: the young master Raṭṭhapāla has arrived." "If you speak the truth, girl, I will make you a free woman." Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father; having approached, she said to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father: "Please know, householder: the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, it seems, has arrived."
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating that old porridge while leaning against a wall. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, he said to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "Is it possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you are eating old porridge? Shouldn't you, dear Raṭṭhapāla, go to your own house?" "Where is our house, householder, for us who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did go to your house, householder; there we received neither alms nor a refusal; on the contrary, we received abuse." "Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go to the house." "Enough, householder, my meal for today is done." "Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, consent to tomorrow's meal." The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented by silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, having understood the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's consent, approached his own house; having approached, he had a large heap of gold and money made and covered it with mats, and then addressed the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives: "Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with the ornaments with which you were adorned when you were dear and pleasing to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla in the past."
translations.mn82:21: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, when the night had passed, had sumptuous food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own house, and announced the time to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready."
translations.mn82:22: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, approached his own father's house; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, having uncovered that heap of gold and money, said to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother's wealth; another is paternal wealth; another is ancestral wealth. It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, to enjoy wealth and to make merit. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit." "If you would act according to my words, householder, having loaded this heap of gold and money onto carts and having them taken away, you would have it dumped in the middle of the Ganges river. Why is that? Because, householder, from this cause, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise for you."
translations.mn82:23: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives, each taking hold of his feet, said to Venerable Raṭhapāla: 'What kind of nymphs are they, dear sir, for whose sake you lead the holy life?' 'Sisters, we do not lead the holy life for the sake of nymphs.' 'Venerable Raṭhapāla addresses us as "sister"!' they fainted right there and fell down.
translations.mn82:24: Then Venerable Raṭhapāla said to his father: 'Householder, if food is to be given, give it; do not harass us.' 'Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.' Then Venerable Raṭhapāla's father served and satisfied Venerable Raṭhapāla with his own hands with choice hard and soft food. Then Venerable Raṭhapāla, having eaten and washed his bowl and hands, standing right there, spoke these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then Venerable Raṭhapāla, having spoken these verses while standing, went to King Koravya's deer park; having gone, he sat down at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed the gamekeeper: 'Clear the deer park, good gamekeeper; we will go to see the beautiful grounds.' 'Yes, lord,' replied the gamekeeper to King Koravya, and while clearing the deer park, he saw Venerable Raṭhapāla sitting at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Having seen him, he went to King Koravya; having gone, he said to King Koravya: 'Your deer park is cleared, lord. There is here a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading family in this same Thullakoṭṭhita, whom you were constantly praising; he is sitting at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding.' 'Well then, good gamekeeper, enough of the park grounds for today. Now we will pay homage to Master Raṭṭhapāla.'
translations.mn82:28: Then King Koravya, having said, 'Distribute all the prepared food and drink there,' had fine carriages harnessed, mounted a fine carriage, and set out from Thullakoṭṭhita with fine carriages and the great pomp of a king to see Venerable Raṭhapāla. He went by carriage as far as the ground allowed, then dismounted from the carriage and approached Venerable Raṭhapāla on foot with a large retinue. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Raṭhapāla. When the courteous and friendly talk was finished, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭhapāla: 'Let Master Raṭhapāla sit on this elephant rug.' 'Enough, great king, you sit; I am sitting on my own seat.' King Koravya sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: 'Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss, possessed of which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. What four? Loss through aging, loss through illness, loss of wealth, loss of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita went to the Blessed One; having gone, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after an exchange of friendly and courteous talk, sat down to one side; some raised their hands in añjali towards the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One's presence and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: 'These, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of loss, possessed of which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. You do not have these. Knowing or seeing or hearing what, did Master Raṭṭhapāla go forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:35: 'Great king, there are four summaries of the Dhamma proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, knowing and seeing and hearing which I went forth from the home life into homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading family in that same Thullakoṭṭhita, was sitting in that assembly. Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla thought: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life, bright as a polished conch shell. What if I shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:6: Then, soon after the well-to-do brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had left, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure like a polished shell. I wish, venerable sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. Let the Blessed One give me the going forth." "But, Raṭṭhapāla, have you obtained permission from your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness?" "No, venerable sir, I have not obtained permission from my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness." "Raṭṭhapāla, the Tathāgatas do not give the going forth to a son without the permission of his parents." "Then, venerable sir, I will act in such a way that my parents will give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness."
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One dwelled at Opāsāda, in the deva forest, the sāla forest, to the north of Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large assembly of brahmins, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was concluded, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Blessed One was sitting having exchanged some courteous and amiable talk with some elderly brahmins. Now at that time a young brahmin student named Kāpaṭika, young, shaven-headed, sixteen years old, a master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, he was fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man, was sitting in that assembly. He interrupted the talk of the elderly brahmins while they were conversing with the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rebuked the young student Kāpaṭika: "Venerable Bhāradvāja, do not interrupt the talk of the elderly brahmins while they are conversing. Wait until the talk is finished." When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said this to the Blessed One: "Let not Master Gotama rebuke the young student Kāpaṭika. The young student Kāpaṭika is a clansman, learned, wise, a good speaker; he is capable of discussing this statement with Master Gotama."
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was dwelling at Opāsāda, a crown property given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal grant, a brahmin gift, teeming with living beings, rich in grass, wood, water, and grain.
translations.mn95:20: When, upon examining him, he sees that he is purified from states that cause delusion; then he places faith in him. Having faith, he approaches him. Having approached, he pays respect to him. Paying respect, he gives ear. Giving ear, he hears the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he memorizes it. Having memorized the teachings, he examines their meaning. Examining their meaning, he gains a reflective acceptance of those teachings. When he has gained a reflective acceptance of those teachings, zeal arises. With zeal aroused, he applies his will. Having applied his will, he scrutinizes. Having scrutinized, he strives. Resolutely striving, he realizes with the body the supreme truth and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom. To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is an awakening to truth; to this extent one awakens to truth; to this extent we describe awakening to truth. But as yet there is no final arrival at truth."
translations.mn95:33: "But, Master Gotama, what quality is helpful for approaching? We ask Master Gotama about the quality that is helpful for approaching." "For approaching, Bhāradvāja, faith is helpful. If faith does not arise, one does not approach. But because faith arises, therefore one approaches. Therefore, for approaching, faith is helpful."
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī had gone up to the upper terrace of his mansion for his midday rest. The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in groups and flocks, heading north towards the deva forest, the sāla forest. Seeing this, he addressed his steward: "Why, good steward, are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in groups and flocks, heading north towards the deva forest, the sāla forest?"
translations.mn9:11: "And what, friend, is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking a new existence. What four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. With the origin of craving comes the origin of nutriment; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of nutriment. This Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration."
translations.mn9:12: "When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, he abolishes the underlying tendency to aversion, he uproots the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' he abandons ignorance and arouses true knowledge, and in this very life he makes an end of suffering. To this extent also, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma."
translations.mn9:15: And what, friend, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, friend, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friend, is the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, friend, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friend, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This, friend, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friend, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view ... right concentration. This, friend, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: 'Right view, right view,' it is said, friend. To what extent, friend, is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma? 'We would come from afar, friend, to learn the meaning of this statement from Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will remember it.' 'Then, friend, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: Saying, 'Good, friend,' those bhikkhus, having approved and rejoiced in Venerable Sāriputta's words, asked him a further question: 'But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?'
translations.mn9:3: When, friend, a noble disciple understands the unwholesome and the root of the unwholesome, and understands the wholesome and the root of the wholesome—to that extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friend, is the unwholesome, what is the root of the unwholesome, what is the wholesome, what is the root of the wholesome? Killing living beings, friend, is unwholesome; taking what is not given is unwholesome; sexual misconduct is unwholesome; false speech is unwholesome; malicious speech is unwholesome; harsh speech is unwholesome; gossip is unwholesome; covetousness is unwholesome; ill will is unwholesome; wrong view is unwholesome. This, friend, is called the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friend, is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is a root of the unwholesome, hatred is a root of the unwholesome, delusion is a root of the unwholesome. This, friend, is called the root of the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friend, is the root of the wholesome? Non-greed is a root of the wholesome, non-hatred is a root of the wholesome, non-delusion is a root of the wholesome. This, friend, is called the root of the wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friend, is a taint, what is the origin of taints, what is the cessation of taints, what is the path leading to the cessation of taints? There are, friend, these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the origin of ignorance there is the origin of taints; with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of taints; this Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of taints; that is, right view ... right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands the unwholesome, thus understands the root of the unwholesome, thus understands the wholesome, thus understands the root of the wholesome, then, having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having eliminated the underlying tendency to aversion, having rooted out the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, he here and now makes an end of suffering. To that extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.sn1.10:2: 'For those dwelling in the forest, peaceful, leading the holy life, eating a single meal a day: by what is their complexion so serene?'
translations.sn1.10:3: 'They do not sorrow over the past, nor do they yearn for the future. They sustain themselves with what is present: hence their complexion is so serene.
translations.sn1.17:1: 'Hard to do and hard to endure is the ascetic life for the incompetent; for many are the obstacles there where the fool sinks down.'
translations.sn1.17:2: 'For how many days would one practice the ascetic life if one does not restrain the mind? One would sink down at every step, under the sway of one's thoughts.'
translations.sn1.17:3: 'Like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its own shell, a bhikkhu should restrain his thoughts, not dependent, not harming others, fully quenched, he would blame no one.'
translations.sn1.18:1: 'Is there any person in the world restrained by shame, who avoids blame like a fine horse avoids the whip?'
translations.sn1.18:2: 'Few are those restrained by shame, who always live mindfully; having reached the end of suffering, they fare evenly amidst the uneven.'
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then, when the night was advanced, a certain deity of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Blessed One: 'How, dear sir, did you cross the flood?' 'By not halting, friend, and by not straining I crossed the flood.' 'But how, dear sir, by not halting and by not straining did you cross the flood?' 'When I halted, friend, then I sank; but when I strained, then I was swept away. It is in this way, friend, that by not halting and by not straining I crossed the flood.'
translations.sn1.1:2: 'After a long time I see a brahmin fully quenched, who by not halting and not straining has crossed over attachment in the world.'
translations.sn1.1:3: This is what that deity said. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, thinking, 'The Teacher has approved of me,' paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he disappeared right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Grove. Then, in the morning, Venerable Samiddhi, having risen early, approached the Tapodā to bathe his limbs. Having bathed his limbs in the Tapodā and emerged, he stood in one robe drying his limbs. Then a certain deity, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Tapodā, approached Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, she stood in the air and addressed Venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: "You beg without having enjoyed, monk, for indeed you do not beg after having enjoyed; having enjoyed, monk, then beg, lest time pass you by."
translations.sn1.20:20: "Beings perceive what can be expressed, established in what can be expressed; not fully understanding what can be expressed, they come under the yoke of Death.
translations.sn1.20:21: But having fully understood what can be expressed, one does not conceive of one who expresses; for that is not for him, by which they could speak of him; if you know, speak, O spirit."
translations.sn1.20:22: "Indeed, venerable sir, I do not understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One."
translations.sn1.20:23: "One who conceives himself as equal, superior, or inferior, by that he would dispute; unshaken among the three discriminations, 'equal' or 'superior' does not exist for him; if you know, speak, O spirit."
translations.sn1.20:25: "He abandoned reckoning, did not fall into conceit, he cut off craving here for name-and-form; him, with bonds cut, free from distress, without longing, seeking, they did not find; gods and humans here or beyond, in heavens or in all abodes.
translations.sn1.20:3: "I do not know the time, the time is hidden, not seen; therefore I beg without having enjoyed, lest time pass me by."
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, having descended to the ground, said to Venerable Samiddhi: "You are young, monk, gone forth, with black hair, endowed with youth, in the prime of life, not having indulged in sensual pleasures. Enjoy, monk, human sensual pleasures; do not abandon the visible benefit and pursue what is of time."
translations.sn1.20:5: "I do not, friend, abandon the visible benefit and pursue what is of time. Rather, friend, I abandon what is of time and pursue the visible benefit. For, friend, sensual pleasures of time have been described by the Blessed One as full of suffering, full of despair; the danger herein is greater. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced individually by the wise."
translations.sn1.20:6: "And how, monk, are sensual pleasures of time described by the Blessed One as full of suffering, full of despair, the danger herein greater? How is this Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced individually by the wise?"
translations.sn1.20:7: "I, friend, am newly gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to explain in detail. This Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Grove. Approach the Blessed One and ask about this matter. As the Blessed One explains to you, so you should remember it."
translations.sn1.20:8: "It is not easy, monk, for us to approach that Blessed One, surrounded as he is by other powerful deities. But if you, monk, approach the Blessed One and ask about this matter, we too will come to hear the Dhamma." "Yes, friend," Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity and approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Samiddhi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.21:2: "As if struck by a sword, as if his head were on fire, a mindful monk should wander forth for the abandoning of sensual desire."
translations.sn1.21:3: "As if struck by a sword, as if his head were on fire, a mindful monk should wander forth for the abandoning of identity view."
translations.sn1.25:1: "A monk who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, bearing his final body, might say 'I speak,' or might say 'They speak of me.'"
translations.sn1.25:2: "A monk who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, bearing his final body, might say 'I speak,' or might say 'They speak of me;' having understood the convention in the world as skilled, he would speak merely in accordance with convention."
translations.sn1.25:3: "A monk who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, bearing his final body, having approached conceit, might he say 'I speak,' or might say 'They speak of me'?"
translations.sn1.25:4: "For one who has abandoned conceit, there are no bonds, all bonds of conceit are dispelled; that wise one, transcending conceiving, might say 'I speak.'
translations.sn1.25:5: He might say 'They speak of me,' having understood the convention in the world as skilled; he would speak merely in accordance with convention."
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, when the night had advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.2:5: "With the destruction of delight in existence, with the cessation of perception and consciousness, with the cessation and appeasement of feelings, thus indeed, friend, I know the release, the liberation, the seclusion of beings."
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, when the night had advanced, several deities from the Satullapa group, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.36:2: "Faith is a person's companion; if he does not dwell in faithlessness, fame and renown come to him, and he goes to heaven after leaving the body."
translations.sn1.36:4: "He should abandon anger, renounce conceit, transcend all fetters; him, not clinging to name-and-form, possessing nothing, attachments do not pursue."
translations.sn1.36:5: "The foolish, unwise people indulge in heedlessness; but the wise one guards heedfulness as the best treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: Do not indulge in heedlessness, do not delight in intimacy with sensual pleasures; the heedful one, meditating, attains supreme happiness."
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer park. At that time the Blessed One's foot was injured by a stone splinter. Severe, indeed, were the feelings that arose in the Blessed One—bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, severe, acute, disagreeable, unpleasant; yet the Blessed One, mindful and fully aware, endured them without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having folded his outer robe in four, lay down on his right side in the lion posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and fully aware.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows and precepts, practicing harsh austerity for a hundred years—their minds are not rightly liberated; of inferior nature, they do not go beyond.
translations.sn1.38:11: For one who desires conceit, there is no taming here; for the uncomposed, there is no sagehood. Dwelling alone in the forest, heedless, one cannot cross the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, well-composed within, pure in heart, everywhere fully liberated; dwelling alone in the forest, heedful, one can cross the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred Satullapa deities, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One in the middle of the night; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity uttered this inspired utterance in the Blessed One's presence: "Indeed, the ascetic Gotama is a nāga; like a nāga, he endures arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, severe, acute, disagreeable, unpleasant, mindful and fully aware, without being distressed."
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity uttered this inspired utterance in the Blessed One's presence: "Indeed, the ascetic Gotama is a lion; like a lion, he endures arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, severe, acute, disagreeable, unpleasant, mindful and fully aware, without being distressed."
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity uttered this inspired utterance in the Blessed One's presence: "See the concentration well-developed and the mind well-liberated, not bent forward, not bent back, and not held in check by forceful suppression. Who would think to surpass such a man-nāga, man-lion, man-thoroughbred, man-bull, man-bearer of burdens, man-tamed, except through lack of vision?"
translations.sn1.38:9: Those who practice the five Vedas for a hundred years, ascetic brahmins—their minds are not rightly liberated; of inferior nature, they do not go beyond.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then a certain deity, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One in the middle of the night; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity spoke these verses in the Blessed One's presence:
translations.sn1.41:4: What is given yields pleasant fruit, but what is not given does not do so; thieves take it, kings take it, fire burns it, it is lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then in the end one leaves it, the body together with its possessions; having understood this, the wise person should enjoy and give. Having given and enjoyed according to one's means, blameless, one goes to a heavenly state.
translations.sn1.42:1: "What giving gives strength? What giving gives beauty? What giving gives happiness? What giving gives vision? And who is the giver of all? Explain this to me, as I ask."
translations.sn1.42:2: "Food-giving gives strength, cloth-giving gives beauty; vehicle-giving gives happiness, lamp-giving gives vision.
translations.sn1.42:3: And he is the giver of all, who gives a dwelling; he also gives the deathless, who teaches the Dhamma."
translations.sn1.51:1: "What is good until old age? What is good when established? What is the treasure of humans? What is hard for thieves to steal?"
translations.sn1.51:2: "Virtue is good until old age, faith is good when established; wisdom is the treasure of humans, merit is hard for thieves to steal."
translations.sn1.55:1: "What produces a person? What runs about for him? What enters into saṁsāra? What is his great fear?"
translations.sn1.55:2: "Craving produces a person, his mind runs about; a being enters into saṁsāra, suffering is his great fear."
translations.sn1.56:1: "What produces a person? What runs about for him? What enters into saṁsāra? From what is he not freed?"
translations.sn1.56:2: "Craving produces a person, his mind runs about; a being enters into saṁsāra, from suffering he is not freed."
translations.sn1.57:1: "What produces a person? What runs about for him? What enters into saṁsāra? What is his refuge?"
translations.sn1.57:2: "Craving produces a person, his mind runs about; a being enters into saṁsāra, kamma is his refuge."
translations.sn1.59:1: "What is a person's companion? What directs him? Delighting in what does a mortal become freed from all suffering?"
translations.sn1.59:2: "Faith is a person's companion, and wisdom directs him; delighting in Nibbāna, a mortal becomes freed from all suffering."
translations.sn1.62:1: "By what is the world led? By what is it dragged along? For the sake of what one thing are all under control?"
translations.sn1.62:2: "By mind the world is led, by mind it is dragged along; for the sake of this one thing, mind, all are under control."
translations.sn1.63:2: "By craving the world is led, by craving it is dragged along; for the sake of this one thing, craving, all are under control."
translations.sn1.64:1: "What is the fetter of the world? What is its wandering about? By abandoning what is it called Nibbāna?"
translations.sn1.64:2: "Delight is the fetter of the world, thought is its wandering about; by abandoning craving, it is called Nibbāna."
translations.sn1.65:1: "What is the bond of the world? What is its wandering about? By abandoning what does one cut off all bonds?"
translations.sn1.65:2: "Delight is the bond of the world, thought is its wandering about; by abandoning craving, one cuts off all bonds."
translations.sn1.69:1: "By what is the world bound? By the removal of what is it freed? By abandoning what does one cut off all bonds?"
translations.sn1.69:2: "By desire the world is bound, by the removal of desire it is freed; by abandoning desire, one cuts off all bonds."
translations.sn1.71:2: "Having cut off what does one sleep happily? Having cut off what does one not sorrow? What one thing's slaughter do you approve of, Gotama?"
translations.sn1.71:3: "Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not sorrow. The slaughter of anger, O deity, with its poisonous root and honeyed tip—this the noble ones praise; for having cut it off, one does not sorrow."
translations.sn1.73:1: "What here is a person's best wealth? What well-practiced brings happiness? What indeed is the sweetest of tastes? How living do they declare the best life?"
translations.sn1.73:2: "Faith is here the best wealth for a person; well-practiced Dhamma brings happiness; truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes; they say a life lived with wisdom is the best."
translations.sn1.7:2: "Those whose teachings are not understood are led into the doctrines of others; asleep, they do not awaken; it is time for them to awaken."
translations.sn1.7:3: "Those whose teachings are well understood are not led into the doctrines of others; fully awakened, rightly knowing, they fare evenly in the uneven."
translations.sn1.8:2: "Those whose teachings are well forgotten are led into the doctrines of others; asleep, they do not awaken; it is time for them to awaken."
translations.sn1.8:3: "Those whose teachings are not forgotten are not led into the doctrines of others; fully awakened, rightly knowing, they fare evenly in the uneven."
translations.sn11.14:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rajagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the devas of the Thirty-three: 'Do not, dear sirs, find fault with this young deva. For, dear sirs, this young deva, formerly being a human being, undertook faith, undertook virtue, undertook learning, undertook generosity, undertook wisdom in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathagata. Having undertaken faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathagata, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the devas of the Thirty-three. He outshines the other devas in beauty and glory.' Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, conciliating the devas of the Thirty-three, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: "Therefore the wise should devote themselves to faith and virtue, confidence and insight into the Dhamma, remembering the instruction of the Buddhas."
translations.sn11.15:1: At Savatthi in Jeta's Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: "What, venerable sir, is a delightful park for humans?"
translations.sn11.15:2: "Parks, shrines, woods, and well-made lotus ponds are not worth a sixteenth part of a delightful park for humans."
translations.sn11.22:1: At Savatthi in Jeta's Grove. There ... he said this: "Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a certain yakkha, ugly and misshapen, was sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas. There, bhikkhus, the devas of the Thirty-three grumbled, complained, and protested: 'It is wonderful, sir, it is amazing! This yakkha, ugly and misshapen, is sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas.' However much, bhikkhus, the devas of the Thirty-three grumbled, complained, and protested, that much more handsome, good-looking, and lovely did that yakkha become.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approached that anger-eating yakkha; having approached, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, kneeling down with his right knee on the ground, he extended his joined palms in reverential salutation towards that anger-eating yakkha and announced his name three times: 'I am Sakka, dear sir, lord of the devas; I am Sakka, dear sir, lord of the devas.' However much, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, announced his name, that much uglier and more misshapen did that yakkha become. Having become uglier and more misshapen, he then and there disappeared. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, having sat down in his own seat, conciliating the devas of the Thirty-three, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: "'My mind is not easily upset, nor am I easily led by anger; I do not get angry for long, nor does anger persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry, I do not speak harshly, nor do I praise my virtues; I restrain myself, seeing my own good.'"
translations.sn11.24:2: "Bhikkhus, there are these two fools. One who does not see a transgression as a transgression, and one who does not properly accept the confession of a transgression according to the Dhamma—these, bhikkhus, are the two fools. Bhikkhus, there are these two wise ones. One who sees a transgression as a transgression, and one who properly accepts the confession of a transgression according to the Dhamma—these, bhikkhus, are the two wise ones.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once upon a time, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, conciliating the devas of the Thirty-three in the Sudhamma assembly hall, on that occasion recited this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: "'Let anger not overpower you; do not become hostile towards friends; do not blame the blameless; do not speak divisive words; for anger crushes evil people like a mountain.'"
translations.sn11.3:1: At Savatthi. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you do not recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.' For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Dhamma, whatever fear, terror, or horror there may be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you do not recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Sangha, whatever fear, terror, or horror there may be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the Tathagata is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, fearless, undaunted, not prone to flight." This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:
translations.sn11.3:13: "In the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, bhikkhus, recollect the Buddha; there will be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you do not recollect the Buddha, the foremost in the world, the bull among men, then recollect the Dhamma, well taught, leading out.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you do not recollect the Dhamma, well taught, leading out, then recollect the Sangha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: Thus, bhikkhus, recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, there will be no fear, terror, or horror."
translations.sn11.3:2: "Once upon a time, monks, a battle between the devas and the asuras had broken out. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the devas of the Thirty-three:
translations.sn11.3:3: 'If, dear sirs, fear, terror, or hair-raising should arise in the devas who have gone to battle, at that time you should look up to my banner. For if you look up to my banner, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there may be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look up to my banner, then you should look up to the banner of the deva-king Pajāpati. For if you look up to the banner of the deva-king Pajāpati, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there may be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? Because, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion; he is fearful, terrified, alarmed, and prone to flee.
translations.sn11.3:9: But I, monks, say this: 'If, monks, when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, fear, terror, or hair-raising should arise, at that time you should recollect me: "Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, a fully enlightened Buddha, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One." For if you recollect me, monks, whatever fear, terror, or hair-raising there may be, that will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: He acts for the good of both, for his own and the other's; knowing the other is provoked, he mindfully becomes calm.
translations.sn11.5:14: But when, monks, the verses spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, were spoken, the devas applauded, and the asuras were silent. Then, monks, the retinues of both the devas and the asuras said this: 'Verses were spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras. And those are with rod and weapon, thus there is quarreling, thus dispute, thus conflict. Verses were spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas. And those are without rod and without weapon, thus there is no quarreling, thus no dispute, thus no conflict. Victory is by the well-spoken words of Sakka, lord of the devas.' Thus, monks, victory was by the well-spoken words of Sakka, lord of the devas."
translations.sn11.5:2: 'Fools would break out even more, if there were no restrainer; therefore, with a harsh rod, the wise one should restrain the fool.'
translations.sn11.5:3: But when, monks, the verse spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, was spoken, the asuras applauded, and the devas were silent. Then, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, said to Sakka, lord of the devas: 'Speak a verse, lord of the devas.' When this was said, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: 'This indeed, I think, is the restraint of a fool: knowing the other is provoked, one mindfully becomes calm.'
translations.sn11.5:5: But when, monks, the verse spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, was spoken, the devas applauded, and the asuras were silent. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to Vepacitti, lord of the asuras: 'Speak a verse, Vepacitti.' When this was said, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: 'This indeed I see as a fault of forbearance, Vāsava, when a fool thinks, "He forbears out of fear of me"; the stupid one attacks more, like a cow fleeing more and more.'
translations.sn11.5:8: 'Let him think what he will, whether or not he forbears out of fear of me; the highest good is the good of both, nothing greater than patience is found.
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park … "There are, monks, these four nutriments for the sustenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the sustenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence.
translations.sn12.12:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. "There are, monks, these four nutriments for the sustenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the sustenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence."
translations.sn12.15:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said this to the Blessed One: "'Right view, right view,' it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is there right view?"
translations.sn12.15:2: "This world, Kaccāna, for the most part relies on the duality of existence and non-existence. But, Kaccāna, for one who sees with right wisdom the origin of the world as it really is, non-existence in the world does not occur. For one who sees with right wisdom the cessation of the world as it really is, existence in the world does not occur. This world, Kaccāna, is for the most part bound by clinging, grasping, and adherence. But this one does not approach that clinging, grasping, mental adherence, and underlying tendency, does not grasp, does not adhere: 'This is my self.' 'Only suffering arises when it arises, and suffering ceases when it ceases'— he does not doubt, is not perplexed; his knowledge about this is independent of others. To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One: "We would ask the venerable Gotama about a certain point, if the venerable Gotama would grant us the opportunity for an answer to the question." "It is not the time for a question now, Kassapa; we have entered among the houses."
translations.sn12.17:5: "Kassapa, saying from the outset, 'One acts, one experiences,' thus asserting 'suffering is self-made,' leads to eternalism. Kassapa, saying when one is assailed by feelings, 'Another acts, another experiences,' thus asserting 'suffering is other-made,' leads to annihilationism. Kassapa, without going to either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; ... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what was overturned, ... 'those with eyes see forms,' so too has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the Blessed One's presence, may I receive the full ordination."
translations.sn12.17:7: "Kassapa, one who was formerly a member of another sect and desires the going forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, desires the full ordination, lives on probation for four months. At the end of four months, if the monks are satisfied, they give the going forth, give the full ordination into the monkhood. But I recognize differences among individuals."
translations.sn12.18:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded the greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: "Timbaruka, saying from the outset, 'That feeling, that one feels,' thus asserting 'pleasure and pain are self-made,' I do not speak thus. Timbaruka, saying when one is assailed by feelings, 'One feeling, another feels,' thus asserting 'pleasure and pain are other-made,' I do not speak thus. Timbaruka, without going to either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; ... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.19:1: "Monks, for a fool hindered by ignorance and bound by craving, this body has thus come to be. So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus there is this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact, the six sense bases, through which contact the fool experiences pleasure and pain, or through one of them.
translations.sn12.19:2: "Monks, for a wise person hindered by ignorance and bound by craving, this body has thus come to be. So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus there is this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact, the six sense bases, through which contact the wise person experiences pleasure and pain, or through one of them.
translations.sn12.19:3: "Herein, monks, what is the distinction, the disparity, the difference between the wise person and the fool?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, have the Blessed One as refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it."
translations.sn12.19:5: "Monks, the ignorance by which a fool is hindered and the craving by which he is bound, by which this body has come to be—that ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, that craving has not been exhausted. For what reason? Because, monks, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool is reborn in a body; being reborn in a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. 'He is not freed from suffering,' I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: "And what, monks, is the supporting condition for craving? 'Feeling' should be said. ... 'Contact' should be said. ... 'The six sense bases' should be said. ... 'Name-and-form' should be said. ... 'Consciousness' should be said. ... 'Volitional formations' should be said. Monks, I say volitional formations have a supporting condition, not without a supporting condition. And what, monks, is the supporting condition for volitional formations? 'Ignorance' should be said.
translations.sn12.23:6: "Thus, monks, with ignorance as supporting condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as supporting condition, consciousness; with consciousness as supporting condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as supporting condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as supporting condition, contact; with contact as supporting condition, feeling; with feeling as supporting condition, craving; with craving as supporting condition, clinging; with clinging as supporting condition, existence; with existence as supporting condition, birth; with birth as supporting condition, suffering; with suffering as supporting condition, faith; with faith as supporting condition, gladness; with gladness as supporting condition, rapture; with rapture as supporting condition, tranquility; with tranquility as supporting condition, happiness; with happiness as supporting condition, concentration; with concentration as supporting condition, knowledge and vision of things as they really are; with knowledge and vision of things as they really are as supporting condition, disenchantment; with disenchantment as supporting condition, dispassion; with dispassion as supporting condition, liberation; with liberation as supporting condition, knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: "Just as, monks, when heavy rain falls on a mountain top, the water flows down according to the slope, filling the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies are full, they fill the small lakes; when the small lakes are full, they fill the large lakes; when the large lakes are full, they fill the small rivers; when the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers; when the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, the Venerable Bhūmijo approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded the greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmijo said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: "Ānanda, when there is body, due to bodily volition, pleasure and pain arise internally. Ānanda, when there is speech, due to verbal volition, pleasure and pain arise internally. Ānanda, when there is mind, due to mental volition, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by ignorance."
translations.sn12.25:11: Ānanda, one either intentionally produces that bodily formation on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally; or others produce that bodily formation on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally; or one produces that bodily formation with clear comprehension on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally; or one produces that bodily formation without clear comprehension on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain are created by oneself. And there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain are created by another. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain are created by both oneself and another. And there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain arise without a cause, by chance. Now, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say about this? What does he declare? How should we answer so that we would speak in accordance with what the Blessed One has said and not misrepresent him with what is untrue, and so that our explanation would be in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable consequence of our assertion would give ground for criticism?
translations.sn12.25:3: Friend, the Blessed One has said that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Speaking thus, one would be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said and not misrepresenting him with what is untrue, and one's explanation would be in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable consequence of one's assertion would give ground for criticism.
translations.sn12.25:4: In this case, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain are created by oneself—that too is dependent on contact. Those who... teach that pleasure and pain are created by another... Those who... teach that pleasure and pain are created by both oneself and another... Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain arise without a cause, by chance—that too is dependent on contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: In this case, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain are created by oneself—it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact. Those who... teach that pleasure and pain are created by another... Those who... teach that pleasure and pain are created by both oneself and another... Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and teach that pleasure and pain arise without a cause, by chance—it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: Good, good, Ānanda. That is how Sāriputta would answer rightly when answering. Ānanda, I have said that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Speaking thus, one would be speaking in accordance with what I have said and not misrepresenting me with what is untrue, and one's explanation would be in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable consequence of one's assertion would give ground for criticism.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention: this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements: this is called form. Thus this name and this form are together called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, bhikkhus, are volitional formations? There are these three kinds of volitional formations: bodily volitional formation, verbal volitional formation, mental volitional formation. These are called volitional formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is existence? There are these three kinds of existence: sense-sphere existence, form-sphere existence, formless-sphere existence. This is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? There are these four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self. This is called clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: "Sāriputta, this was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: 'Those who have understood the Dhamma, and the various trainees here: being prudent, explain their conduct, dear sir, when asked.'
translations.sn12.31:3: Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this statement stated in brief be seen in detail?" When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta was silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: "Sāriputta, do you see: 'This has come to be'?" "Venerable sir, one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be,' one is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of what has come to be. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be with that as its nutriment.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be with that as its nutriment,' one is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of its nutriment. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,' one is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, for the cessation of what is subject to cessation. Thus, venerable sir, one is a trainee."
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, venerable sir, is one a person who has understood the Dhamma? Venerable sir, one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is what has come to be.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is what has come to be,' one is liberated through non-clinging by being disenchanted with, dispassionate toward, and ceasing what has come to be. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has nutriment as its source.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has nutriment as its source,' one is liberated through non-clinging by being disenchanted with, dispassionate toward, and ceasing what has nutriment as its source. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,' one is liberated through non-clinging by being disenchanted with, dispassionate toward, and ceasing what is subject to cessation. Thus, venerable sir, one is a person who has understood the Dhamma. So, venerable sir, that which was said in the Parayana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.35:1: At Savatthi. 'With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness ... ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.' When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'What, venerable sir, is aging-and-death, and for whom is there this aging-and-death?' 'Not a valid question,' the Blessed One said. 'Bhikkhu, whether one says, 'What is aging-and-death, and for whom is there this aging-and-death?' or whether one says, 'Aging-and-death is one thing, and for someone else there is this aging-and-death,' both these statements are essentially the same; they differ only in phrasing. If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is the same as the body,' then the holy life cannot be lived. If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another,' then the holy life cannot be lived. Without veering toward either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death.'
translations.sn12.35:2: 'What, venerable sir, is birth, and for whom is there this birth?' 'Not a valid question,' the Blessed One said. 'Bhikkhu, whether one says, 'What is birth, and for whom is there this birth?' or whether one says, 'Birth is one thing, and for someone else there is this birth,' both these statements are essentially the same; they differ only in phrasing.
