If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is the same as the body,' then the holy life cannot be lived. If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another,' then the holy life cannot be lived. Without veering toward either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With existence as condition, birth.'
translations.sn12.35:3: 'What, venerable sir, is existence, and for whom is there this existence?' 'Not a valid question,' the Blessed One said. 'Bhikkhu, whether one says, 'What is existence, and for whom is there this existence?' or whether one says, 'Existence is one thing, and for someone else there is this existence,' both these statements are essentially the same; they differ only in phrasing. If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is the same as the body,' then the holy life cannot be lived; if, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another,' then the holy life cannot be lived. Without veering toward either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With clinging as condition, existence' ... ... 'With craving as condition, clinging' ... 'With feeling as condition, craving' ... 'With contact as condition, feeling' ... 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact' ... 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases' ... 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form' ... 'With volitional formations as condition, consciousness.'
translations.sn12.35:4: 'What, venerable sir, are volitional formations, and for whom are there these volitional formations?' 'Not a valid question,' the Blessed One said. 'Bhikkhu, whether one says, 'What are volitional formations, and for whom are there these volitional formations?' or whether one says, 'Volitional formations are one thing, and for someone else there are these volitional formations,' both these statements are essentially the same; they differ only in phrasing. If, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is the same as the body,' then the holy life cannot be lived; if, bhikkhu, there is the view: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another,' then the holy life cannot be lived. Without veering toward either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations.'
translations.sn12.35:5: But, bhikkhu, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever various kinds of writhing, wriggling, and vacillation there are—'What is aging-and-death, and for whom is there this aging-and-death?' or 'Aging-and-death is one thing, and for someone else there is this aging-and-death' or 'The soul is the same as the body' or 'The soul is one thing, the body is another'—all these are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no more subject to future arising.
translations.sn12.35:7: But, bhikkhu, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever various kinds of writhing, wriggling, and vacillation there are—What is existence? ... ... What is clinging? ... What is craving? ... What is feeling? ... What is contact? ... What are the six sense bases? ... What is name-and-form? ... What is consciousness? ... ...
translations.sn12.38:1: At Savatthi. 'Bhikkhus, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency toward: this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is supported and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: If, bhikkhus, one does not intend and does not plan, but still has a tendency, this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is supported and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.44:1: At Savatthi. 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the origin and the passing away of the world. Listen to that and attend closely, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: "And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world."
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds ... Dependent on the nose and odors ... Dependent on the tongue and tastes ... Dependent on the body and tactile objects ... Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling ... with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: "And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of existence ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world."
translations.sn12.46:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: "What then, Master Gotama, does the one who acts also experience [the result]?" "'The one who acts is the one who experiences,' brahmin, is one extreme."
translations.sn12.46:3: "Then, Master Gotama, does one act and another experience?" "'One acts and another experiences,' brahmin, is the second extreme. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness ... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.51:10: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not to be clung to, he understands it as not to be delighted in. If he feels a painful feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not to be clung to, he understands it as not to be delighted in. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent, he understands it as not to be clung to, he understands it as not to be delighted in. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
translations.sn12.51:11: When feeling a feeling terminating with the body, he understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with the body.' When feeling a feeling terminating with life, he understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with life.' He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; the bodily remains will be left over.'
translations.sn12.51:12: "Just as, bhikkhus, a man might take a hot clay pot from a potter's kiln and place it on level ground. The heat there would then subside right there, and the potsherds would be left over. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when feeling a feeling terminating with the body, understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with the body.' When feeling a feeling terminating with life, he understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with life.' He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; the bodily remains will be left over.'"
translations.sn12.51:13: "What do you think, bhikkhus, would a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed still generate a meritorious volitional formation, or a demeritorious volitional formation, or an imperturbable volitional formation?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.51:14: "But with the complete non-existence of volitional formations, with the cessation of volitional formations, would consciousness be discerned?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.51:2: "To what extent, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu, when investigating, investigate for the complete destruction of suffering?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it." "Then listen, bhikkhus, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when investigating, investigates thus: 'This manifold and diverse suffering that arises in the world, aging-and-death: what is the source, the origin, the birth, the origin of this suffering? When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? When what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?' Investigating, he understands thus: 'This manifold and diverse suffering that arises in the world, aging-and-death: this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, is born from birth, originates from birth. When birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be; when birth does not exist, aging-and-death does not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging-and-death, he understands the origin of aging-and-death, he understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and he understands the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death. And he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then further, investigating, he investigates: 'But this birth, what is its source, its origin, what gives birth to it, what is its origin? When what exists does birth come to be? When what does not exist does birth not come to be?' Investigating, he understands thus: 'Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin, is born from existence, originates from existence. When existence exists, birth comes to be; when existence does not exist, birth does not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the way leading to the cessation of birth. Practicing accordingly, he is a follower of the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing rightly for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, further, investigating, he investigates: 'But what is the cause of becoming? ... What is the cause of clinging? ... What is the cause of craving? ... What is the cause of feeling? ... What is the cause of contact? ... What is the cause of the six sense bases? ... What is the cause of name-and-form? ... What is the cause of consciousness? ... What is the cause of these volitional formations? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their source? When what exists do volitional formations come to be? When what does not exist do volitional formations not come to be?' Investigating thus, he understands: 'Volitional formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, ignorance as their source. When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; when ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands volitional formations, he understands the origin of volitional formations, he understands the cessation of volitional formations, and he understands the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations. Practicing accordingly, he is a follower of the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing rightly for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of volitional formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: Monks, a person who is subject to ignorance, if he performs a meritorious volitional formation, his consciousness goes to a meritorious state. If he performs a demeritorious volitional formation, his consciousness goes to a demeritorious state. If he performs an imperturbable volitional formation, his consciousness goes to an imperturbable state. But when, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance and arisen to true knowledge, then, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, he does not perform a meritorious volitional formation, nor a demeritorious volitional formation, nor an imperturbable volitional formation. Not performing, not willing, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.sn12.52:2: Monks, suppose a great mass of fire were burning, requiring ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads of fuel. And a man from time to time would throw dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood into it. Thus, monks, that great mass of fire, with that sustenance, with that fuel, would burn for a long time. So too, monks, when one dwells contemplating the gratification in things that are liable to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: Monks, when one dwells contemplating the danger in things that are liable to clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving comes cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: At Savatthi. 'Monks, when one dwells contemplating the gratification in things that are liable to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, becoming ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Monks, suppose there is a great tree. And whatever roots it has going downward and whatever roots going sideways, all draw the sap upward. Thus, monks, that great tree, with that sustenance, with that fuel, would stand for a long time. So too, monks, when one dwells contemplating the gratification in things that are liable to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: Monks, when one dwells contemplating the danger in things that are liable to clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving comes cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming ... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park ... 'Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body made of the four great elements. For what reason? Because growth and decline, taking up and putting down, are seen in this body made of the four great elements. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But, monks, regarding what is called mind, intellect, or consciousness, an untaught ordinary person is unable to become disenchanted, unable to become dispassionate, unable to become liberated. For what reason? Because for a long time it has been held, cherished, and grasped by the untaught ordinary person: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore, an untaught ordinary person is unable to become disenchanted, unable to become dispassionate, unable to become liberated regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:3: Monks, it would be better for an untaught ordinary person to take as self this body made of the four great elements, rather than the mind. For what reason? This body made of the four great elements is seen standing for one year, for two years, for three years, for four years, for five years, for ten years, for twenty years, for thirty years, for forty years, for fifty years, for a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: There, monks, a learned noble disciple carefully and wisely attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; ... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.62:3: There, monks, a learned noble disciple carefully and wisely attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' Monks, with pleasant-feeling contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very pleasant-feeling contact, whatever feeling that is born from that pleasant-feeling contact, that pleasant feeling ceases and subsides. With painful-feeling contact as condition, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that very painful-feeling contact, whatever feeling that is born from that painful-feeling contact, that painful feeling ceases and subsides. With neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, whatever feeling that is born from that neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, monks, from the rubbing together and friction of two sticks, heat is generated and fire is produced. But when those two sticks are separated and set apart, the heat generated from them ceases and subsides; so too, monks, with pleasant-feeling contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very pleasant-feeling contact, whatever feeling that is born from that pleasant-feeling contact, that pleasant feeling ceases and subsides. ... with painful-feeling contact as condition ... with neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, whatever feeling that is born from that neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, monks, would they take food for play, for intoxication, for adornment, or for embellishment?" "No, venerable sir." "Would they not take food only for the purpose of crossing the desert?" "Yes, venerable sir." "In the same way, monks, I say that edible food should be seen as such. Monks, when edible food is fully understood, the desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. When the desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter by which a noble disciple, bound by that fetter, would come back to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, monks, should contact nutriment be seen? Suppose, monks, a flayed cow were to stand leaning against a wall. The creatures living in the wall would devour it. If it were to stand leaning against a tree, the creatures living in the tree would devour it. If it were to stand leaning against water, the creatures living in the water would devour it. If it were to stand leaning against the air, the creatures living in the air would devour it. For wherever, monks, that flayed cow were to stand leaning, the creatures living there would devour it. In the same way, monks, I say that contact nutriment should be seen as such. Monks, when contact nutriment is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, monks, should mental volition nutriment be seen? Suppose, monks, there was a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man's height, full of coals that were blazing, flame-less, and smokeless. Then a man would come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. Then two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him toward that pit of glowing coals. Then, monks, that man would have a will to be far away, an aspiration to be far away, an inclination to be far away. Why is that? Because, monks, that man would think: 'If I fall into this pit of glowing coals, I will thereby meet death or deadly suffering.' In the same way, monks, I say that mental volition nutriment should be seen as such. Monks, when mental volition nutriment is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: Monks, if there is lust, delight, and craving for edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness becomes established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is future renewed existence. Where there is future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, that, monks, I say is sorrowful, lamentable, and full of despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Just as, monks, a painter or a painter's apprentice, with dye or lac or turmeric or indigo or crimson, would create the figure of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts, on a well-polished board or wall or cloth; even so, monks, when there is passion, delight, and craving for nutriment in the form of edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is future renewed existence. Where there is future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, that, monks, I say is sorrowful, full of despair, and full of anguish.
translations.sn12.64:6: Monks, when there is no passion, no delight, no craving for nutriment in the form of edible food, consciousness does not become established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no future renewed existence. Where there is no future renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, that, monks, I say is sorrowless, despairless, and free from anguish.
translations.sn12.64:8: Just as, monks, in a peaked house or a hall with a peak, there are windows to the north, south, or east. When the sun rises, a ray of light enters through a window; where would it become established? On the western wall, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no western wall, where would it become established? On the ground, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no ground, where would it become established? In the water, venerable sir. If, monks, there were no water, where would it become established? It would not become established, venerable sir. Even so, monks, when there is no passion, no delight, no craving for nutriment in the form of edible food ...
translations.sn12.65:1: At Savatthi. Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me: Alas, this world has fallen into trouble, in that it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn. And yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death. When will the escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be known? Then, monks, it occurred to me: When what exists does aging and death come to be? What is the condition for aging and death? Then, monks, through careful attention, there came to me a breakthrough by wisdom: When there is birth, aging and death come to be; with birth as condition, aging and death.
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, monks, it occurred to me: This consciousness turns back from name-and-form; it does not go beyond. Just so far may one be born, age, die, pass away, or be reborn, that is: with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. 'Origin, origin'—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, monks, it occurred to me: When what does not exist does consciousness not come to be? With the cessation of what does consciousness cease? Then, monks, through careful attention, there came to me a breakthrough by wisdom: When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn12.65:6: Then, monks, it occurred to me: I have attained the path to enlightenment, that is: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact ... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. 'Cessation, cessation'—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
translations.sn12.65:7: Just as, monks, a man walking in a forest, in a wood, might see an ancient path, an ancient road, traveled by people of the past. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of the past, with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, a delightful place. Then, monks, that man would inform the king or a royal minister: 'Please, sir, you should know that while walking in a forest, in a wood, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road, traveled by people of the past. I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of the past, with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, a delightful place. Sir, you should restore that city.' Then, monks, the king or the royal minister would restore that city. And that city would later become successful, prosperous, populous, filled with people, attained to growth and expansion. Even so, monks, I saw the ancient path, the ancient road, traveled by the rightly enlightened ones of the past.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammasadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: Monks. Venerable sir, those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: Do you all, monks, reflect upon reflection? When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: I, venerable sir, reflect upon reflection. But how, monk, do you reflect upon reflection? Then that monk explained. As that monk explained, he did not satisfy the Blessed One's mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Sublime One! The Blessed One should speak about the intermediate contemplation. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it." "Then, Ānanda, listen and attend closely. I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, contemplating further, one contemplates with intermediate contemplation: 'But where does this craving arise and become established when it arises, where does it settle when it settles?' Contemplating, one understands thus: 'Whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing, there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles. And what in the world is agreeable and pleasing? The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasing; there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles. The ear in the world is agreeable and pleasing ... The nose in the world is agreeable and pleasing ... The tongue in the world is agreeable and pleasing ... The body in the world is agreeable and pleasing ... The mind in the world is agreeable and pleasing; there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles.'
translations.sn12.66:6: For, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past regarded whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased clinging. Those who increased clinging increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they were not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:7: For, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will regard whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase clinging. Those who increase clinging will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not be freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they will not be freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:8: For, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present regard whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase clinging. Those who increase clinging increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.67:1: On one occasion Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to Venerable Sāriputta: "What, friend Sāriputta, is aging-and-death self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or arisen without cause, spontaneously?" "Friend Koṭṭhita, aging-and-death is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor arisen without cause, spontaneously. Rather, with birth as condition, aging-and-death."
translations.sn12.67:2: "What, friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or arisen without cause, spontaneously?" "Friend Koṭṭhita, birth is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor arisen without cause, spontaneously. Rather, with existence as condition, birth."
translations.sn12.67:4: "What, friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or arisen without cause, spontaneously?" "Friend Koṭṭhita, consciousness is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor arisen without cause, spontaneously. Rather, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness."
translations.sn12.67:5: "Just now we understood Venerable Sāriputta's statement thus: 'Friend Koṭṭhita, name-and-form is not self-made, not other-made, not both self-made and other-made, nor arisen without cause, spontaneously. Rather, with consciousness as condition, name-and-form.'"
translations.sn12.67:7: "But how, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be seen?" "Well then, friend, I will give you a simile. For by means of a simile, some wise people understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, friend, there were two sheaves of reeds leaning against each other. In the same way, friend: with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. If, friend, one were to pull away one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall; and if one were to pull away the other, the first would fall. In the same way, friend: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact ... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering."
translations.sn12.67:8: "It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta! It is amazing, friend Sāriputta! How well this was spoken by Venerable Sāriputta. And we rejoice in Venerable Sāriputta's statement on these thirty-six grounds:
translations.sn12.68:13: "Then is Venerable Nārada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?" "'Cessation of existence is nibbāna' is, friend, seen by me with right wisdom as it really is, but I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed. Suppose, friend, there was a well along a desert road, but there was neither a rope nor a water bucket. Then a man might come along, oppressed and afflicted by the heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. He would look into the well. He would indeed have knowledge of 'water,' but he would not dwell having contacted it with his body. In the same way, friend, 'cessation of existence is nibbāna' is seen by me with right wisdom as it really is, but I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed."
translations.sn12.68:6: "Then is Venerable Musīla an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?" When this was said, Venerable Musīla remained silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. There ... "Bhikkhus, the great ocean draws in the great rivers; the great rivers, drawing in, draw in the small rivers; the small rivers, drawing in, draw in the great lakes; the great lakes, drawing in, draw in the small lakes. In the same way, bhikkhus, ignorance draws in volitional formations; volitional formations, drawing in, draw in consciousness; consciousness, drawing in, draws in name-and-form; name-and-form, drawing in, draws in the six sense bases; the six sense bases, drawing in, draw in contact; contact, drawing in, draws in feeling; feeling, drawing in, draws in craving; craving, drawing in, draws in clinging; clinging, drawing in, draws in existence; existence, drawing in, draws in birth; birth, drawing in, draws in aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Now on that occasion the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, esteemed, and he obtained robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. The Saṅgha of bhikkhus was also honored, respected, revered, venerated, esteemed, and they obtained robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, not respected, not revered, not venerated, not esteemed, and they did not obtain robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites.
translations.sn12.70:10: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus, seeing thus, do you dwell having contacted with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:11: "Now here, venerable ones, is this statement and your non-attainment of these states; how is this, friend?" "We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susīma."
translations.sn12.70:12: "I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the venerable ones. It would be good if the venerable ones would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the venerable ones." "Whether you understand, friend Susīma, or whether you do not understand, still we are liberated by wisdom."
translations.sn12.70:13: Then Venerable Susīma rose from his seat and went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Susīma reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with those bhikkhus. "First, Susīma, there is knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma; afterwards, knowledge of nibbāna."
translations.sn12.70:14: "I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One." "Whether you understand, Susīma, or whether you do not understand, still first there is knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma; afterwards, knowledge of nibbāna.
translations.sn12.70:16: "Therefore, Susīma, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all form should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Any kind of feeling whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all feeling should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Any kind of perception whatsoever ... Any kind of volitional formations whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all volitional formations should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susīma, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; in liberation, there arises the knowledge: 'Liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.sn12.70:18: 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death'—do you see this, Susīma?" "Yes, venerable sir." "'With existence as condition, birth'—do you see this, Susīma?" "Yes, venerable sir." "'With clinging as condition, existence'—do you see this, Susīma?" "Yes, venerable sir." "'With craving as condition, clinging'—do you see this, Susīma?" "Yes, venerable sir." "'With feeling as condition, craving'... 'With contact as condition, feeling'... 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact'... 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases'... 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form'... 'With volitional formations as condition, consciousness'... 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations'—do you see this, Susīma?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.70:2: Now at that time the wanderer Susīma was residing at Rājagaha together with a large company of wanderers. Then the company of the wanderer Susīma said to the wanderer Susīma: "Come, friend Susīma, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. You, having learned the Dhamma, will teach us. We, having learned the Dhamma, will teach it to householders. Thus we too will become honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, revered, and gain robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites." "Yes, friends," replied the wanderer Susīma to his company. Then he approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Susīma said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline."
translations.sn12.70:21: "But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you wield the various kinds of psychic potency: having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; you dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; you walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, you travel in space like a bird; with your hand you touch and stroke the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; you exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.70:25: "But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having contacted with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.70:27: Then the Venerable Susīma, having fallen with his head at the Blessed One's feet, said to the Blessed One: "A transgression has overcome me, venerable sir, in that I was so foolish, so confused, so unskillful as to go forth as a thief of the Dhamma in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline. May the Blessed One, venerable sir, accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future."
translations.sn12.70:3: Then the Venerable Ānanda, taking the wanderer Susīma, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, this wanderer Susīma says thus: 'Friend Ānanda, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.'" "Well then, Ānanda, give Susīma the going forth." The wanderer Susīma received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the full admission.
translations.sn12.70:5: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you wield the various kinds of psychic potency: having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; you dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; you walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, you travel in space like a bird; with your hand you touch and stroke the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; you exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:6: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, do you hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:7: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you understand the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with your own mind: 'A mind with lust is a mind with lust,' you understand; 'A mind without lust is a mind without lust,' you understand; 'A mind with hate is a mind with hate,' you understand; 'A mind without hate is a mind without hate,' you understand; 'A mind with delusion is a mind with delusion,' you understand; 'A mind without delusion is a mind without delusion,' you understand; 'A contracted mind is a contracted mind,' you understand; 'A distracted mind is a distracted mind,' you understand; 'An exalted mind is an exalted mind,' you understand; 'An unexalted mind is an unexalted mind,' you understand; 'A surpassable mind is a surpassable mind,' you understand; 'An unsurpassable mind is an unsurpassable mind,' you understand; 'A concentrated mind is a concentrated mind,' you understand; 'An unconcentrated mind is an unconcentrated mind,' you understand; 'A liberated mind is a liberated mind,' you understand; 'An unliberated mind is an unliberated mind,' you understand?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:8: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you recollect your manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was, so named, of such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was, so named, of such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here.' Thus with their aspects and details you recollect your manifold past lives?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:9: "But, venerable ones, knowing thus, seeing thus, do you with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions: 'Indeed, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view. After death, at the breaking up of the body, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell. But these beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, holding right view, undertaking actions based on right view. After death, at the breaking up of the body, they have reappeared in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, do you see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions?" "No, friend."
translations.sn16.11:1: On one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary.
translations.sn16.11:10: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'I will establish keen shame and fear of wrongdoing towards the elders, the newly ordained, and those of middle standing.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself.
translations.sn16.11:11: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will attend to it, take it to heart, and concentrate on it with my whole mind, listening to the Dhamma with an attentive ear.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself.
translations.sn16.11:12: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasure will not be neglected by me.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself."
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, having given me this exhortation, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. For seven days, friend, I ate the country's almsfood as a debtor; on the eighth day, final knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One stepped off the road and went to the foot of a certain tree. Then, friend, I spread my outer robe made of patches fourfold and said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit. That would be for my long-term welfare and happiness.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting, the Blessed One said to me: 'Soft, Kassapa, is this outer robe of yours made of patches.' 'Venerable sir, let the Blessed One accept my outer robe made of patches out of compassion.' 'But will you then, Kassapa, wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes?' 'I will wear the Blessed One's worn-out hempen rag-robes, venerable sir.' So, friend, I gave my outer robe made of patches to the Blessed One. And I took to wearing the Blessed One's worn-out hempen rag-robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, through the destruction of the taints, have realized for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, I dwell therein. If one were to think, friend, of covering a seven-jeweled nāga or a nāga worth half a kingdom with a palm leaf, one might think of covering my six direct knowledges with a palm leaf."
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time, about thirty of the Venerable Ānanda's resident pupils, mostly young men, had given up the training and returned to the lower life. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having wandered on tour in the Southern Hills as long as he pleased, approached Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary, and the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Venerable Ānanda: "For how many reasons, friend Ānanda, did the Blessed One lay down the rule about eating among families in groups of three?"
translations.sn16.11:3: "For three reasons, Venerable Kassapa, the Blessed One laid down the rule about eating among families in groups of three: for the restraint of evil persons, for the ease of well-behaved monks, and lest those with evil wishes, relying on a faction, might cause a schism in the Sangha, and out of compassion for families. These, Venerable Kassapa, are the three reasons for which the Blessed One laid down the rule about eating among families in groups of three."
translations.sn16.11:4: "Then why, friend Ānanda, do you wander on tour with these newly ordained monks who are unrestrained in their sense faculties, immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness? You wander, one would think, destroying the crop; you wander, one would think, destroying families. Your following is crumbling, friend Ānanda; your new recruits are falling away. And this youngster does not know his measure."
translations.sn16.11:6: The bhikkhunī Thullanandā heard: "It is said that the Venerable Mahākassapa has disparaged the Venerable Ānanda, the sage of the Videhas, by calling him a youngster."
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, displeased, uttered this displeased speech: "What now? Does the Venerable Mahākassapa, formerly a member of another sect, think he can disparage the Venerable Ānanda, the sage of the Videhas, by calling him a youngster?" The Venerable Mahākassapa heard the bhikkhunī Thullanandā making this statement.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Indeed, friend Ānanda, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā has spoken a rash, thoughtless word. For, friend, since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, I do not recall having acknowledged any other teacher except the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Before, friend, while I was still a householder, this thought occurred to me: 'Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is open. It is not easy for one living at home to lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life, polished like a conch shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?' Then, friend, some time later, having had a robe made from patches of cloth, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, dedicating myself to those in the world who are arahants.'
translations.sn16.13:2: 'Just as, Kassapa, genuine gold does not disappear as long as counterfeit gold does not appear in the world. But when, Kassapa, counterfeit gold appears in the world, then genuine gold disappears. So too, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear as long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma does not appear in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma appears in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.'
translations.sn16.13:4: 'There are, Kassapa, five detrimental things that lead to the decay and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers dwell without respect, without deference for the Teacher; they dwell without respect, without deference for the Dhamma; they dwell without respect, without deference for the Saṅgha; they dwell without respect, without deference for the training; they dwell without respect, without deference for concentration. These, Kassapa, are the five detrimental things that lead to the decay and disappearance of the true Dhamma.'
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard. At one time Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahākassapa. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahākassapa: 'It is said, friend Kassapa, that one who is without ardor and without fear of wrongdoing is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of achieving the unsurpassed security from bondage; but one who has ardor and fear of wrongdoing is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of achieving the unsurpassed security from bondage.'
translations.sn16.2:3: 'And how, friend, is one without fear of wrongdoing? Here, friend, a bhikkhu does not fear wrongdoing thus: 'May unarisen bad unwholesome states not arise in me'; he does not fear wrongdoing thus: 'May arisen bad unwholesome states not persist in me'; he does not fear wrongdoing thus: 'May unarisen wholesome states arise in me'; he does not fear wrongdoing thus: 'May arisen wholesome states not cease in me.' Thus, friend, one is without fear of wrongdoing. Thus, friend, one who is without ardor and without fear of wrongdoing is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of achieving the unsurpassed security from bondage.'
translations.sn16.2:4: 'And how, friend, is one with ardor? Here, friend, a bhikkhu arouses ardor thus: 'May unarisen bad unwholesome states not arise in me'; he arouses ardor thus: 'May arisen bad unwholesome states be abandoned in me'; he arouses ardor thus: 'May unarisen wholesome states arise in me'; he arouses ardor thus: 'May arisen wholesome states be maintained in me.' Thus, friend, one is with ardor.'
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard ... at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to Venerable Mahākassapa as he was sitting to one side: 'You are now old, Kassapa, and these rough hempen rag-robes must be burdensome to you. Therefore, Kassapa, wear householder's robes, accept invitational meals, and dwell close to me.'
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Now on that occasion a certain bhikkhu named Thera was a lone-dweller and one who praised dwelling alone. He would enter the village for alms alone, return alone, sit in seclusion alone, and undertake walking meditation alone. Then several bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, a certain bhikkhu named Thera is a lone-dweller and one who praises dwelling alone.'
translations.sn21.10:3: 'There is, Thera, this dwelling alone; I do not say there is not. But, Thera, listen to how dwelling alone is fulfilled in detail, attend carefully; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' he replied. 'And how, Thera, is dwelling alone fulfilled in detail? Here, Thera, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and desire and lust for present acquisitions of a self are well subdued. Thus, Thera, dwelling alone is fulfilled in detail.'
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus.' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: "Here, friend, while I was in seclusion, withdrawn, such a thought arose in my mind: 'Noble silence, noble silence is spoken of. What, then, is noble silence?' Then, friend, it occurred to me: 'Here, a monk, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, with internal clarity and unification of mind, free from initial and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is born of concentration and filled with rapture and happiness. This is called noble silence.' So, friend, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, with internal clarity and unification of mind, free from initial and sustained thought, I entered and dwelled in the second jhāna, which is born of concentration and filled with rapture and happiness. While I was dwelling in this way, friend, perceptions accompanied by thought and attention assailed me."
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: "Friend monks." "Friend," those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: "Here, friend, while I was in seclusion, withdrawn, such a thought arose in my mind: 'Is there anything in the world whose change and alteration would cause sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair to arise in me?' Then, friend, it occurred to me: 'There is nothing in the world whose change and alteration would cause sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair to arise in me.'"
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary, in the same dwelling. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. After exchanging courteous and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: "Your faculties are clear, friend Moggallāna; your complexion is pure and bright. Surely Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spent the day in a pleasant abiding?" "I spent the day, friend, in a gross abiding. However, I had a Dhamma discussion." "With whom did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma discussion?" "I had a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One, friend." "But, friend, the Blessed One is far away now, dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by psychic power, or did the Blessed One approach Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by psychic power?" "I did not approach the Blessed One by psychic power, friend, nor did the Blessed One approach me by psychic power. However, my divine eye and divine ear element were purified as far as the Blessed One, and the Blessed One's divine eye and divine ear element were purified as far as me." "But how did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One?"
translations.sn21.3:3: "Here, friend, I said to the Blessed One: 'One with aroused energy, one with aroused energy is spoken of, Venerable Sir. To what extent, Venerable Sir, is one with aroused energy?' When this was said, friend, the Blessed One said to me: 'Here, Moggallāna, a monk dwells with aroused energy: "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, let the flesh and blood in the body dry up, but I will not relax my energy until I achieve what can be achieved by manly strength, manly energy, manly exertion." Thus, Moggallāna, one is with aroused energy.' Thus, friend, I had a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One."
translations.sn21.3:6: "Sāriputta is foremost in wisdom, in virtue and in peace; even a monk who has gone beyond, he might be the highest."
translations.sn21.6:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Having seen him, he addressed the monks: "Do you see, monks, that monk coming, ugly, unsightly, deformed, despised by the monks?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "That monk, monks, is of great power and great might, and that attainment is not easily obtained which that monk has not attained before. For the sake of which goal clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life he has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, and having entered upon it, he dwells." The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: "Swans, herons, and peacocks, elephants, and spotted deer—all fear the lion; there is no equal in body."
translations.sn21.8:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's maternal cousin, having put on well-pressed robes, having applied eye ointment, and taking a bright bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Venerable Nanda: "It is not fitting, Nanda, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness that you should put on well-pressed robes, apply eye ointment, and carry a bright bowl. This, Nanda, is fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness: that you should be a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and dwell without concern for sensual pleasures." The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: "When shall I see Nanda as a forest-dweller, a rag-robe wearer, subsisting on others' leftovers, without concern for sensual pleasures?"
translations.sn21.9:1: At Savatthi. Then Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One's paternal cousin, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side, miserable and sad, shedding tears. Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Tissa: "Why, Tissa, are you sitting to one side miserable and sad, shedding tears?" "Because, venerable sir, the monks have been harassing me on all sides with piercing words." "That is because, Tissa, you are one who speaks but cannot endure speech; it is not fitting for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, that you should be one who speaks but cannot endure speech. This, Tissa, is fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness: that you should be one who speaks and also endures speech."
translations.sn22.100:2: "Monks, have you seen a thing called 'mind'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "That too, monks, the thing called 'mind' is mind-made by mind. Yet even by that mind-made mind, monks, the mind is even more mind-made. Therefore, monks, one should frequently reflect on one's own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.' By the defilement of mind, monks, beings are defiled; by the purification of mind, beings are purified."
translations.sn22.100:3: "Monks, I do not perceive any single class of beings as having such a mind as the animals. They too, monks, are mind-made by mind; even by those animal beings, the mind is even more mind-made. Therefore, monks, one should frequently reflect on one's own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.' By the defilement of mind, monks, beings are defiled; by the purification of mind, beings are purified."
translations.sn22.101:1: At Savatthi. "Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And what, monks, does one know and see for the destruction of the taints to occur? 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such are volitional formations ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.' Thus, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs."
translations.sn22.101:2: "For a monk who dwells without applying himself to development, monks, even if such a wish should arise: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!' yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of undevelopment.' Undevelopment of what? Undevelopment of the four establishments of mindfulness, undevelopment of the four right efforts, undevelopment of the four bases for spiritual power, undevelopment of the five faculties, undevelopment of the five powers, undevelopment of the seven factors of enlightenment, undevelopment of the Noble Eightfold Path."
translations.sn22.101:3: "Suppose, monks, there is a hen with eight or ten or twelve eggs. And she has not properly sat on them, properly incubated them, properly nurtured them. Even if that hen should have such a wish: 'Oh, that my chicks might break through the eggshell with their claws or beak and hatch safely!' yet those chicks are incapable of breaking through the eggshell with their claws or beak and hatching safely. Why is that? Because, monks, that hen with eight or ten or twelve eggs has not properly sat on them, properly incubated them, properly nurtured them. So too, monks, for a monk who dwells without applying himself to development, even if such a wish should arise: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!' yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of undevelopment.' Undevelopment of what? Undevelopment of the four establishments of mindfulness ... the Noble Eightfold Path."
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas on Crocodile Hill, in the deer park at Bhesakala Grove. Then the householder Nakulapita approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapita said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. One is obsessed with the idea: 'I am feeling, my feeling.' That feeling of his changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of feeling, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:11: One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. One is obsessed with the idea: 'I am perception, my perception.' That perception of his changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of perception, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:12: One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations. One is obsessed with the idea: 'I am volitional formations, my volitional formations.' Those volitional formations of his change and become otherwise. With the change and alteration of volitional formations, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:13: They regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. They dwell obsessed by the notion: 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.' When that consciousness of theirs changes and becomes otherwise, then with the change and alteration of consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus, householder, one is afflicted in body and afflicted in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones and is skilled and disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has seen good persons and is skilled and disciplined in the Dhamma of good persons, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They do not dwell obsessed by the notion: 'I am form, form is mine.' When that form of theirs changes and becomes otherwise, then with the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. Thus, householder, one is afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind.
translations.sn22.1:2: "Venerable sir, I am old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, come to the last stage, and my body is ailing and constantly ill. Yet, venerable sir, I have not seen the Blessed One and the monks worthy of esteem only occasionally. Let the Blessed One advise me, venerable sir; let the Blessed One instruct me, venerable sir, for my welfare and happiness for a long time."
translations.sn22.1:3: "So it is, householder, so it is. This body, householder, is afflicted, a nest of disease, wrapped up. For, householder, if anyone carrying this body around were to claim even a moment's health, what is that but foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: 'Though my body is afflicted, my mind shall be unafflicted.' Thus should you train yourself, householder."
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakulapita, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, approached the Venerable Sariputta. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Sariputta and sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, the Venerable Sariputta said to the householder Nakulapita: "Your faculties are serene, householder; your facial complexion is pure and bright. Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk today in the Blessed One's presence?"
translations.sn22.1:7: "But, householder, didn't it occur to you to question the Blessed One further: 'In what way, venerable sir, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? And in what way is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind?'" "We would come from afar, venerable sir, to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sariputta. It would be good if the Venerable Sariputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement."
translations.sn22.1:8: "Then, householder, listen and attend closely; I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," the householder Nakulapita replied to the Venerable Sariputta. The Venerable Sariputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: "And how, householder, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? Here, householder, an untaught ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They dwell obsessed by the notion: 'I am form, form is mine.' When that form of theirs changes and becomes otherwise, then with the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the bearer of the burden? The person, it should be said. This venerable one of such a name, of such a clan. This, bhikkhus, is called the bearer of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden."
translations.sn22.22:6: "The five aggregates are indeed a burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, and laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans where there is a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha. Then several bhikkhus who were going to the western region approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, we wish to go to the western region, to take up residence in the western region."
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friends, by entering and dwelling upon unwholesome states, there were a pleasant dwelling in this very life, free from vexation, distress, and fever, and if after the breakup of the body, after death, one could expect a good destination, then the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But because, friends, by entering and dwelling upon unwholesome states, there is a painful dwelling in this very life, with vexation, distress, and fever, and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination can be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: "But, bhikkhus, have you taken leave of Sariputta?" "No, venerable sir, we have not taken leave of the Venerable Sariputta." "Take leave of Sariputta, bhikkhus. Sariputta, bhikkhus, is wise, a helper of his fellow monks." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain grove of eḷagalā trees. Then those monks, having delighted in and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and approached Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the western country, to take up residence in the western country. Has the Teacher given us permission?"
translations.sn22.2:5: "Even from afar, friend, we would come to understand the meaning of this statement from Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement." "Then, friends, listen and attend carefully, I will speak." "Yes, friend," those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One … Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute." "Monk, what one dwells on, that is measured; what is measured, by that one is reckoned. What one does not dwell on, that is not measured; what is not measured, by that one is not reckoned." "Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Fortunate One!"
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard— at one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs, at Kuraraghara on the Papāta mountain. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhakavagga, in the Questions of Māgaṇḍiya:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not devoid of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, not abandoned desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving for them. Thus, householder, one is not devoid of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one devoid of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, abandoned desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving for them. Thus, householder, one is devoid of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one placing something in front?
