Here, householder, someone thinks thus: 'May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling, such perception, such volitional formations, such consciousness in the future.' Thus, householder, one is placing something in front.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, does one engage in disputation with people? Here, householder, someone engages in talk of this sort: 'You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What should be said first you said last; what should be said last you said first. What I have thought out is consistent; what you have thought out is inconsistent. Your thesis has been refuted; you are defeated. Go, try to salvage your thesis, or disentangle yourself if you can.' Thus, householder, one engages in disputation with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: 'Having abandoned home, roaming homeless, Not making intimacies in the village; Devoid of sensual pleasures, placing nothing in front, How would one engage in disputation with people?'
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one a home-roamer? Being bound, infatuated, and attached to the sign of form as a home— this, householder, is called a 'home-roamer.' (Similarly for sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.) Thus, householder, one is a home-roamer.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one intimate in the village? Here, householder, someone lives associating with householders, rejoicing with them and sorrowing with them, happy when they are happy and sad when they are sad, and involves himself in their affairs when they arise. Thus, householder, one is intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one not intimate in the village? Here, householder, a monk lives not associating with householders, not rejoicing with them nor sorrowing with them, not happy when they are happy nor sad when they are sad, and does not involve himself in their affairs when they arise. Thus, householder, one is not intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins who regard the self in various ways, all regard the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one among them. Which five? Here, bhikkhus, an untaught ordinary person, who has no regard for noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for superior persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. (Similarly for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.)
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this view and the underlying tendency 'I am' are not abandoned. And, bhikkhus, when the underlying tendency 'I am' is not abandoned, there is descent of the five faculties— the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty. There is, bhikkhus, mind, there are mental phenomena, there is the element of ignorance. Touched by feeling born of contact with ignorance, the untaught ordinary person thinks: 'I am'; 'I am this'; 'I will be'; 'I will not be'; 'I will be with form'; 'I will be formless'; 'I will be percipient'; 'I will be non-percipient'; 'I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.'
translations.sn22.48:1: Setting at Savatthi. 'Monks, I will teach the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging. Listen to this. And what, monks, are the five aggregates? Whatever, monks, is form—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the form aggregate. Whatever feeling ... whatever perception ... whatever volitional formations—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle ... this is called the volitional formations aggregate. Whatever consciousness—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate. These, monks, are called the five aggregates.
translations.sn22.53:1: Setting at Savatthi. 'Monks, one who clings is not freed; one who does not cling is freed. If, monks, consciousness were to stand based on form, supported by form, established on form, sprinkled with delight, it would attain growth, increase, and expansion. If consciousness were to stand based on feeling ... based on perception ... based on volitional formations, supported by volitional formations, established on volitional formations, sprinkled with delight, it would attain growth, increase, and expansion.
translations.sn22.53:2: Monks, if anyone were to say: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from volitional formations, I will describe the coming, going, passing away, arising, growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness'—that is not possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If, monks, consciousness were to stand based on form, supported by form, established on form, sprinkled with delight, it would attain growth, increase, and expansion. If consciousness were to stand based on feeling ... based on perception ... based on volitional formations, supported by volitional formations, established on volitional formations, sprinkled with delight, it would attain growth, increase, and expansion.
translations.sn22.55:1: Setting at Savatthi. There the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: 'A monk who is resolved thus: "It might not be, and it might not be for me; it will not be, and it will not be for me"—such a monk can cut off the lower fetters.' When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: 'But how, venerable sir, can a monk who is resolved thus: "It might not be, and it might not be for me; it will not be, and it will not be for me"—cut off the lower fetters?'
translations.sn22.55:10: 'But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that immediately there is the destruction of the taints?' 'Here, monk, an untaught ordinary person becomes fearful where there is no ground for fear. This fear, monk, arises for an untaught ordinary person: "It might not be, and it might not be for me; it will not be, and it will not be for me."
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not understand as it really is: 'Form is suffering' as 'Form is suffering'; feeling is suffering ... perception is suffering ... volitional formations are suffering ... consciousness is suffering as 'Consciousness is suffering'.
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not understand as it really is: 'Form is non-self' as 'Form is non-self'; feeling is non-self as 'Feeling is non-self'; perception is non-self as 'Perception is non-self'; volitional formations are non-self as 'Volitional formations are non-self'; consciousness is non-self as 'Consciousness is non-self'.
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not understand as it really is: 'Form is conditioned' as 'Form is conditioned'; feeling is conditioned ... perception is conditioned ... volitional formations are conditioned ... consciousness is conditioned as 'Consciousness is conditioned'. He does not understand as it really is: 'Form will cease to be'. Feeling will cease to be ... perception will cease to be ... volitional formations will cease to be ... consciousness will cease to be.
translations.sn22.55:8: He understands as it really is: 'Form is impermanent' as 'Form is impermanent'. Feeling is impermanent ... perception is impermanent ... volitional formations are impermanent ... consciousness is impermanent as 'Consciousness is impermanent'. Form is suffering ... consciousness is suffering ... Form is non-self ... consciousness is non-self ... Form is conditioned ... consciousness is conditioned as 'Consciousness is conditioned'. He understands as it really is: 'Form will cease to be'. Feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness will cease to be.
translations.sn22.55:9: With the cessation of form, with the cessation of feeling, with the cessation of perception, with the cessation of volitional formations, with the cessation of consciousness—thus, monk, a monk who is resolved thus: "It might not be, and it might not be for me; it will not be, and it will not be for me"—can cut off the lower fetters.' 'Venerable sir, it is said: "A monk who is resolved thus can cut off the lower fetters."
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, monks, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, monks, is called consciousness. With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness. This Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, that is: right view ... right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: For, bhikkhus, any ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness, having directly known the cessation of consciousness, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, are practising for disenchantment, for dispassion, for cessation regarding consciousness—they are practising well. Those who are practising well have gained a foothold in this Dhamma and Discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? I directly knew form, I directly knew the origin of form, I directly knew the cessation of form, I directly knew the way leading to the cessation of form; I directly knew feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, I directly knew the origin of consciousness, I directly knew the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew the way leading to the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.56:5: But, bhikkhus, any ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known form in this way... having directly known the way leading to the cessation of form in this way, are liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form—they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Savatthi. "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is skilled in seven cases and a triple investigator is called in this Dhamma and Discipline a consummate one, one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in seven cases? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, understands the way leading to the cessation of form; understands the gratification of form, understands the danger of form, understands the escape from form; understands feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness; understands the gratification of consciousness, understands the danger of consciousness, understands the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, bhikkhus, are volitional formations? There are these six classes of volition: volition regarding forms... volition regarding mental phenomena. These, bhikkhus, are called volitional formations. With the arising of contact there is the arising of volitional formations; with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of volitional formations. This Noble Eightfold Path itself is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations, that is: right view... right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: But, bhikkhus, any ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way; having directly known the gratification of consciousness in this way, having directly known the danger of consciousness in this way, having directly known the escape from consciousness in this way, are liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness—they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled in seven cases.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, bhikkhus, is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. This, bhikkhus, is called form. With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of form; with the cessation of nutriment there is the cessation of form. This Noble Eightfold Path itself is the way leading to the cessation of form, that is: right view... right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: But, bhikkhus, any ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known form in this way, having directly known the origin of form in this way, having directly known the cessation of form in this way, having directly known the way leading to the cessation of form in this way; having directly known the gratification of form in this way, having directly known the danger of form in this way, having directly known the escape from form in this way, are liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form—they are well liberated. Those who are well liberated are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, bhikkhus, is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact. This, bhikkhus, is called feeling. With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling; with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling. This Noble Eightfold Path itself is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, that is: right view... right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling—this is the gratification of feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of feeling. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Savatthi. "Bhikkhus, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called perfectly enlightened because he is liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form. And a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, liberated by wisdom, is called liberated by wisdom because he is liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form.
translations.sn22.58:3: The Tathagata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called perfectly enlightened because he is liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding perception... volitional formations... consciousness. And a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, liberated by wisdom, is called liberated by wisdom because he is liberated through non-clinging by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness.
translations.sn22.59:10: Whatever consciousness—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn22.59:7: Therefore, monks, whatever form—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn22.5:11: One does not delight in, welcome, or cling to consciousness. For one who does not delight in, welcome, or cling to consciousness, the delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight, clinging ceases ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, monks, is the origin of form, the origin of feeling, the origin of perception, the origin of volitional formations, the origin of consciousness? Here, monks, a monk delights, welcomes, and clings.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what does one delight in, welcome, and cling to? One delights in, welcomes, and clings to form. For one delighting in, welcoming, and clinging to form, delight arises. That delight in form is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: One delights in feeling ... one delights in perception ... one delights in volitional formations ... one delights in, welcomes, and clings to consciousness. For one delighting in, welcoming, and clinging to consciousness, delight arises. That delight in consciousness is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition ... thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what does one not delight in, not welcome, and not cling to? One does not delight in, welcome, or cling to form. For one not delighting in, not welcoming, and not clinging to form, the delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases ... thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One ... Having sat down to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: "Venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa says this: 'There is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.' What does the Blessed One say about this?"
translations.sn22.60:3: "There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause and condition. There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition."
translations.sn22.60:4: "But what, venerable sir, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings? How are beings defiled with cause and condition?"
translations.sn22.60:5: "If, Mahāli, form were exclusively suffering, immersed in suffering, steeped in suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings would not become enamored with form. But because, Mahāli, form is pleasurable, immersed in pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings become enamored with form; being enamored, they are bound; being bound, they become defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: If, Mahāli, consciousness were exclusively suffering, immersed in suffering, steeped in suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings would not become enamored with consciousness. But because, Mahāli, consciousness is pleasurable, immersed in pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings become enamored with consciousness; being enamored, they are bound; being bound, they become defiled. This too, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings. Thus too beings are defiled with cause and condition."
translations.sn22.60:9: "But what, venerable sir, is the cause and condition for the purification of beings? How are beings purified with cause and condition?" "If, Mahāli, form were exclusively pleasurable, immersed in pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because, Mahāli, form is suffering, immersed in suffering, steeped in suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings become disenchanted with form; being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, there arises the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' One understands: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' As far, monks, as there are abodes of beings, as far as the peak of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, that is, the arahants."
translations.sn22.76:4: "Truly happy are the arahants, in whom craving is not found; the 'I am' conceit is cut off, the net of delusion is torn apart.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates, they fare in the true Dhamma; praised by the good, they are the Buddha's own sons.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures, trained in the three trainings, the great heroes wander, having abandoned fear and terror.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with the ten factors, great nagas, composed; these indeed are the best in the world, in whom craving is not found.
translations.sn22.76:9: The knowledge of the non-learner has arisen, this is the last body; that which is the essence of the holy life, in that there is no further condition."
translations.sn22.79:1: At Savatthi. "Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect various past lives, all of them recollect the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one among them. Which five? 'I had such form in the past'—thus, monks, recollecting, one recollects just form. 'I had such feeling in the past'—thus, monks, recollecting, one recollects just feeling. 'I had such perception in the past'... 'I had such volitional formations in the past'... 'I had such consciousness in the past'—thus, monks, recollecting, one recollects just consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: 'Now I am being devoured by consciousness. In the past too I was devoured by consciousness in just the same way, as I am now devoured by present consciousness. And if I were to delight in future consciousness, I would in the future be devoured by consciousness in just the same way, as I am now devoured by present consciousness.' Reflecting thus, he becomes dispassionate towards past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and is practicing for the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: Therein, monks, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'Now I am being devoured by form. In the past too I was devoured by form in just the same way, as I am now devoured by present form. And if I were to delight in future form, I would in the future be devoured by form in just the same way, as I am now devoured by present form.' Reflecting thus, he becomes dispassionate towards past form, does not delight in future form, and is practicing for the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Park. Then the Blessed One, having dismissed the Sangha of monks on some business, dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, on returning from his alms round, he went to the Great Wood for the day's abiding. Having entered the Great Wood, he sat down at the foot of a beluva sapling for the day's abiding.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the brahma Sahampati, having understood the Blessed One's consent, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side towards him, and disappeared right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the Banyan Tree Park; having gone, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One produced such a feat of psychic power that those monks, feeling ashamed, would come to him in twos and threes. And those monks, feeling ashamed, came to the Blessed One in twos and threes; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to those monks:
translations.sn22.80:6: "This, monks, is the extreme of livelihoods, namely, going for alms. This, monks, is a curse in the world: 'You wander for alms, bowl in hand.' Yet, monks, clansmen undertake it for a purpose, for the sake of a purpose; not compelled by kings, not compelled by thieves, not owing debt, not out of fear, not for the sake of livelihood; but rather: 'We are afflicted by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; afflicted by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.'
translations.sn22.80:7: Thus, monks, this clansman has gone forth. But he is covetous, intensely desirous of sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt intentions, muddle-minded, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, scatter-brained, with faculties uncontrolled. Just as, monks, a firebrand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, serves no purpose as fuel in the village or in the forest. Just so, monks, do I describe this person: deprived of the benefits of a householder and not fulfilling the goal of the ascetic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: There are these two views, monks: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Herein, monks, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'Is there anything in the world that I could cling to without fault?' He understands thus: 'There is nothing in the world that I could cling to without fault. For if I were to cling, I would cling only to form, only to feeling, only to perception, only to volitional formations, only to consciousness. For me, clinging would be a condition for existence; existence a condition for birth; birth a condition for aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair to come to be. Such would be the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn22.81:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambi in Ghosita's Park. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kosambi for alms. Having walked for alms in Kosambi, after the meal, on returning from his alms round, he himself put his dwelling in order, took his bowl and robe, and without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Sangha of monks, set out on tour alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not regard form as self, nor feeling as self, nor perception as self, nor volitional formations as self, nor consciousness as self; but he holds such a view: 'That self is the world; after death I shall be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change.' That, monks, eternalist view is a volitional formation. And that volitional formation, what is its source?... Thus, monks, for one who knows thus, who sees thus, there is immediately the destruction of the taints.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, traveling by stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One stayed at the foot of a Bhaddasāla tree. Then several monks approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging greetings and courteous talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to Venerable Ānanda: 'It has been a long time, friend Ānanda, since we have heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One in person; we wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One in person.'
translations.sn22.82:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra's Mother, together with a great Sangha of monks. Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day, the fifteenth, the full moon night, the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Sangha of monks.
translations.sn22.82:10: 'What, venerable sir, is the gratification of form, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, what is the danger, what is the escape?' 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on form—this is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form. Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness—this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.' 'Good, venerable sir,' that monk, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: 'How, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that in regard to this body with consciousness and in regard to all external signs, I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer occur?' 'Whatever form, bhikkhu, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all form with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever volitional formations... whatever consciousness, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all consciousness with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Thus, bhikkhu, knowing thus, seeing thus, in regard to this body with consciousness and in regard to all external signs, I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer occur.'
translations.sn22.82:12: Now on that occasion, a certain monk had this thought: 'So, it seems, form is non-self, feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self; then how will actions done by what is non-self affect the self?' Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in that monk's mind, addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.82:13: 'It is possible, bhikkhus, that some foolish person here, unknowing, immersed in ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think to outrun the Teacher's instruction. 'So, it seems, form is non-self, feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self. Then how will actions done by what is non-self affect the self?' You have been well instructed by me, bhikkhus, with questioning and counter-questioning on various points regarding these things.
translations.sn22.82:4: 'But, venerable sir, what is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'These five aggregates subject to clinging, bhikkhu, have desire as their root.' ... 'Is clinging the same as these five aggregates subject to clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'Neither is clinging the same as these five aggregates subject to clinging, bhikkhu, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging; rather, the desire and lust there is the clinging there.' 'Good, venerable sir,' that monk... asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: 'But, venerable sir, could there be diversity in desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'There could be, bhikkhu,' the Blessed One said. 'Here, bhikkhu, someone thinks thus: 'May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling... such perception... such volitional formations... such consciousness in the future.' Thus, bhikkhu, there could be diversity in desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging.' 'Good, venerable sir,' that monk... asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: 'What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the perception aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the volitional formations aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the consciousness aggregate?' 'The four great elements, bhikkhu, are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the volitional formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the manifestation of the consciousness aggregate.' 'Good, venerable sir,' that monk... asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: "But how, venerable sir, does identity view come to be?" "Here, bhikkhu, an untaught ordinary person, who has no regard for the noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for superior persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They regard feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That is how, bhikkhu, identity view comes to be." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu replied ... and asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: "But how, venerable sir, does identity view not come to be?" "Here, bhikkhu, a learned noble disciple, who has regard for the noble ones and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma, who has regard for superior persons and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form. They do not regard feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness. That is how, bhikkhu, identity view does not come to be." "Good, venerable sir," that bhikkhu replied ... and asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Savatthi. There the Venerable Ananda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus." "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ananda. The Venerable Ananda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: "Just as, friend Ananda, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, would look at their own facial reflection in a clean bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, with clinging, not without clinging; so too, friend Ananda, with clinging there is the thought 'I am,' not without clinging. With clinging to feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness there is the thought 'I am,' not without clinging.
translations.sn22.84:10: "This simile, Tissa, was made by me to convey the meaning. And this is the meaning here: 'a person unskilled in the path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the ordinary person. 'A person skilled in the path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'A forked path,' Tissa, this is a designation for doubt. 'The left-hand path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, that is: wrong view ... wrong concentration. 'The right-hand path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view ... right concentration. 'The dense jungle,' Tissa, this is a designation for ignorance. 'The great low-lying marsh,' Tissa, this is a designation for sensual pleasures. 'The deep precipice,' Tissa, this is a designation for anger and despair. 'The pleasant even ground,' Tissa, this is a designation for Nibbana. Delight, Tissa, delight, Tissa. I by exhortation, I by guidance, I by instruction."
translations.sn22.84:5: "Good, good, Tissa. For that is how it is, Tissa. As is the case for one who has not removed lust for volitional formations, who has not removed desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for consciousness, for him, with the change and alteration of that consciousness, arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair." "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.sn22.84:6: "Good, good, Tissa. For that is how it is, Tissa. As is the case for one who has not removed lust for consciousness. What do you think, Tissa, for one who has removed lust, desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving for form, for him, with the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn22.85:1: On one occasion the Venerable Sariputta was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park. Now on that occasion a bhikkhu named Yamaka had come to hold such a pernicious view: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body, does not exist after death."
translations.sn22.85:10: "What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathagata as form ... feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness?" "No, friend."
translations.sn22.85:11: "What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathagata as that which is formless ... feelingless ... perceptionless ... non-volitional ... non-conscious?" "No, friend." "Then, friend Yamaka, when the Tathagata is not apprehended by you as real and actual here in this very life, is it fitting for you to declare: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body, does not exist after death'?"
translations.sn22.85:12: "Formerly, friend Sariputta, when I was ignorant, I held that pernicious view; but now, having heard this Dhamma exposition of the Venerable Sariputta, I have abandoned that pernicious view and have penetrated the Dhamma."
translations.sn22.85:16: They do not understand as it really is: 'Impermanent form is impermanent form.' They do not understand as it really is: 'Impermanent feeling is impermanent feeling.' They do not understand as it really is: 'Impermanent perception is impermanent perception.' They do not understand as it really is: 'Impermanent volitional formations are impermanent volitional formations.' They do not understand as it really is: 'Impermanent consciousness is impermanent consciousness.'
translations.sn22.85:19: They do not understand as it really is: 'Conditioned form is conditioned form.' They do not understand as it really is: 'Conditioned feeling ... conditioned perception ... conditioned volitional formations ... conditioned consciousness is conditioned consciousness.'
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand form as a murderer: 'Form is a murderer.' They do not truly understand feeling as a murderer: 'Feeling is a murderer.' ... They do not truly understand perception as a murderer: 'Perception is a murderer.' ... They do not truly understand volitional formations as murderers: 'Volitional formations are murderers.' They do not truly understand consciousness as a murderer: 'Consciousness is a murderer.'
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach form, cling to it, and take a stand: 'This is mine.' They approach feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness, cling to it, and take a stand: 'This is mine.' These five aggregates subject to clinging, when approached and clung to, lead to harm and suffering for a long time.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as: 'Form is impermanent.' They truly understand impermanent feeling ... impermanent perception ... impermanent volitional formations ... impermanent consciousness as: 'Consciousness is impermanent.'
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand non-self form as: 'Form is non-self.' They truly understand non-self feeling ... non-self perception ... non-self volitional formations ... non-self consciousness as: 'Consciousness is non-self.'
translations.sn22.85:5: When those monks were unable to dissuade Venerable Yamaka from that evil view, then those monks rose from their seats and went to Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Venerable Sāriputta, such an evil view has arisen in the monk named Yamaka: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.' It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta would approach the monk Yamaka out of compassion.' Venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to Venerable Yamaka; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Yamaka ... and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: 'Is it true, friend Yamaka, that such an evil view has arisen in you: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death'?' 'Yes, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.'
translations.sn22.85:9: 'What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?' 'No, friend.' 'Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?' 'No, friend.' 'In feeling ... apart from feeling ... in perception ... apart from perception ... in volitional formations ... apart from volitional formations ... in consciousness, do you regard the Tathāgata as in consciousness?' 'No, friend.' 'Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from consciousness?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn22.86:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time Venerable Anurādha was dwelling not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut. Then several wanderers of other sects approached Venerable Anurādha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Anurādha. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'Friend Anurādha, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—does the Tathāgata, when describing him, describe him in these four ways: 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'?'
translations.sn22.86:10: 'What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form ... feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:11: 'What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard this one who is formless ... feelingless ... perceptionless ... without volitional formations ... without consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:12: 'And since, Anurādha, the Tathāgata is not apprehended by you as true and real here and now, is it fitting for you to declare: 'That Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—the Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him otherwise than in these four ways: 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or ... 'does not exist,' or ... 'both exists and does not exist,' or ... 'neither exists nor does not exist after death'?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: 'Friends, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—the Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him otherwise than in these four ways: 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'.' When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'This monk must be newly gone forth, or if an elder, he is foolish and incompetent.' Then, having disparaged Venerable Anurādha as newly gone forth and foolish, the wanderers of other sects rose from their seats and departed.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then, soon after those wanderers of other sects had left, this thought occurred to Venerable Anurādha: 'If those wanderers of other sects were to question me further, how should I answer so that I would speak in accordance with the words of the Blessed One and not misrepresent him with falsehood, and so that my explanation would be in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable consequence of my assertion would give ground for criticism?'
translations.sn22.86:8: "What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?" "No, venerable sir." "Feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as the Tathāgata?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn22.86:9: "What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?" "No, venerable sir." "Apart from form, do you regard the Tathāgata?" "No, venerable sir." "In feeling... apart from feeling... in perception... apart from perception... in volitional formations... apart from volitional formations... in consciousness... apart from consciousness, do you regard the Tathāgata?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn22.89:10: "Just as, friend, the scent of a blue lotus, a white lotus, or a red lotus. If someone were to say: 'The scent belongs to the petals' or 'the scent belongs to the color' or 'the scent belongs to the filaments,' would they be speaking correctly?" "No, friend." "Then how, friend, would one answer correctly?" "'The scent belongs to the flower,' friend, would be the correct answer." "So too, friend, I do not say 'I am' form, nor do I say 'I am' apart from form. I do not say 'I am' feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, nor do I say 'I am' apart from consciousness. Yet, friend, in the five aggregates subject to clinging, I have attained 'I am,' but I do not regard 'this I am.'"
translations.sn22.89:11: "Although, friend, a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still there remains in him: the latent tendency to conceit 'I am,' the desire 'I am,' the underlying tendency 'I am' not yet uprooted. Then, at a later time, he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.' As he dwells thus contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever latent tendency to conceit 'I am,' desire 'I am,' underlying tendency 'I am' that remained in him, that too is uprooted."
translations.sn22.89:12: "Just as, friend, a cloth that is soiled and stained. Its owners give it to a washerman. The washerman scrubs it with salt earth, lye, or cow dung, and rinses it in clear water. Although the cloth becomes clean and pure, still there remains in it a latent scent of salt earth, lye, or cow dung not yet removed. The washerman returns it to the owners. The owners place it in a sweet-scented box. Whatever latent scent of salt earth, lye, or cow dung remained in it, that too is removed. So too, friend, although a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still there remains in him a latent tendency to conceit 'I am,' desire 'I am,' underlying tendency 'I am' not yet uprooted. Then, at a later time, he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.' As he dwells thus contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever latent tendency to conceit 'I am,' desire 'I am,' underlying tendency 'I am' that remained in him, that too is uprooted."
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the elder monks said to Venerable Khemaka: "We did not ask Venerable Khemaka with the intention of troubling him, but Venerable Khemaka was able to explain in detail the teaching of the Blessed One, to teach it, to proclaim it, to establish it, to open it up, to analyze it, to make it clear. Indeed, Venerable Khemaka has explained in detail the teaching of the Blessed One, taught it, proclaimed it, established it, opened it up, analyzed it, made it clear."
translations.sn22.90:1: On one occasion several elder monks were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Channa emerged from seclusion, took a key, and approaching the elder monks from dwelling to dwelling, said to them: "Let the venerable elders advise me, instruct me, give me a Dhamma talk so that I may see the Dhamma."
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the elder monks said to Venerable Channa: "Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is non-self; feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are non-self."
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: "I too think thus: 'Form is impermanent, feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is impermanent; form is non-self, feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all phenomena are non-self.' Yet my mind does not leap forward, settle, become steady, or become resolved in the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Agitation and clinging arise; the mind turns back, thinking: 'Then what will be my self?' But one who sees the Dhamma does not think thus. Who will teach me the Dhamma so that I may see the Dhamma?"
translations.sn22.90:4: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: "This Venerable Ānanda is dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park, praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by wise fellow practitioners, and he is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma. And I have that much confidence in Venerable Ānanda. Why don't I go to Venerable Ānanda?" Then Venerable Channa, having put his lodging in order and taking his bowl and robe, went to Kosambī, to Ghosita's Park, to Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda... and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.90:8: "Even with this much we are pleased with Venerable Channa, that Venerable Channa has revealed and cut off the stake. Lend an ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma." Then, just from that, a sublime joy and happiness arose in Venerable Channa: "It seems I am capable of understanding the Dhamma."
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, I do not dispute with the world; the world disputes with me. A proponent of the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. That which is agreed upon as nonexistent in the world by the wise, I too say 'it does not exist.' That which is agreed upon as existent in the world by the wise, I too say 'it exists.'
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, bhikkhus, is agreed upon as existent in the world by the wise, which I say 'it exists'? Form, bhikkhus, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is agreed upon as existent in the world by the wise; I too say 'it exists.' Feeling... Perception... Volitional formations... Consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is agreed upon as existent in the world by the wise; I too say 'it exists.' This, bhikkhus, is what is agreed upon as existent in the world by the wise; I too say 'it exists.'
translations.sn22.94:4: There is, bhikkhus, a world-phenomenon in the world, which the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully understands; having fully awakened to and fully understood it, he declares it, teaches it, makes it known, establishes it, reveals it, explains it, and makes it plain.
translations.sn22.94:7: Bhikkhus, one who, when the Tathāgata is declaring, teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, explaining, and making plain in such a way, does not know and does not see—what shall I do with that foolish ordinary person, blind, sightless, unknowing, unseeing?
translations.sn22.95:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjhā on the bank of the river Ganges. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.95:10: In whatever way one scrutinizes, wisely examines, it appears empty, hollow to one who sees it wisely.
translations.sn22.95:11: And concerning this body, taught by the one of vast wisdom, see form abandoned, the giving up of the three things.
translations.sn22.95:12: When vitality, heat, and consciousness depart from this body, then it lies cast away, food for others, without consciousness.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, this illusion, the prattle of fools. This is called a murderer; here no essence is found.
translations.sn22.95:2: "Suppose, bhikkhus, this river Ganges were carrying along a great mass of foam. A person with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and wisely examine it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it would appear merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in a mass of foam? So too, bhikkhus, whatever form there is, past, future, or present... whether far or near—a bhikkhu sees it, scrutinizes it, wisely examines it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it appears merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in form?
translations.sn22.95:3: "Suppose, bhikkhus, in the autumn, when it is raining in large drops, a water bubble appears and bursts on the water. A person with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and wisely examine it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it would appear merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in a water bubble? So too, bhikkhus, whatever feeling there is, past, future, or present... whether far or near—a bhikkhu sees it, scrutinizes it, wisely examines it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it appears merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:4: "Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A person with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and wisely examine it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it would appear merely empty, hollow, insubstantial... For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in a mirage? So too, bhikkhus, whatever perception there is...
translations.sn22.95:5: "Suppose, bhikkhus, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he would see a large plantain trunk, straight, fresh, without a fruit-bud core. He would cut it down at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would remove the outer skin. As he removes the outer skin, he would not find even sapwood, much less heartwood. A person with good eyesight would see it, scrutinize it, and wisely examine it. To him, seeing it, scrutinizing it, wisely examining it, it would appear merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in a plantain trunk? So too, bhikkhus, whatever volitional formations there are, past, future, or present... whether far or near—a bhikkhu sees them, scrutinizes them, wisely examines them. To him, seeing them, scrutinizing them, wisely examining them, they appear merely empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be, bhikkhus, in volitional formations?
translations.sn22.95:6: Just as, monks, a magician or a magician's apprentice might display a magical illusion at a crossroads. A person with good eyesight would see it, examine it, and investigate it properly. As they see it, examine it, and investigate it properly, it would appear to them as empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in an illusion? In the same way, monks, whatever consciousness—past, future, or present... whether far or near—a monk sees, examines, and investigates properly. As they see it, examine it, and investigate it properly, it appears to them as empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are liberated. In liberation, there arises the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' ... They understand: 'There is no more for this state of being.'
translations.sn22.95:9: Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a bubble, perception like a mirage, volitional formations like a plantain trunk, consciousness like an illusion—so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Savatthi. Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Is there, venerable sir, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity? Is there, venerable sir, any feeling... any perception... any volitional formations... any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity?" "There is not, monk, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity. There is not, monk, any feeling... any perception... any volitional formations... any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity."
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a small lump of cow dung in his hand, said to that monk: "Even to this extent, monk, there is no acquisition of individual existence that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity. If, monk, even this acquisition of individual existence were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, monk, even this acquisition of individual existence is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.
translations.sn22.96:3: In the past, monk, I was a king, an anointed khattiya. When I was that king, an anointed khattiya, I had eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusavati as the capital. I had eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand mansions, with the Great Assembly Hall as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand couches, made of ivory, heartwood, gold, silver, covered with long-haired rugs, with coverlets of antelope hide, with canopies above and red cushions at both ends. I had eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold ornaments, with gold banners, covered with gold netting, with Uposatha the elephant king as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold ornaments, with gold banners, covered with gold netting, with Valahaka the horse king as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with gold ornaments, with gold banners, covered with gold netting, with the Vejayanta chariot as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand jewels, with the jewel treasure as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand women, with Queen Subhadda as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand khattiyas, as attendants, with the jewel-treasure as the foremost. I had eighty-four thousand cows, with tethers of fine cloth and bronze milk pails. I had eighty-four thousand bolts of cloth, of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, fine cotton. I had eighty-four thousand dishes of food, offered morning and evening.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a little bit of dust on the tip of his fingernail, said to that monk: "Even to this extent, monk, there is no form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that for eternity. If, monk, even this much form were permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because, monk, even this much form is not permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned."
translations.sn35.101:4: Just as, monks, whatever grass, sticks, branches, and leaves there are in this Jeta Grove, people might take away, burn, or use as they wish, would you then think: 'People are taking us away, burning us, or using us as they wish'?"
translations.sn35.116:2: Then those monks thought: "This Venerable Ananda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Ananda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which was stated without detailed analysis. Let us approach Venerable Ananda and ask him about this matter."
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those monks approached Venerable Ananda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ananda. After exchanging courteous and memorable words, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to Venerable Ananda:
translations.sn35.116:5: "Just as, friend, a person in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass over the root and trunk of a great tree standing with heartwood, thinking that the heartwood should be sought among the branches and leaves; such is the case with you venerables: having bypassed the Blessed One when he is present, you think that we should be asked about this matter. For, friend, the Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen—he is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the holy one; he is the proclaimer, the expounder, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathagata. And indeed, the time was such that you should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. You should have remembered whatever the Blessed One would have explained."
translations.sn35.116:6: "Certainly, friend Ananda, the Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen—he is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the holy one; he is the proclaimer, the expounder, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathagata. And indeed, the time was such that we should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. We should have remembered whatever the Blessed One would have explained. However, Venerable Ananda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Ananda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which was stated without detailed analysis. Please explain, Venerable Ananda, without making it burdensome."
translations.sn35.116:7: "Then listen, friends, pay careful attention, I will speak." "Yes, friend," those monks replied to Venerable Ananda. Venerable Ananda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: "Yes, friend," those monks, having agreed to Venerable Ananda, rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: "Before my enlightenment, monks, when I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: 'Those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously been experienced by the mind—past, ceased, changed—my mind frequently goes and inclines toward them, whether in the present, a little, or in the future.' Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: 'Regarding those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously been experienced by the mind—past, ceased, changed—I should guard my mind with diligence, mindfulness, and mental protection.' Therefore, monks, for you too, regarding those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously been experienced by the mind—past, ceased, changed—your mind frequently goes and inclines toward them, whether in the present, a little, or in the future. Therefore, monks, for you too, regarding those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously been experienced by the mind—past, ceased, changed—you should guard your mind with diligence, mindfulness, and mental protection. Therefore, monks, that base should be understood where the eye ceases and perception of forms ceases; that base should be understood ... where the tongue ceases and perception of tastes ceases; that base should be understood ... where the mind ceases and perception of mental phenomena ceases; that base should be understood." Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rajagaha on Vulture's Peak. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: "What is the cause, venerable sir, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbana in this very life? And what is the cause, venerable sir, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final Nibbana in this very life?"
translations.sn35.118:2: "There are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing lust. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, then for him, delighting in them, welcoming them, and remaining attached to them, consciousness becomes dependent on that and grasping occurs. A monk with grasping, lord of the devas, does not attain final Nibbana ...
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, lord of the devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue ... There are, lord of the devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing lust. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, then for him, delighting in them, welcoming them, and remaining attached to them, consciousness becomes dependent on that and grasping occurs. A monk with grasping, lord of the devas, does not attain final Nibbana. This is the cause, lord of the devas, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbana in this very life.
translations.sn35.118:4: And there are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing lust. If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, then for him, not delighting in them, not welcoming them, and not remaining attached to them, consciousness does not become dependent on that and grasping does not occur. A monk without grasping, lord of the devas, attains final Nibbana ...
translations.sn35.127:1: On one occasion Venerable Pindola Bharadvaja was staying at Kosambi, in Ghosita's Park. Then King Udena approached Venerable Pindola Bharadvaja; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Pindola Bharadvaja. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, King Udena said to Venerable Pindola Bharadvaja: "What is the cause, Master Bharadvaja, what is the reason why these young monks, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, who have not played around with sensual pleasures, lead the holy life that is complete and pure for their entire life, and they succeed in it?" "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: 'Come, monks, regard a mother-like woman as a mother, regard a sister-like woman as a sister, regard a daughter-like woman as a daughter.' This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, who have not played around with sensual pleasures, lead the holy life that is complete and pure for their entire life, and they succeed in it."
translations.sn35.127:2: "The mind is fickle, Master Bharadvaja. Sometimes lustful thoughts arise even towards mother-like women, sister-like women, daughter-like women. Is there, Master Bharadvaja, another cause, another reason why these young monks, black-haired ... succeed in it?"
translations.sn35.127:3: "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: 'Come, monks, reflect on this very body from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin, full of various kinds of impurity: In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.' This too, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks, black-haired ... succeed in it." "For those monks, Master Bharadvaja, who have developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom, that is easy. But for those monks, Master Bharadvaja, who have undeveloped body, undeveloped virtue, undeveloped mind, undeveloped wisdom, that is difficult. Sometimes, Master Bharadvaja, when one thinks, 'I will attend to the unattractive,' the attractive comes instead. Is there, Master Bharadvaja, another cause, another reason why these young monks, black-haired ... succeed in it?"
translations.sn35.127:4: "This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: 'Come, monks, dwell with your sense doors guarded. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or its features. Since, if you dwell with the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in, practice restraint for its restraint. Guard the eye faculty; undertake restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear ... Having smelled an odor with the nose ... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue ... Having felt a tactile object with the body ... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or its features. Since, if you dwell with the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in, practice restraint for its restraint. Guard the mind faculty; undertake restraint of the mind faculty.' This too, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, who have not played around with sensual pleasures, lead the holy life that is complete and pure for their entire life, and they succeed in it."
translations.sn35.136:2: "Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, tactile objects, and mental phenomena—all of these are said to be as far as they exist.
translations.sn35.136:3: In the world with its gods, these are considered happiness; but where these cease, that is considered suffering by them.
translations.sn35.136:4: The noble ones have seen happiness as the cessation of identity; this goes against what the whole world sees.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others call happiness, that the noble ones call suffering; what others call suffering, that the noble ones know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: See this Dhamma hard to understand, here the foolish are confused; for those shrouded there is darkness, blindness for those who do not see.
translations.sn35.136:7: But for those who see, it is open, like light for those with vision; those unskilled in the Dhamma's path do not understand what is near.
translations.sn35.136:8: By those obsessed with craving for existence, following craving for existence, fallen under Māra's sway, this Dhamma is not well understood.
translations.sn35.63:1: At Savatthi. Then Venerable Migajala approached the Blessed One ... Sitting to one side, Venerable Migajala said to the Blessed One: "'One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone,' it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, does one dwell alone, and to what extent does one dwell with a companion?"
translations.sn35.69:1: On one occasion Venerable Sariputta and Venerable Upasena were staying at Rajagaha in the Cool Grove, at the Snake's Hood Grotto. Now on that occasion a snake had bitten Venerable Upasena on the body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: "Come, friends, lift this body onto a cot and carry it outside. Before this body is scattered right here, like a handful of chaff."
translations.sn35.74:1: At Savatthi. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One ... Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, in such-and-such a dwelling there is a certain monk who is new, not well-known, sick, suffering, gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that monk out of compassion."
translations.sn35.74:12: "Good, good, monk. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me for the fading away of lust. For the fading away of lust, monk, is the Dhamma taught by me. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?"
translations.sn35.74:18: "But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it proper to regard that thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard the news and the talk of illness, and knowing that the monk was unknown, approached that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he stirred on his bed. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: 'Enough, monk, do not stir on your bed. There are these seats prepared, I will sit there.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to that monk: 'I hope you are bearing up, monk, I hope you are getting by? I hope that painful feelings are subsiding, not increasing, and that their subsiding is evident, not their increase?'
translations.sn35.74:3: 'No, venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by; strong painful feelings are increasing for me, not subsiding; their increase is evident, not their subsiding.'
translations.sn35.75:7: 'Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging.'
translations.sn35.75:8: 'Good, good, monk. It is good that you, monk, understand the Dhamma taught by me to be for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging. For, monk, the Dhamma has been taught by me for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging.'
translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached ... sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.88:12: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a stick, then I will think thus: "These people of Sunāparanta are good, indeed these people of Sunāparanta are very good, in that they do not give me a blow with a knife." Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:14: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a knife, then I will think thus: "These people of Sunāparanta are good, indeed these people of Sunāparanta are very good, in that they do not take my life with a sharp knife." Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:16: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp knife, then I will think thus: "There are disciples of the Blessed One who, being distressed and ashamed and disgusted with the body and life, seek for someone to take their life; but I have obtained this without having sought for someone to take my life." Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:17: 'Good, good, Puṇṇa. You will be able, Puṇṇa, endowed with this taming and peacefulness, to dwell in the Sunāparanta country. Now, Puṇṇa, when you think it is time.'
translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, put his lodging in order, and taking his bowl and robe, set out on a journey to the Sunāparanta country. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at the Sunāparanta country. There Venerable Puṇṇa dwelled in the Sunāparanta country. Then, within that rainy season, Venerable Puṇṇa established five hundred male lay followers. Within that rainy season, he established five hundred female lay followers. Within that rainy season, he realized the three knowledges. Within that rainy season, he attained final Nibbāna.
