translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks approached the Blessed One ... sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, that clansman named Puṇṇa, who was exhorted by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has passed away. What is his destination, what is his future state?'
translations.sn35.88:4: 'Puṇṇa, having been exhorted by me with this brief exhortation, in which country will you dwell?' 'Venerable sir, there is a country called Sunāparanta; I will dwell there.'
translations.sn35.88:5: 'Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta are rough; Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta are harsh. If, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, what will you think then?'
translations.sn35.88:6: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, then I will think thus: "These people of Sunāparanta are good, indeed these people of Sunāparanta are very good, in that they do not give me a blow with the hand." Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:8: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with the hand, then I will think thus: "These people of Sunāparanta are good, indeed these people of Sunāparanta are very good, in that they do not give me a blow with a clod." Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approached the Blessed One ... sitting to one side, Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.95:10: 'And here, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen, there will be merely the seen; in the heard, merely the heard; in the sensed, merely the sensed; in the cognized, merely the cognized. When, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, in the cognized merely the cognized, then, Māluṅkyaputta, you will not be 'by that.' When, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'by that,' then, Māluṅkyaputta, you will not be 'therein.' When, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not 'therein,' then, Māluṅkyaputta, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.'
translations.sn35.95:12: 'Having seen a form with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign, He experiences it with mind enthralled, And clings to it firmly.'
translations.sn35.95:13: 'For him feelings increase, Born of the form; He is tormented by longing and vexation, His mind is afflicted; Thus he accumulates suffering, And Nibbāna is said to be far away.'
translations.sn35.95:14: 'Having heard a sound with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign, He experiences it with mind enthralled, And clings to it firmly.'
translations.sn35.95:16: 'Having smelled an odor with mindfulness lost, Attending to the pleasing sign, He experiences it with mind enthralled, And clings to it firmly.'
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, mindfulness is lost, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of desire, they feel, and they cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:2: "Now, what shall we say to the young monks here? For you, monk, are old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of life, yet you ask for advice in brief."
translations.sn35.95:20: Having contacted a contact, mindfulness is lost, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of desire, they feel, and they cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known a mental object, mindfulness is lost, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of desire, they feel, and they cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:24: They do not lust after forms, having seen a form with mindfulness; with a mind detached, they feel, and they do not cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:25: As they see a form, and as they experience a feeling; it decreases, it does not accumulate, thus they live mindfully; thus, having diminished suffering, nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:26: They do not lust after sounds, having heard a sound with mindfulness; with a mind detached, they feel, and they do not cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:27: As they hear a sound, and as they experience a feeling; it decreases, it does not accumulate, thus they live mindfully; thus, having diminished suffering, nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:28: They do not lust after odors, having smelled an odor with mindfulness; with a mind detached, they feel, and they do not cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:3: "Although, venerable sir, I am old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of life. Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the Fortunate One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I may understand the meaning of the Blessed One's words. So that I may become an heir of the Blessed One's words."
translations.sn35.95:30: They do not lust after flavors, having tasted a flavor with mindfulness; with a mind detached, they feel, and they do not cling to it.
translations.sn35.95:35: As they know a mental object, and as they experience a feeling; it decreases, it does not accumulate, thus they live mindfully; thus, having diminished suffering, nibbāna is said to be near."
translations.sn35.95:36: "Venerable sir, I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One said in brief in this detailed way." "Good, good, Mālukyaputta. Good indeed, Mālukyaputta, that you understand the meaning of what I said in brief in this detailed way:
translations.sn35.95:4: "What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Regarding those forms cognizable by the eye, not seen, not seen before, you do not see, nor will you see them? Is there in you any desire, lust, or affection for them?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn35.95:9: "Regarding those mental objects cognizable by the mind, not known, not known before, you do not know, nor will you know them? Is there in you any desire, lust, or affection for them?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn36.19:12: "And what, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime? Here, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime. Those, Ānanda, who would say: 'This is the ultimate peace, happiness, and pleasure experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime."
translations.sn36.19:15: "And what, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime? Here, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime."
translations.sn36.19:7: "And what, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime? Here, Ānanda, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime. Those, Ānanda, who would say: 'This is the ultimate peace, happiness, and pleasure experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime."
translations.sn36.19:8: "And what, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the subsiding of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime. Those, Ānanda, who would say: 'This is the ultimate peace, happiness, and pleasure experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime."
translations.sn36.19:9: "And what, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body, that which the noble ones describe as 'dwelling in happiness with equanimity and mindfulness,' enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime. Those, Ānanda, who would say: 'This is the ultimate peace, happiness, and pleasure experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a happiness other than this, more excellent and sublime."
translations.sn36.21:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said this to the Blessed One: "There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: 'Whatever this individual person experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by what was done in the past.' What does Master Gotama say about this?"
translations.sn36.21:2: "Sīvaka, some feelings arise from bile. This should be known by oneself, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise from bile. This is accepted as truth in the world, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise from bile. In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold the view and say: 'Whatever this individual experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is due to past action.' They go beyond what is known by oneself and what is accepted as truth in the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong."
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent! ... I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha. From today, may Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life."
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: "What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the way leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the way leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?"
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, monks, is spiritual joy? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This is called, monks, spiritual joy.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, monks, is spiritual joy that is more spiritual? When, monks, a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion, joy arises. This is called, monks, spiritual joy that is more spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, monks, is spiritual happiness? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' This is called, monks, spiritual happiness.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, monks, is spiritual happiness that is more spiritual? When, monks, a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion, happiness and gladness arise. This is called, monks, spiritual happiness that is more spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This is called, monks, spiritual equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity that is more spiritual? When, monks, a monk whose taints are destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion, equanimity arises. This is called, monks, spiritual equanimity that is more spiritual.
translations.sn36.4:2: One who does not endure these arisen painful feelings, bodily feelings that take life, trembles when touched by them.
translations.sn36.4:3: He wails and laments, weak and powerless; he does not rise up from the abyss, nor does he gain a foothold.
translations.sn36.6:2: But, monks, a learned noble disciple, when touched by a painful feeling, does not sorrow, grieve, or lament; he does not weep beating his breast and become distraught. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one does not feel a feeling, whether pleasant or painful, even though learned; and this is the great distinction between the wise one and the ordinary person, the skilled one.
translations.sn36.6:5: For one who has understood the Dhamma, learned, seeing this world and the next, desirable things do not stir the mind, nor is there aversion towards the undesirable.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, monks, is a monk mindful? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings ... mind in mind ... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. That is how, monks, a monk is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending? Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking aside; when bending and stretching; when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; when eating, drinking, consuming food, and tasting; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent. That is how, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension. Mindful and clearly comprehending, monks, a monk should await the time. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If, monks, while a monk is dwelling thus mindful, clearly aware, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a pleasant feeling arises in him, he understands: 'This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. This pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on an impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen body—how could it be permanent?' He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, contemplating vanishing, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, contemplating vanishing, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment, the underlying tendency to lust for the body and pleasant feeling is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: 'It is impermanent,' he understands: 'It is not clung to,' he understands: 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a painful feeling... If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: 'It is impermanent,' he understands: 'It is not clung to,' he understands: 'It is not delighted in.' If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. Feeling a feeling terminating with the body, he understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with the body.' Feeling a feeling terminating with life, he understands: 'I feel a feeling terminating with life.' He understands: 'With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.'
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer park. Now on that occasion the Blessed One's foot had been cut by a stone sliver. Severe pains assailed the Blessed One—bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, racking, severe, disagreeable, unpleasant. But the Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly aware, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one leg overlapping the other, mindful and clearly aware. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: "Are you lying down in lethargy, or are you intoxicated with poetry? Don't you have sufficient goals? Alone in a secluded dwelling place, are you sleeping because you are drowsy?"
translations.sn4.13:3: "I do not lie down in lethargy, nor am I intoxicated with poetry. Having attained the goal, I am sorrowless. Alone in a secluded dwelling place, I lie down full of compassion for all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: Even those with a dart stuck in the chest, piercing the heart again and again—they too, afflicted by the dart, obtain sleep here. Therefore I do not sleep, I who am dart-free.
translations.sn4.13:5: I am not afraid to be awake, nor do I fear to sleep. Day and night do not oppress me. I see no decline for myself anywhere in the world. Therefore I sleep, full of compassion for all beings."
translations.sn4.18:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at the brahmin village of Pañcasālā. Now on that occasion in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā there were gifts for the young maidens. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Pañcasālā for alms. Now on that occasion the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā had been possessed by Māra the Evil One: 'Don't let the ascetic Gotama obtain alms.'
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered Pañcasālā for alms with a bowl as clean as when he had washed it, and he departed with a bowl as clean as when he had washed it. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and said to him: 'So, ascetic, did you obtain alms?' 'Was it you, Evil One, who made it so that I would not obtain alms?' 'Then, venerable sir, let the Blessed One enter Pañcasālā for alms a second time. I will make it so that the Blessed One obtains alms.'
translations.sn4.19:4: "What they call mine, and those who say 'mine'—if your mind is among these, ascetic, you will not escape me."
translations.sn4.19:5: "What they call is not mine, those who say are not me. Thus, Evil One, know this: you will not even see my path."
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd's Banyan Tree, newly enlightened. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'I am truly freed from that difficult practice. Good that I am freed from that useless difficult practice. Good that I, steadfast, have attained enlightenment.'
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his mind the reflection in the Blessed One's mind, approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: "Having deviated from ascetic practices by which young men purify themselves, impure you think yourself pure; you have missed the path to purity."
translations.sn4.1:6: "Having developed virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the path to enlightenment, I have reached supreme purity; you are defeated, End-maker!"
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, 'The Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me,' sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in a forest hut in the Himalayan region. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'Is it possible to exercise rulership righteously: without killing and without instigating others to kill, without confiscating and without instigating others to confiscate, without sorrowing and without causing sorrow?'
translations.sn4.20:3: "Even if it were a mountain of gold, made entirely of gold, not even double that would suffice for one person. Knowing this, one should conduct oneself accordingly.
translations.sn4.20:4: Having seen suffering and its source, how could a person incline towards sensual pleasures? Having understood that attachment in the world is a snare, a person should train for the removal of that very attachment."
translations.sn4.21:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Silāvatī. Now at that time several monks were dwelling not far from the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then Māra the Evil One, having assumed the form of a brahmin, with a large matted hair-knot, wearing an antelope hide garment, old, bent like a roof rafter, breathing heavily, taking a staff of udumbara wood, approached those monks; having approached, he said this to those monks: "You, sirs, have gone forth while young, lads, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, not having dallied with sensual pleasures. Enjoy, sirs, human sensual pleasures. Do not abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what is a matter of time." "We do not, brahmin, abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what is a matter of time. Rather, we abandon what is a matter of time to pursue what is visible here and now. For, brahmin, sensual pleasures have been called by the Blessed One as having much suffering, much despair, with greater danger in this. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be experienced individually by the wise." When this was said, Māra the Evil One shook his head, lolled his tongue, furrowed his brow into three lines on his forehead, and departed leaning on his staff.
translations.sn4.24:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā, on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the foot of the goatherd's banyan tree. Now at that time Māra the Evil One had been following the Blessed One for seven years, seeking an opportunity but not finding one. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One with a verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: "Not having found any enjoyment there, the wind-sower departed; Like a crow attacking a rock, we are disappointed in Gotama."
translations.sn4.24:2: "Are you sunk in sorrow, meditating in the forest? Have you lost wealth, or do you long for it? Or have you done some wrong in the village? Why do you not make friends with people? No one makes friends with you."
translations.sn4.24:3: "Having dug up the root of sorrow entirely, I meditate sorrowless, without wrongdoing; Having cut off all craving and the babble of existence, I meditate, taintless, with bonds of negligence cut."
translations.sn4.24:6: "If you have discovered the path, safe, leading to the deathless, go alone, depart; why instruct another?"
translations.sn4.24:7: "Those people who are crossing over ask about the far shore; Being asked, I explain to them the truth, which is without impediments."
translations.sn4.24:8: "Just as, venerable sir, there might be a lotus pond not far from a village or town. And there might be a crab there. Then, venerable sir, several boys or girls, having left that village or town, would approach that lotus pond; having approached, they would take that crab out of the water and place it on dry land. Whatever limb that crab, venerable sir, might extend, those boys or girls would cut it off, break it, and smash it with a stick or a potsherd. Thus, venerable sir, with all its limbs cut off, broken, and smashed, that crab would be unable to return to that lotus pond. In the same way, venerable sir, all those diversions, deceptions, and agitations have been cut off, broken, and smashed by the Blessed One. I am now unable, venerable sir, to approach the Blessed One again, that is, seeking an opportunity." Then Māra the Evil One, in the presence of the Blessed One, spoke these verses of disappointment:
translations.sn4.24:9: "The crow circled around the rock that looked like fat: 'Perhaps we'll find something soft here, perhaps there might be some savor.'
translations.sn4.25:10: 'The Arahant, the Fortunate One in the world, is not easily led by lust; He has transcended Māra's realm, therefore I sorrow greatly.'
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Blessed One with a verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: "Having attained the goal, the peace of the heart, Having conquered the army of the pleasant and agreeable; I meditate alone, having awakened to happiness, Therefore I do not make friends with people; No one makes friends with me."
translations.sn4.25:16: "How does a monk often dwell here, Having crossed the five floods, having crossed the sixth here? How, often meditating, are perceptions of sensual pleasures Kept at bay, not obtaining a hold?"
translations.sn4.25:17: "With body calmed, with mind well liberated, Not constructing, mindful, homeless; Having understood the Dhamma, meditating without thought, He does not waver, does not recall, is not sluggish.
translations.sn4.25:2: "Why are you despondent, dear? For which man do you sorrow? We will bind him with the snare of lust, Like a forest elephant; Having bound him, we will bring him, He will be under your control."
translations.sn4.25:20: "Having cut off craving, traveling with the multitude, Many faithful will certainly travel; Indeed, this homeless one will lead much of humanity, Having cut off, beyond the realm of the King of Death."
translations.sn4.25:23: "Fools, with lotus stalks, You strike the mountain; With nails you dig the mountain, With iron teeth you eat.
translations.sn4.25:24: Like splitting a rock with your head, You would sink into the nether world; Like bumping into a stump with your chest, You would be disappointed in Gotama."
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said this to the Blessed One: "We will serve at your feet, ascetic." Then the Blessed One paid no attention, as one liberated in the supreme destruction of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, having withdrawn to one side, considered thus: "Men's inclinations are diverse. Suppose we each create a hundred, a hundred forms of a maiden." Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, each created a hundred, a hundred forms of a maiden, and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said this to the Blessed One: "We will serve at your feet, ascetic." The Blessed One paid no attention to that too, as one liberated in the supreme destruction of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.8:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.8:2: "One with sons delights in sons, A cattle-owner delights in cattle likewise; Acquisitions are a man's delight, Indeed, one without acquisitions does not delight."
translations.sn4.8:3: "One who has children grieves because of children, likewise one who has cattle grieves because of cattle; attachments are the grief of man, indeed one who has no attachments does not grieve."
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Now at that time the bhikkhunī Khemā, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, had taken up residence at a rest house between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, while traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, took up residence for one night at that rest house between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: "Come, good man, go to the rest house and find out if there is any ascetic or brahmin there whom I could visit today."
translations.sn44.1:2: "Yes, lord," that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having wandered through the entire rest house, he did not see any ascetic or brahmin whom King Pasenadi of Kosala could visit. However, that man saw the bhikkhunī Khemā who had taken up residence at the rest house. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he said to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
translations.sn44.1:3: "There is no ascetic or brahmin at the rest house, lord, whom you could visit. But, lord, there is a bhikkhunī named Khemā, a disciple of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And this lady has such a good reputation: 'She is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, skilled in discussion.' May the lord visit her."
translations.sn44.1:6: "Then, great king, I will question you about this same matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, great king: Is there any accountant, calculator, or reckoner who is able to count the grains of sand in the Ganges river—so many grains of sand, so many hundreds of grains, so many thousands of grains, so many hundreds of thousands of grains?" "No, venerable lady." "Is there any accountant, calculator, or reckoner who is able to measure the water in the great ocean—so many gallons of water, so many hundreds of gallons, so many thousands of gallons, so many hundreds of thousands of gallons?" "No, venerable lady." "Why is that?" "Because, venerable lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom." "So too, great king, that form by which one might describe the Tathāgata—that form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and made incapable of arising in the future. The Tathāgata is liberated from reckoning in terms of form, great king, deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. 'The Tathāgata exists after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death' does not apply.
translations.sn44.1:9: That consciousness by which one might describe the Tathāgata—that consciousness has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and made incapable of arising in the future. The Tathāgata is liberated from reckoning in terms of consciousness, great king, deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. 'The Tathāgata exists after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death' does not apply." Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having delighted in and approved of the bhikkhunī Khemā's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Khemā, circumambulated her, and departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: "Ignorance, bhikkhus, is the forerunner in the attainment of unwholesome states, followed by lack of shame and fear of wrongdoing. For one who is immersed in ignorance, bhikkhus, for the unwise, wrong view arises; for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises; for one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises; for one with wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; for one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; for one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; for one with wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in a Sakyan town named Nagaraka. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Half of the holy life, venerable sir, is good friendship, good companionship, good association."
translations.sn45.2:2: "Not so, Ānanda, not so, Ānanda. The entire holy life, Ānanda, is good friendship, good companionship, good association. It is to be expected, Ānanda, of a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, good associates—that he will develop the noble eightfold path, that he will cultivate the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, good associates develop the noble eightfold path, cultivate the noble eightfold path? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and matures in relinquishment; he develops right intention, which is based on seclusion ... he develops right speech ... he develops right action ... he develops right livelihood ... he develops right effort ... he develops right mindfulness ... he develops right concentration, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and matures in relinquishment. Thus, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, good associates develops the noble eightfold path, cultivates the noble eightfold path."
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi leaving Sāvatthī in an all-white chariot drawn by white mares. The yoked horses were white, the ornaments were white, the chariot was white, the fittings were white, the reins were white, the goad-stick was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the garments were white, the sandals were white, and he was being fanned with a white chowrie. Seeing him, people said: 'Indeed, sir, that is a divine vehicle! Indeed, sir, it has the appearance of a divine vehicle!'
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will and non-harming, seclusion is his weapon; Endurance is his armor, it leads to safety from bondage.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from his alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: "It is possible, Ānanda," the Blessed One said. "This, Ānanda, is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path: 'the divine vehicle,' and also 'the Dhamma vehicle,' and also 'the unsurpassed victory in battle.'"
translations.sn45.4:8: "One for whom faith and wisdom are always yoked together as the burden; Conscience is the pole, mind is the yoke-tie, mindfulness is the charioteer and guard.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot is furnished with virtue, the axle is meditation, energy is the wheels; Equanimity is the burden-bearing yoke, non-desire is the covering.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Noble Eightfold Path, analyzing it. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? That which, bhikkhus, is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called, bhikkhus, right view.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? That which, bhikkhus, is intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-harming—this is called, bhikkhus, right intention.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? That which, bhikkhus, is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called, bhikkhus, right speech.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? That which, bhikkhus, is abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is called, bhikkhus, right action.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood—this is called, bhikkhus, right livelihood.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right effort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts and strives his mind for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts and strives his mind for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts and strives his mind for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts and strives his mind for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states—this is called, bhikkhus, right effort.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, bhikkhus, is right mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world—this is called, bhikkhus, right mindfulness.
translations.sn46.11:1: "Just as, bhikkhus, whatever beings assume the four postures—walking at times, standing at times, sitting at times, lying down at times—all of them assume these four postures dependent on the earth, established on the earth; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, dependent on virtue, established in virtue, develops the seven factors of enlightenment, makes much of the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.sn46.14:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Now on that occasion Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pipphali Cave, sick, afflicted, gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, emerging from seclusion in the evening, approached Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he sat down on a prepared seat. Sitting, the Blessed One said this to Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: "I hope you are bearing up, Kassapa, I hope you are enduring? I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?" "Venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not enduring. Strong painful feelings are increasing in me, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness dependent on seclusion... (develops) the enlightenment factor of equanimity dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. Thus developed, bhikkhus, thus made much of, the seven factors of enlightenment lead to the abandoning of the things that fetter.
translations.sn46.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas, where there is a town of the Sumbhas named Setaka. Then Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One... (and) sitting to one side, Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: "It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir. How much I have done, venerable sir, and how much affection, respect, shame, and fear of wrongdoing I have for the Blessed One. For, venerable sir, when I was formerly a householder, I was not much esteemed by the Dhamma, not much esteemed by the Sangha. But seeing affection, respect, shame, and fear of wrongdoing for the Blessed One, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.'"
translations.sn46.30:3: "Then, venerable sir, having gone to an empty place, turning over and examining these five aggregates subject to clinging upside down and all around, I truly understood: 'This is suffering' as it really is, 'This is the origin of suffering' as it really is, 'This is the cessation of suffering' as it really is, 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' as it really is. And, venerable sir, the Dhamma has been penetrated by me, the path has been attained by me; which, when developed and cultivated, will lead me, living in such and such a way, to such a state that I will know: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'"
translations.sn46.38:1: At the time, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with eager ears, giving attention, applying the whole mind, and inclining the ear, at that time these five hindrances are not present. At that time the seven factors of enlightenment go to fulfillment by development.
translations.sn46.3:1: "Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation—I say, bhikkhus, that seeing them is very helpful; I say, bhikkhus, that listening to them is very helpful; I say, bhikkhus, that approaching them is very helpful; I say, bhikkhus, that attending on them is very helpful; I say, bhikkhus, that recollecting them is very helpful; I say, bhikkhus, that going forth after them is very helpful. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, having heard the Dhamma from such bhikkhus, one dwells secluded in two ways: bodily seclusion and mental seclusion. Dwelling thus secluded, one recollects and ponders that Dhamma."
translations.sn46.3:2: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, dwelling thus secluded, recollects and ponders that Dhamma, at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that Dhamma with wisdom, examines it, and undertakes a thorough inquiry.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy? There is, bhikkhus, the element of initiative, the element of launching, the element of exertion. Giving frequent attention to that—this is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture? There are, bhikkhus, things that are bases for the enlightenment factor of rapture. Giving frequent attention to that—this is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility? There is, bhikkhus, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind. Giving frequent attention to that—this is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration? There is, bhikkhus, the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction. Giving frequent attention to that—this is the non-nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Savatthi for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: "It is too early to walk for alms in Savatthi. Let us go to the park of the wanderers of other sects."
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, bhikkhus, is the method by which, relying on that method, the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen? Mindfulness regarding internal phenomena, that is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; mindfulness regarding external phenomena, that too is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. 'Enlightenment factor of mindfulness'—thus it comes under the recitation. By this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Investigation of internal phenomena with wisdom, examining, and undertaking a thorough inquiry, that is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena; investigation of external phenomena with wisdom, examining, and undertaking a thorough inquiry, that too is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. 'Enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena'—thus it comes under the recitation. By this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Bodily energy, that is the enlightenment factor of energy; mental energy, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy. 'Enlightenment factor of energy'—thus it comes under the recitation. By this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Rapture accompanied by thought and examination, that is the enlightenment factor of rapture; rapture without thought and examination, that too is the enlightenment factor of rapture. 'Enlightenment factor of rapture'—thus it comes under the recitation. By this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:14: Tranquility of body, that is the enlightenment factor of tranquility; tranquility of mind, that too is the enlightenment factor of tranquility. 'Enlightenment factor of tranquility'—thus it comes under the recitation. By this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Monks, concentration with thought and examination is also the concentration enlightenment factor; concentration without thought and examination is also the concentration enlightenment factor. It comes under the heading 'concentration enlightenment factor'. In this way, it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those monks approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. After an exchange of greetings and courteous talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to the monks:
translations.sn46.52:3: "Friend, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma thus to his disciples: 'Come, monks, abandon the five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' We too, friend, teach the Dhamma thus to our disciples: 'Come, friends, abandon the five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' Here, friend, what is the distinction, the difference, the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, in teaching the Dhamma or in instruction?"
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those monks neither approved nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects. Without approving or rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed, thinking: "We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One." Then those monks, after walking for alms in Savatthi and returning from the alms round after the meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: "Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be spoken to thus: 'Friend, is there a method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten, and the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen?' Questioned thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects would not be able to reply and would, furthermore, meet with vexation. For what reason? Because, monks, that is not within their domain. I do not see anyone, monks, in this world with its gods, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathagata or a disciple of the Tathagata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, monks, is the method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten? Monks, sensual desire internally is a hindrance; sensual desire externally is also a hindrance. It comes under the heading 'hindrance of sensual desire'. In this way, it becomes twofold. Monks, ill will internally is a hindrance; ill will externally is also a hindrance. It comes under the heading 'hindrance of ill will'. In this way, it becomes twofold. Monks, sloth is a hindrance; torpor is also a hindrance. It comes under the heading 'hindrance of sloth and torpor'. In this way, it becomes twofold. Monks, restlessness is a hindrance; worry is also a hindrance. It comes under the heading 'hindrance of restlessness and worry'. In this way, it becomes twofold. Monks, doubt about phenomena internally is a hindrance; doubt about phenomena externally is also a hindrance. It comes under the heading 'hindrance of doubt'. In this way, it becomes twofold. This, monks, is the method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: Monks, when the mind is agitated, that is not the time for developing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, not the time for developing the energy enlightenment factor, not the time for developing the rapture enlightenment factor. For what reason? Because, monks, an agitated mind is hard to calm with those states.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, throw dry sticks into it, blow on it with his mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust. Could that man extinguish that great mass of fire?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn46.53:13: But, monks, when the mind is agitated, that is the time for developing the tranquility enlightenment factor, the time for developing the concentration enlightenment factor, the time for developing the equanimity enlightenment factor. For what reason? Because, monks, an agitated mind is easily calmed with those states.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw wet grass into it, throw wet cow dung into it, throw wet sticks into it, blow on it with a water-sprinkler, and sprinkle it with dust. Could that man extinguish that great mass of fire?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.sn46.53:2: "Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be spoken to thus: 'Friend, when the mind is sluggish, which enlightenment factors are untimely for development at that time, and which enlightenment factors are timely for development at that time? And when, friend, the mind is agitated, which enlightenment factors are untimely for development at that time, and which enlightenment factors are timely for development at that time?' Questioned thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects would not be able to reply and would, furthermore, meet with vexation. For what reason? Because, monks, that is not within their domain.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see anyone, monks, in this world with its gods, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathagata or a disciple of the Tathagata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:4: Monks, at a time when the mind is sluggish, that is not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility, not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of concentration, not the time to develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? A sluggish mind, monks, is hard to arouse with those qualities.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to make a small fire blaze up. If he were to throw wet grass on it, wet cow dung, and wet sticks, give it a draught of water, and scatter dust on it, would that man be able to make that small fire blaze up? No, venerable sir.
translations.sn46.53:7: But, monks, at a time when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the time to develop the enlightenment factor of energy, the time to develop the enlightenment factor of rapture. Why is that? A sluggish mind, monks, is easy to arouse with those qualities.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to make a small fire blaze up. If he were to throw dry grass on it, dry cow dung, and dry sticks, give it a draught of air, and not scatter dust on it, would that man be able to make that small fire blaze up? Yes, venerable sir.
translations.sn46.54:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Koliyans, where there was a town of the Koliyans named Haliddavasana. Then, in the morning, a number of monks dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is too early to walk for alms in Haliddavasana. Let us go to the park of the wanderers of other sects.'
translations.sn46.54:11: Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed: 'Friend, how is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by compassion developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by altruistic joy developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by equanimity developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal?' Questioned thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects would be unable to reply and, furthermore, would meet with vexation. Why is that? Because, monks, that is outside their domain. I do not see anyone, monks, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has learned it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how, monks, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' he dwells perceiving the repulsive there. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,' he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive there. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,' he dwells perceiving the repulsive there. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,' he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive there. If he wishes: 'Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,' he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending there. Or else, having entered upon the beautiful liberation, he dwells therein. Monks, I say that the beautiful is the culmination of the liberation of mind by loving-kindness for a wise monk here who has not penetrated to a superior liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how, monks, is the liberation of mind by compassion developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' he dwells perceiving the repulsive there... If he wishes: 'Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,' he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending there. Or else, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Monks, I say that the base of infinite space is the culmination of the liberation of mind by compassion for a wise monk here who has not penetrated to a superior liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how, monks, is the liberation of mind by altruistic joy developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by altruistic joy... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by altruistic joy, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes: 'May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' he dwells perceiving the repulsive there... If he wishes: 'Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,' he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending there. Or else, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Monks, I say that the base of infinite consciousness is the culmination of the liberation of mind by altruistic joy for a wise monk here who has not penetrated to a superior liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: "Friend, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: 'Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, all around, to all as to oneself, pervade the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, all around, to all as to oneself, pervade the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, all around, to all as to oneself, pervade the entire world with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, all around, to all as to oneself, pervade the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.'"
translations.sn46.8:1: On one occasion, Venerable Upavāna and Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Upavāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Upavāna. After exchanging courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: "Friend Upavāna, could a monk know for himself through wise attention: 'The seven factors of enlightenment, well developed by me, lead to dwelling at ease'?" "Friend Sāriputta, a monk could know for himself through wise attention: 'The seven factors of enlightenment, well developed by me, lead to dwelling at ease.'"
translations.sn47.10:1: Then, in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to a certain bhikkhunī's dwelling; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then several bhikkhunīs approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhunīs said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: "Here, Venerable Ānanda, several bhikkhunīs dwelling with well-established minds in the four establishments of mindfulness perceive a supreme distinction between before and after." "That is so, sisters, that is so. For any monk or nun, sisters, who dwells with a well-established mind in the four establishments of mindfulness, it can be expected: 'They will perceive a supreme distinction between before and after.'"
translations.sn47.10:7: Again, Ānanda, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he is contemplating phenomena in phenomena, either bodily fever arises, or mental sluggishness, or the mind is distracted externally. Then, Ānanda, that monk should direct his mind to some inspiring sign. When he directs his mind to some inspiring sign, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. He reflects thus: 'The purpose for which I directed my mind has been achieved. Now I shall withdraw it.' He withdraws it and does not think or examine. He understands: 'I am without thought, without examination, inwardly mindful, I am happy.' Thus, Ānanda, there is development by directing.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, I have taught development by directing, I have taught development without directing. What should be done by a teacher for his disciples out of compassion, seeking their welfare, that I have done for you. These, Ānanda, are the roots of trees, these are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent, lest you regret it later. This is our instruction to you."
translations.sn47.13:1: On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Now at that time, Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans in the village of Nālaka, sick, suffering, gravely ill. And the novice Cunda was attending on Venerable Sāriputta.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then, due to that same illness, Venerable Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna. Then the novice Cunda, taking Venerable Sāriputta's bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī, Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, and approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the novice Cunda said to Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable sir, Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna. This is his bowl and robe."
translations.sn47.13:3: "This matter, friend Cunda, is worthy of being reported to the Blessed One. Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we will report this matter to the Blessed One." "Yes, venerable sir," the novice Cunda replied to Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, this novice Cunda says: 'Venerable sir, Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna; this is his bowl and robe.' But, venerable sir, my body feels as if it were drugged, the directions are not clear to me, and the teachings do not appear to me when I hear: 'Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.'"
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas, in a market town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Once upon a time, monks, an acrobat set up his bamboo pole and said to his apprentice, the young medakathālika: 'Come, my dear medakathālika, climb the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.' 'Yes, teacher,' replied the apprentice medakathālika to the acrobat, and having climbed the bamboo pole, he stood on the teacher's shoulders. Then, monks, the acrobat said to the apprentice medakathālika: 'You, my dear medakathālika, protect me, and I will protect you. Thus, guarding each other, protecting each other, we will show our skills, gain profit, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.' When this was said, monks, the apprentice medakathālika said to the acrobat: 'That, teacher, will not be so. You, teacher, protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus, self-guarded, self-protected, we will show our skills, gain profit, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.'"
translations.sn47.19:2: "That is the right method," the Blessed One said. "Just as the apprentice medakathālika spoke to the teacher. 'I will protect myself,' monks, the foundations of mindfulness should be cultivated; 'I will protect others,' the foundations of mindfulness should be cultivated. Protecting oneself, monks, one protects others; protecting others, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas, in a market town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn47.20:2: "Suppose, monks, a great crowd were to gather, saying, 'The beauty of the land, the beauty of the land!' And suppose that beauty of the land is an extremely captivating dancer, an extremely captivating singer. 'The beauty of the land is dancing and singing,' monks, an even larger great crowd would gather. Then a man might come along, desiring to live, not wishing to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. Someone would say to him: 'Here, good man, is a bowl of oil filled to the brim which you must carry between the great assembly and the beauty of the land. And a man with a drawn sword will follow right behind you. Wherever you spill even a drop, right there he will cut off your head.' What do you think, monks, would that man, ignoring that bowl of oil, bring about heedlessness outwardly?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: "What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma does not last long? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma lasts long?"
translations.sn47.25:2: "It is because of not developing, not making much of the four foundations of mindfulness, brahmin, that after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma does not last long. And it is because of developing, making much of the four foundations of mindfulness, brahmin, that after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma lasts long.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then, in the morning, Venerable Ananda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Sirivaddha; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Sitting, Venerable Ananda said to the householder Sirivaddha: "I hope you are bearing up, householder, I hope you are enduring? I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, that their subsiding is evident and not their increasing?" "I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not enduring. My painful feelings are increasing, venerable sir, not subsiding; their increasing is evident, not their subsiding."
translations.sn47.29:3: "Therefore, householder, you should train thus: 'I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. I will dwell contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.' Thus, householder, you should train."
translations.sn47.33:1: "For anyone, monks, for whom the four foundations of mindfulness are neglected, the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is neglected. For anyone, monks, for whom the four foundations of mindfulness are undertaken, the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is undertaken.
translations.sn47.37:1: "These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating the body in the body, any desire for the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, any desire for feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating mind in mind, any desire for mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: "These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: They dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For one who dwells contemplating mind in mind, the mind becomes fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the establishment of mindfulness, the development of the establishment of mindfulness, and the way leading to the development of the establishment of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the establishment of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings ... he dwells contemplating mind in mind ... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, bhikkhus, is called the establishment of mindfulness."
translations.sn47.40:2: "And what, bhikkhus, is the development of the establishment of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body, dwells contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings ... he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in mind ... he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena, dwells contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, bhikkhus, is called the development of the establishment of mindfulness."
translations.sn47.4:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at the brahmin village of Sālā. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus ... and said:
translations.sn47.4:2: "Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are newly ordained, not long gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline, should be encouraged, settled, and established by you, bhikkhus, in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? 'Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, for the knowledge of the body as it really is; dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, for the knowledge of feelings as they really are; dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, for the knowledge of mind as it really is; dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, for the knowledge of phenomena as they really are.'"
translations.sn47.4:3: "Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are trainees, who have not attained their mind's ideal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, they too dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, for the full understanding of the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings ... for the full understanding of feelings; they dwell contemplating mind in mind ... for the full understanding of mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena ... for the full understanding of phenomena."
translations.sn47.4:4: "Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge, they too dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a mind that is purified, concentrated, one-pointed, detached from the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings ... detached from feelings; they dwell contemplating mind in mind ... detached from mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena ... detached from phenomena."
translations.sn47.6:1: "Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, bhikkhus, the quail, being carried off by the hawk, lamented thus: 'We were indeed unlucky, of little merit, in that we wandered outside our own range into the domain of others. If today we had wandered within our own range, in our own ancestral domain, this hawk would not have been a match for me in a fight.' 'But what, quail, is your own range, your own ancestral domain?' 'It is a field covered with clods, ploughed up.' Then, bhikkhus, the hawk, confident in her own strength, not boasting of her own strength, released the quail: 'Go now, quail, but even having gone there you will not escape me.'"
translations.sn47.6:2: "Then, bhikkhus, the quail went to a field covered with clods, ploughed up, climbed up a large clod, and standing there, challenged the hawk: 'Come for me now, hawk! Come for me now, hawk!' Then, bhikkhus, the hawk, confident in her own strength, not boasting of her own strength, folded both wings and suddenly swooped down upon the quail. When, bhikkhus, the quail knew: 'This hawk has come too close,' then he slipped inside that very clod. Then, bhikkhus, the hawk there dashed her breast against it.
