For so it happens, bhikkhus, to one who wanders outside his own range into the domain of others."
translations.sn47.6:3: "Therefore, bhikkhus, do not wander outside your own range into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his own range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opening, Māra gains a foothold. And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu's outside range, the domain of others? It is the five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, tantalizing; sounds cognizable by the ear ... odors cognizable by the nose ... tastes cognizable by the tongue ... tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, tantalizing. This, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu's outside range, the domain of others."
translations.sn47.7:1: "Bhikkhus, there are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, rough, uneven regions where neither monkeys nor humans roam. There are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, rough, uneven regions where monkeys roam, but not humans. There are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, level, pleasant regions where both monkeys and humans roam. There, bhikkhus, hunters set snares with birdlime on monkey trails to catch monkeys."
translations.sn47.8:2: Indeed, monks, that foolish, unskilled, unwise cook does not take note of his master's sign: 'Today my master likes this kind of sauce, or he reaches for this, or he takes a lot of this, or he praises this. Today my master likes sour sauce, or he reaches for sour, or he takes a lot of sour, or he praises sour. Today my master likes bitter sauce... pungent sauce... sweet sauce... astringent sauce... non-astringent sauce... salty sauce... non-salty sauce, or he reaches for non-salty, or he takes a lot of non-salty, or he praises non-salty.'
translations.sn47.8:4: Indeed, monks, that foolish, unskilled, unwise monk does not gain pleasant dwellings in this very life, nor does he gain mindfulness and full awareness. For what reason? Because, monks, that foolish, unskilled, unwise monk does not take note of the sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Suppose, monks, a wise, skilled, clever cook were to present a king or a royal minister with various kinds of sauces—sour ones, bitter ones, pungent ones, sweet ones, astringent ones, non-astringent ones, salty ones, non-salty ones.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Vajirā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal, on returning from her alms round, she went to the Blind Men's Grove for the day's abiding. Having plunged into the Blind Men's Grove, she sat down at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhunī Vajirā, desiring to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: "By whom has this being been created? Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? Where does the being cease?"
translations.sn5.10:3: Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā thought: "Now who is this that recited a verse—a human or a non-human?" Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā thought: "This is Māra the Evil One, who has recited a verse desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in me, desiring to make me fall away from concentration." Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, having understood, "This is Māra the Evil One," replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: "Why now do you assume 'a being'? Māra, is that a speculative view? This is a mere heap of formations: Here no being is found.
translations.sn5.10:5: For just as, with an assemblage of parts, The word 'chariot' is used, So, when the aggregates are present, There's the convention 'a being.'
translations.sn5.10:6: It's only suffering that comes to be, Suffering that stands and falls away. Nothing but suffering comes to be, Nothing but suffering ceases."
translations.sn5.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal, on returning from her alms round, she went to the Blind Men's Grove, seeking seclusion. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, desiring to make her fall away from seclusion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: "There is no escape in the world, What will you do with seclusion? Enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure; Don't be remorseful later."
translations.sn5.1:3: Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā thought: "Now who is this that recited a verse—a human or a non-human?" Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā thought: "This is Māra the Evil One, who has recited a verse desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in me, desiring to make me fall away from seclusion." Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, having understood, "This is Māra the Evil One," replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: "There is an escape in the world, Which I have well discerned with wisdom. O kinsman of the negligent, Evil One, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes; The aggregates are their chopping block. What you call sensual delight Has become for me non-delight."
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, "Āḷavikā the bhikkhunī knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: "That state which is to be attained by the seers, A place hard to reach, That cannot be attained by a woman With her two-fingered wisdom."
translations.sn5.2:4: "What can the state of a woman do When the mind is well concentrated, When knowledge is proceeding, When one rightly sees into the Dhamma?
translations.sn5.2:5: One to whom it might occur, 'I am a woman' or 'I am a man,' Or 'I am anything at all'— Is fit for Māra to address."
translations.sn5.3:2: "Why now, like a mother bereft of her child, Do you sit alone with tearful face? Having gone into the woods alone, Are you looking for a man?"
translations.sn5.3:3: Then the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī thought: "Now who is this that recited a verse—a human or a non-human?" Then the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī thought: "This is Māra the Evil One, who has recited a verse desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in me, desiring to make me fall away from concentration."
translations.sn5.3:5: "I am one who has completely lost my son; Men are ended for me. I do not sorrow, I do not weep, Nor do I fear you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed in every way, The mass of darkness is shattered. Having conquered the army of Death, I dwell without taints."
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, "Kisāgotamī the bhikkhunī knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Vijayā dressed... and sat down at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhunī Vijayā, desiring to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: "You are young and beautiful, And I too am a youth in my prime. Come, let us enjoy ourselves With the fivefold music."
translations.sn5.4:4: "Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, And delightful tactile objects— I hand them all back to you, Māra; I have no need of them.
translations.sn5.4:5: With this foul body, fragile and breakable, I am disgusted and ashamed; craving for sensual pleasures has been uprooted.
translations.sn5.4:6: And those beings who are attached to form, and those who dwell in the formless, and those peaceful attainments—everywhere darkness is destroyed.
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, having dressed in the morning... stood at the foot of a sal tree in full bloom. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, desiring to make her fall away from concentration, approached her; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā in verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: "Having approached the sal tree with its top in full bloom, you stand alone at its foot, bhikkhunī; you have no companion, foolish one, are you not afraid of rogues?"
translations.sn5.5:4: "Even if a hundred thousand rogues such as you were to come here, I would not stir a hair, I would not be terrified; I am not afraid of you, Māra, even alone.
translations.sn5.5:6: I am one who has mastery over the mind, the bases of psychic power are well developed; I am freed from all bonds, I do not fear you, friend."
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, "The bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā knows me," sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: "Why do you not delight in birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures. Who has persuaded you of this: 'Bhikkhunī, do not delight in birth'?"
translations.sn5.6:3: "For one who is born there is death; being born, one encounters sufferings—bondage, murder, affliction—therefore I do not delight in birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha has taught the Dhamma for the transcendence of birth; for the abandoning of all suffering, he has established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: And those beings who are attached to form, and those who dwell in the formless, not understanding cessation, come again to renewed existence."
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Upacālā, having dressed in the morning... sat down at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Upacālā; having approached, he said to the bhikkhunī Upacālā: "Where do you wish to be reborn, bhikkhunī?" "I do not wish to be reborn anywhere, friend."
translations.sn5.7:2: "The Thirty-three gods and the Yāma gods, and the Tusita gods too; the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who wield power—direct your mind there, and you will experience delight."
translations.sn5.7:3: "The Thirty-three gods and the Yāma gods, and the Tusita gods too; the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who wield power—they are bound by the bond of sensual pleasure, they come again under Māra's control.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is smoking, the whole world is burning, the whole world is shaking.
translations.sn5.7:5: Unshaken, unburning, not frequented by ordinary people, where Māra cannot go—there my mind delights."
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, "The bhikkhunī Upacālā knows me," sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā, having dressed in the morning... sat down at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā; having approached, he said to the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā: "Whose creed do you approve of, bhikkhunī?" "I do not approve of anyone's creed, friend."
translations.sn5.8:2: "For whom have you shaved your head? You appear like a renunciant; yet you do not approve of any creed, why do you wander as if confused?"
translations.sn5.8:3: "Outside here the creeds, they have faith in views; I do not approve of their Dhamma, they are unskilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Freed everywhere, unattached, the One with Vision sees all; attained to the destruction of all kamma, liberated with the destruction of the substrates—he, the Blessed One, is my Teacher, I approve of his teaching."
translations.sn5.9:2: "By whom was this image made? Where is the maker of the image? Where has the image arisen? Where does the image cease?"
translations.sn5.9:4: "This image is not made by oneself, nor is this misery made by another; it has arisen dependent on a cause, with the breakup of the cause it ceases.
translations.sn5.9:6: So too these aggregates and elements, and these six sense bases, have arisen dependent on a cause, with the breakup of the cause they cease."
translations.sn56.11:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus of the group of five:
translations.sn56.11:10: But when, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these Four Noble Truths as they really are in their three phases and twelve aspects was thoroughly purified, then, bhikkhus, I claimed to have attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. And the knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.'"
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless vision of the Dhamma arose in the Venerable Koṇḍañña: "Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation."
translations.sn56.11:13: And so at that moment, at that instant, at that second, the sound spread as far as the brahmā world. And this ten-thousandfold world system shook, quaked, and trembled, and an immeasurable, splendid light appeared in the world surpassing the divine majesty of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: "Bhikkhus, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth. What two? That which is this pursuit of sensual happiness in sensual pleasures, low, vulgar, common, ignoble, unbeneficial; and that which is this pursuit of self-mortification, painful, ignoble, unbeneficial. Avoiding both these extremes, the Tathāgata has awakened to the middle way, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, bhikkhus, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:4: And this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering—in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, release from it, non-attachment. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: this noble eightfold path; that is, right view ... right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:9: And as long as, monks, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are in their three phases and twelve aspects was not thoroughly purified, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
translations.sn56.20:1: “These four, monks, are actual, unerring, not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering’—this, monks, is actual, unerring, not otherwise; ‘this is the origin of suffering’—this is actual, unerring, not otherwise; ‘this is the cessation of suffering’—this is actual, unerring, not otherwise; ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this is actual, unerring, not otherwise. These, monks, are the four that are actual, unerring, not otherwise.
translations.sn56.26:1: “Those, monks, whom you have compassion for, and those who should listen—friends or companions, relatives or kin—you should, monks, urge, settle, and establish them in the true understanding of the four noble truths.
translations.sn56.26:2: Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Those, monks, whom you have compassion for, and those who should listen—friends or companions, relatives or kin—you should, monks, urge, settle, and establish them in the true understanding of these four noble truths.
translations.sn56.27:1: “These, monks, are the four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These, monks, are the four noble truths that are actual, unerring, not otherwise; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.28:1: “These, monks, are the four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. In this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is noble; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion several senior monks were dwelling at Cetā in the Sañjānika forest. Then, after their meal, on returning from almsround, a group of senior monks assembled and sat together in the pavilion, and this conversation arose among them: “Now, friends, does one who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering, see the cessation of suffering, and see the way leading to the cessation of suffering?”
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī, in the sīsapā grove. Then the Buddha, having picked up a few sīsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Which is more: the few sīsapā leaves in my hand, or those in the sīsapā grove above?” “Sir, the few sīsapā leaves that the Buddha picked up in his hand are few, but those in the sīsapā grove above are many more.” “In the same way, mendicants, the things I have directly known but have not taught you are many more. And why haven’t I taught them? Because they aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and extinguishment. That’s why I haven’t taught them.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what have I taught? ‘This is suffering’—that’s what I’ve taught. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—that’s what I’ve taught. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—that’s what I’ve taught. ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’—that’s what I’ve taught.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why have I taught them? Because they are beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and extinguishment. That’s why I’ve taught them.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Suppose, mendicants, there was a person with a life span of a hundred years, who lived for a hundred years. And someone would say to them: ‘Please, mister, in the morning they will strike you with a hundred spears. At midday they will strike you with a hundred spears. And in the evening they will strike you with a hundred spears. And you, mister, being struck by three hundred spears each day, with a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, after a hundred years have passed you will comprehend the four noble truths that you had not comprehended before.’
translations.sn56.35:2: It would be worthwhile, mendicants, for a gentleman to take it up. Why is that? Because this transmigration has no known beginning. No first point is found of blows with spears, blows with swords, blows with axes, blows with hatchets. Even if that were so, mendicants, I do not say that the comprehension of the four noble truths is accompanied by suffering and distress. Rather, I say that the comprehension of the four noble truths is accompanied by pleasure and happiness. What four? The noble truth of suffering … the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: “Suppose, mendicants, a person was to strip all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in India, gather them together in one heap, and make them into stakes. Having made stakes, they would impale the large creatures in the ocean on large stakes, the medium creatures on medium stakes, and the small creatures on small stakes. And the large creatures in the ocean would not be exhausted.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in India would be used up and exhausted. But there are far more small creatures in the ocean, which are hard to impale on stakes. Why is that? Because of the subtlety of their bodies. So vast, mendicants, is the plane of loss. So great is the escape from such a vast plane of loss for a person accomplished in view, who truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Come, mendicants, let’s go to Inspiration Peak for the day’s meditation.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. Then the Buddha together with several mendicants went to Inspiration Peak. A certain mendicant saw the great precipice at Inspiration Peak. Seeing it, he said to the Buddha: “Sir, this precipice is truly huge and terrifying. Sir, is there any precipice more huge and terrifying than this one?” “There is, mendicant, a precipice more huge and terrifying than this one.”
translations.sn56.42:2: “But sir, what precipice is more huge and terrifying than this one?” “Any ascetics or brahmins who do not truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering,’ they delight in conditions that lead to rebirth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Delighting in such conditions, they generate conditions that lead to rebirth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Having generated such conditions, they fall into the precipice of rebirth, the precipice of old age, the precipice of death, the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from rebirth, old age, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.”
translations.sn56.45:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw many Licchavi youths in the assembly hall practicing archery, shooting arrows from a distance through a tiny keyhole, shot after shot without missing. Having seen this, it occurred to him: "These Licchavi youths are trained, indeed well trained, in that they can shoot arrows from a distance through a tiny keyhole, shot after shot without missing."
translations.sn56.45:3: "What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and challenging: to shoot an arrow from a distance through a tiny keyhole, shot after shot without missing, or to pierce the tip of a hair split into seven parts with the tip of another hair?" "This, venerable sir, is more difficult and challenging: to pierce the tip of a hair split into seven parts with the tip of another hair." "But, Ānanda, they pierce something even harder to pierce who penetrate as it really is: 'This is suffering' ... 'This is the origin of suffering' ... 'This is the cessation of suffering' ... 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.'"
translations.sn56.46:1: "There is, bhikkhus, an inter-cosmic void, an abyss, unconfined, a darkness, a murky darkness, where even the light of the moon and the sun, so powerful and mighty, does not reach."
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "That darkness is great, venerable sir, that darkness is indeed great. Is there, venerable sir, any other darkness greater and more terrifying than this darkness?" "There is, bhikkhu, another darkness greater and more terrifying than this darkness."
translations.sn56.48:2: "So too, bhikkhus, it is by chance that one obtains the human state. So too, bhikkhus, it is by chance that a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. So too, bhikkhus, it is by chance that the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world. This human state has been obtained, bhikkhus; a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world."
translations.sn56.48:1: "Suppose, monks, this great earth were entirely covered with water. There a person would throw a yoke with a single hole. The eastern wind would drive it westward, the western wind would drive it eastward, the northern wind would drive it southward, the southern wind would drive it northward. There would be a blind turtle. It would come up to the surface only once every hundred years. What do you think, monks, would that blind turtle, coming up to the surface only once every hundred years, be able to insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole?" "It would be a rare chance, venerable sir, that the blind turtle, coming up to the surface only once every hundred years, would insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole."
